1459::CODE;;Parameters
1460::CODE;;----------
1461::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
1462::CODE;;The input samples. Internally, it will be converted to
1463::CODE;;``dtype=np.float32`` and if a sparse matrix is provided
1464::CODE;;to a sparse ``csr_matrix``.
1465::CODE;;Returns
1466::CODE;;-------
1467::CODE;;p : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_classes)
1468::CODE;;The class log-probabilities of the input samples. The order of the
1469::CODE;;classes corresponds to that in the attribute :term:`classes_`.
1470::CODE;;Raises
1471::CODE;;------
1472::CODE;;AttributeError
1473::CODE;;If the ``loss`` does not support probabilities.
1479::CODE;;This method allows monitoring (i.e. determine error on testing set)
1480::CODE;;after each stage.
1481::CODE;;Parameters
1482::CODE;;----------
1483::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
1484::CODE;;The input samples. Internally, it will be converted to
1485::CODE;;``dtype=np.float32`` and if a sparse matrix is provided
1486::CODE;;to a sparse ``csr_matrix``.
1487::CODE;;Yields
1488::CODE;;------
1489::CODE;;y : generator of ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
1490::CODE;;The predicted value of the input samples.
1503::CODE;;This estimator builds an additive model in a forward stage-wise fashion; it
1504::CODE;;allows for the optimization of arbitrary differentiable loss functions. In
1505::CODE;;each stage a regression tree is fit on the negative gradient of the given
1506::CODE;;loss function.
1507::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` is a much faster variant
1508::CODE;;of this algorithm for intermediate and large datasets (`n_samples >= 10_000`) and
1509::CODE;;supports monotonic constraints.
1510::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gradient_boosting>`.
1511::CODE;;Parameters
1512::CODE;;----------
1513::CODE;;loss : {'squared_error', 'absolute_error', 'huber', 'quantile'}, \
1514::CODE;;default='squared_error'
1515::CODE;;Loss function to be optimized. 'squared_error' refers to the squared
1516::CODE;;error for regression. 'absolute_error' refers to the absolute error of
1517::CODE;;regression and is a robust loss function. 'huber' is a
1518::CODE;;combination of the two. 'quantile' allows quantile regression (use
1519::CODE;;`alpha` to specify the quantile).
1520::CODE;;See
1521::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_gradient_boosting_quantile.py`
1522::CODE;;for an example that demonstrates quantile regression for creating
1523::CODE;;prediction intervals with `loss='quantile'`.
1524::CODE;;learning_rate : float, default=0.1
1525::CODE;;Learning rate shrinks the contribution of each tree by `learning_rate`.
1526::CODE;;There is a trade-off between learning_rate and n_estimators.
1527::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[0.0, inf)`.
1528::CODE;;n_estimators : int, default=100
1529::CODE;;The number of boosting stages to perform. Gradient boosting
1530::CODE;;is fairly robust to over-fitting so a large number usually
1531::CODE;;results in better performance.
1532::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
1533::CODE;;subsample : float, default=1.0
1534::CODE;;The fraction of samples to be used for fitting the individual base
1535::CODE;;learners. If smaller than 1.0 this results in Stochastic Gradient
1536::CODE;;Boosting. `subsample` interacts with the parameter `n_estimators`.
1537::CODE;;Choosing `subsample < 1.0` leads to a reduction of variance
1538::CODE;;and an increase in bias.
1539::CODE;;Values must be in the range `(0.0, 1.0]`.
1540::CODE;;criterion : {'friedman_mse', 'squared_error'}, default='friedman_mse'
1541::CODE;;The function to measure the quality of a split. Supported criteria are
1542::CODE;;"friedman_mse" for the mean squared error with improvement score by
1543::CODE;;Friedman, "squared_error" for mean squared error. The default value of
1544::CODE;;"friedman_mse" is generally the best as it can provide a better
1545::CODE;;approximation in some cases.
1546::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1547::CODE;;min_samples_split : int or float, default=2
1548::CODE;;The minimum number of samples required to split an internal node:
1549::CODE;;- If int, values must be in the range `[2, inf)`.
1550::CODE;;- If float, values must be in the range `(0.0, 1.0]` and `min_samples_split`
1551::CODE;;will be `ceil(min_samples_split * n_samples)`.
1552::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.18
1553::CODE;;Added float values for fractions.
1554::CODE;;min_samples_leaf : int or float, default=1
1555::CODE;;The minimum number of samples required to be at a leaf node.
1556::CODE;;A split point at any depth will only be considered if it leaves at
1557::CODE;;least ``min_samples_leaf`` training samples in each of the left and
1558::CODE;;right branches. This may have the effect of smoothing the model,
1559::CODE;;especially in regression.
1560::CODE;;- If int, values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
1561::CODE;;- If float, values must be in the range `(0.0, 1.0)` and `min_samples_leaf`
1562::CODE;;will be `ceil(min_samples_leaf * n_samples)`.
1563::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.18
1564::CODE;;Added float values for fractions.
1565::CODE;;min_weight_fraction_leaf : float, default=0.0
1566::CODE;;The minimum weighted fraction of the sum total of weights (of all
1567::CODE;;the input samples) required to be at a leaf node. Samples have
1568::CODE;;equal weight when sample_weight is not provided.
1569::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[0.0, 0.5]`.
1570::CODE;;max_depth : int or None, default=3
1571::CODE;;Maximum depth of the individual regression estimators. The maximum
1572::CODE;;depth limits the number of nodes in the tree. Tune this parameter
1573::CODE;;for best performance; the best value depends on the interaction
1574::CODE;;of the input variables. If None, then nodes are expanded until
1575::CODE;;all leaves are pure or until all leaves contain less than
1576::CODE;;min_samples_split samples.
1577::CODE;;If int, values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
1578::CODE;;min_impurity_decrease : float, default=0.0
1579::CODE;;A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
1580::CODE;;greater than or equal to this value.
1581::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[0.0, inf)`.
1582::CODE;;The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::
1583::CODE;;N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
1584::CODE;;- N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)
1585::CODE;;where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
1586::CODE;;samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
1587::CODE;;left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.
1588::CODE;;``N``, ``N_t``, ``N_t_R`` and ``N_t_L`` all refer to the weighted sum,
1589::CODE;;if ``sample_weight`` is passed.
1590::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
1591::CODE;;init : estimator or 'zero', default=None
1592::CODE;;An estimator object that is used to compute the initial predictions.
1593::CODE;;``init`` has to provide :term:`fit` and :term:`predict`. If 'zero', the
1594::CODE;;initial raw predictions are set to zero. By default a
1595::CODE;;``DummyEstimator`` is used, predicting either the average target value
1596::CODE;;(for loss='squared_error'), or a quantile for the other losses.
1597::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
1598::CODE;;Controls the random seed given to each Tree estimator at each
1599::CODE;;boosting iteration.
1600::CODE;;In addition, it controls the random permutation of the features at
1601::CODE;;each split (see Notes for more details).
1602::CODE;;It also controls the random splitting of the training data to obtain a
1603::CODE;;validation set if `n_iter_no_change` is not None.
1604::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
1605::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
1606::CODE;;max_features : {'sqrt', 'log2'}, int or float, default=None
1607::CODE;;The number of features to consider when looking for the best split:
1608::CODE;;- If int, values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
1609::CODE;;- If float, values must be in the range `(0.0, 1.0]` and the features
1610::CODE;;considered at each split will be `max(1, int(max_features * n_features_in_))`.
1611::CODE;;- If "sqrt", then `max_features=sqrt(n_features)`.
1612::CODE;;- If "log2", then `max_features=log2(n_features)`.
1613::CODE;;- If None, then `max_features=n_features`.
1614::CODE;;Choosing `max_features < n_features` leads to a reduction of variance
1615::CODE;;and an increase in bias.
1616::CODE;;Note: the search for a split does not stop until at least one
1617::CODE;;valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to
1618::CODE;;effectively inspect more than ``max_features`` features.
1619::CODE;;alpha : float, default=0.9
1620::CODE;;The alpha-quantile of the huber loss function and the quantile
1621::CODE;;loss function. Only if ``loss='huber'`` or ``loss='quantile'``.
1622::CODE;;Values must be in the range `(0.0, 1.0)`.
1623::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
1624::CODE;;Enable verbose output. If 1 then it prints progress and performance
1625::CODE;;once in a while (the more trees the lower the frequency). If greater
1626::CODE;;than 1 then it prints progress and performance for every tree.
1627::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[0, inf)`.
1628::CODE;;max_leaf_nodes : int, default=None
1629::CODE;;Grow trees with ``max_leaf_nodes`` in best-first fashion.
1630::CODE;;Best nodes are defined as relative reduction in impurity.
1631::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[2, inf)`.
1632::CODE;;If None, then unlimited number of leaf nodes.
1633::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
1634::CODE;;When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit
1635::CODE;;and add more estimators to the ensemble, otherwise, just erase the
1636::CODE;;previous solution. See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
1637::CODE;;validation_fraction : float, default=0.1
1638::CODE;;The proportion of training data to set aside as validation set for
1639::CODE;;early stopping. Values must be in the range `(0.0, 1.0)`.
1640::CODE;;Only used if ``n_iter_no_change`` is set to an integer.
1641::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
1642::CODE;;n_iter_no_change : int, default=None
1643::CODE;;``n_iter_no_change`` is used to decide if early stopping will be used
1644::CODE;;to terminate training when validation score is not improving. By
1645::CODE;;default it is set to None to disable early stopping. If set to a
1646::CODE;;number, it will set aside ``validation_fraction`` size of the training

1650::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
1651::CODE;;See
1652::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_gradient_boosting_early_stopping.py`.
1653::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
1654::CODE;;tol : float, default=1e-4
1655::CODE;;Tolerance for the early stopping. When the loss is not improving
1656::CODE;;by at least tol for ``n_iter_no_change`` iterations (if set to a

1658::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[0.0, inf)`.
1659::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
1660::CODE;;ccp_alpha : non-negative float, default=0.0
1661::CODE;;Complexity parameter used for Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning. The
1662::CODE;;subtree with the largest cost complexity that is smaller than
1663::CODE;;``ccp_alpha`` will be chosen. By default, no pruning is performed.
1664::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[0.0, inf)`.
1665::CODE;;See :ref:`minimal_cost_complexity_pruning` for details. See
1666::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_tree_plot_cost_complexity_pruning.py`
1667::CODE;;for an example of such pruning.
1668::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
1669::CODE;;Attributes
1670::CODE;;----------
1671::CODE;;n_estimators_ : int
1672::CODE;;The number of estimators as selected by early stopping (if
1673::CODE;;``n_iter_no_change`` is specified). Otherwise it is set to
1674::CODE;;``n_estimators``.
1675::CODE;;n_trees_per_iteration_ : int
1676::CODE;;The number of trees that are built at each iteration. For regressors, this is
1677::CODE;;always 1.
1678::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.4.0
1679::CODE;;feature_importances_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
1680::CODE;;The impurity-based feature importances.
1681::CODE;;The higher, the more important the feature.
1682::CODE;;The importance of a feature is computed as the (normalized)
1683::CODE;;total reduction of the criterion brought by that feature. It is also
1684::CODE;;known as the Gini importance.
1685::CODE;;Warning: impurity-based feature importances can be misleading for
1686::CODE;;high cardinality features (many unique values). See
1687::CODE;;:func:`sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance` as an alternative.
1688::CODE;;oob_improvement_ : ndarray of shape (n_estimators,)
1689::CODE;;The improvement in loss on the out-of-bag samples
1690::CODE;;relative to the previous iteration.
1691::CODE;;``oob_improvement_[0]`` is the improvement in
1692::CODE;;loss of the first stage over the ``init`` estimator.
1693::CODE;;Only available if ``subsample < 1.0``.
1694::CODE;;oob_scores_ : ndarray of shape (n_estimators,)
1695::CODE;;The full history of the loss values on the out-of-bag
1696::CODE;;samples. Only available if `subsample < 1.0`.
1697::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
1698::CODE;;oob_score_ : float
1699::CODE;;The last value of the loss on the out-of-bag samples. It is
1700::CODE;;the same as `oob_scores_[-1]`. Only available if `subsample < 1.0`.
1701::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
1702::CODE;;train_score_ : ndarray of shape (n_estimators,)
1703::CODE;;The i-th score ``train_score_[i]`` is the loss of the
1704::CODE;;model at iteration ``i`` on the in-bag sample.
1705::CODE;;If ``subsample == 1`` this is the loss on the training data.
1706::CODE;;init_ : estimator
1707::CODE;;The estimator that provides the initial predictions. Set via the ``init``
1708::CODE;;argument.
1709::CODE;;estimators_ : ndarray of DecisionTreeRegressor of shape (n_estimators, 1)
1710::CODE;;The collection of fitted sub-estimators.
1711::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
1712::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
1713::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1714::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
1715::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
1716::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
1717::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
1718::CODE;;max_features_ : int
1719::CODE;;The inferred value of max_features.
1720::CODE;;See Also
1721::CODE;;--------
1722::CODE;;HistGradientBoostingRegressor : Histogram-based Gradient Boosting
1723::CODE;;Classification Tree.
1724::CODE;;sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeRegressor : A decision tree regressor.
1725::CODE;;sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor : A random forest regressor.
1726::CODE;;Notes
1727::CODE;;-----
1728::CODE;;The features are always randomly permuted at each split. Therefore,
1729::CODE;;the best found split may vary, even with the same training data and
1730::CODE;;``max_features=n_features``, if the improvement of the criterion is
1731::CODE;;identical for several splits enumerated during the search of the best
1732::CODE;;split. To obtain a deterministic behaviour during fitting,
1733::CODE;;``random_state`` has to be fixed.
1734::CODE;;References
1735::CODE;;----------
1736::CODE;;J. Friedman, Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting
1737::CODE;;Machine, The Annals of Statistics, Vol. 29, No. 5, 2001.
1738::CODE;;J. Friedman, Stochastic Gradient Boosting, 1999
1739::CODE;;T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman.
1740::CODE;;Elements of Statistical Learning Ed. 2, Springer, 2009.

23::CODE;;def _find_binning_thresholds(col_data, max_bins):
43::CODE;;missing_mask = np.isnan(col_data)
44::CODE;;if missing_mask.any():

50::CODE;;if len(distinct_values) <= max_bins:
51::CODE;;midpoints = distinct_values[:-1] + distinct_values[1:]
52::CODE;;midpoints *= 0.5

61::CODE;;X_DTYPE

63::CODE;;assert midpoints.shape[0] == max_bins - 1
66::CODE;;np.clip(midpoints, a_min=None, a_max=ALMOST_INF, out=midpoints)
67::CODE;;return midpoints

63::CODE;;Update equals:
64::CODE;;loss.fit_intercept_only(y_true - raw_prediction)
65::CODE;;This is only applied if loss.differentiable is False.
66::CODE;;Note: It only works, if the loss is a function of the residual, as is the
67::CODE;;case for AbsoluteError and PinballLoss. Otherwise, one would need to get
68::CODE;;the minimum of loss(y_true, raw_prediction + x) in x. A few examples:
69::CODE;;- AbsoluteError: median(y_true - raw_prediction).
70::CODE;;- PinballLoss: quantile(y_true - raw_prediction).
71::CODE;;More background:
72::CODE;;For the standard gradient descent method according to "Greedy Function
73::CODE;;Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine" by Friedman, all loss functions but the
74::CODE;;squared loss need a line search step. BaseHistGradientBoosting, however, implements
75::CODE;;a so called Newton boosting where the trees are fitted to a 2nd order
76::CODE;;approximations of the loss in terms of gradients and hessians. In this case, the
77::CODE;;line search step is only necessary if the loss is not smooth, i.e. not
78::CODE;;differentiable, which renders the 2nd order approximation invalid. In fact,
79::CODE;;non-smooth losses arbitrarily set hessians to 1 and effectively use the standard
80::CODE;;gradient descent method with line search.
100::CODE;;`raw_predictions` is typically a precomputed array to avoid redundant
101::CODE;;state-wise computations fitting with early stopping enabled: in this case
102::CODE;;`raw_predictions` is incrementally updated whenever we add a tree to the
103::CODE;;boosted ensemble.
104::CODE;;Note: this makes fitting HistGradientBoosting* models inherently non thread
105::CODE;;safe at fit time. However thread-safety at fit time was never guaranteed nor
106::CODE;;enforced for scikit-learn estimators in general.
107::CODE;;Thread-safety at prediction/transform time is another matter as those
108::CODE;;operations are typically side-effect free and therefore often thread-safe by
109::CODE;;default for most scikit-learn models and would like to keep it that way.
110::CODE;;Therefore this context manager should only be used at fit time.
111::CODE;;TODO: in the future, we could explore the possibility to extend the scorer
112::CODE;;public API to expose a way to compute vales from raw predictions. That would
113::CODE;;probably require also making the scorer aware of the inverse link function
114::CODE;;used by the estimator which is typically private API for now, hence the need
115::CODE;;for this patching mechanism.

1287::CODE;;@property
1288::CODE;;def n_iter_(self):
1294::CODE;;This estimator is much faster than
1295::CODE;;:class:`GradientBoostingRegressor<sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor>`
1296::CODE;;for big datasets (n_samples >= 10 000).
1297::CODE;;This estimator has native support for missing values (NaNs). During
1298::CODE;;training, the tree grower learns at each split point whether samples
1299::CODE;;with missing values should go to the left or right child, based on the
1300::CODE;;potential gain. When predicting, samples with missing values are
1301::CODE;;assigned to the left or right child consequently. If no missing values
1302::CODE;;were encountered for a given feature during training, then samples with
1303::CODE;;missing values are mapped to whichever child has the most samples.
1304::CODE;;See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_hgbt_regression.py` for a
1305::CODE;;usecase example of this feature.
1306::CODE;;This implementation is inspired by
1307::CODE;;`LightGBM <https://github.com/Microsoft/LightGBM>`_.
1308::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <histogram_based_gradient_boosting>`.
1309::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
1310::CODE;;Parameters
1311::CODE;;----------
1312::CODE;;loss : {'squared_error', 'absolute_error', 'gamma', 'poisson', 'quantile'}, \
1313::CODE;;default='squared_error'
1314::CODE;;The loss function to use in the boosting process. Note that the
1315::CODE;;"squared error", "gamma" and "poisson" losses actually implement
1316::CODE;;"half least squares loss", "half gamma deviance" and "half poisson
1317::CODE;;deviance" to simplify the computation of the gradient. Furthermore,
1318::CODE;;"gamma" and "poisson" losses internally use a log-link, "gamma"
1319::CODE;;requires ``y > 0`` and "poisson" requires ``y >= 0``.
1320::CODE;;"quantile" uses the pinball loss.
1321::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.23
1322::CODE;;Added option 'poisson'.
1323::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.1
1324::CODE;;Added option 'quantile'.
1325::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.3
1326::CODE;;Added option 'gamma'.
1327::CODE;;quantile : float, default=None
1328::CODE;;If loss is "quantile", this parameter specifies which quantile to be estimated
1329::CODE;;and must be between 0 and 1.
1330::CODE;;learning_rate : float, default=0.1
1331::CODE;;The learning rate, also known as *shrinkage*. This is used as a
1332::CODE;;multiplicative factor for the leaves values. Use ``1`` for no
1333::CODE;;shrinkage.
1334::CODE;;max_iter : int, default=100
1335::CODE;;The maximum number of iterations of the boosting process, i.e. the
1336::CODE;;maximum number of trees.
1337::CODE;;max_leaf_nodes : int or None, default=31
1338::CODE;;The maximum number of leaves for each tree. Must be strictly greater
1339::CODE;;than 1. If None, there is no maximum limit.
1340::CODE;;max_depth : int or None, default=None
1341::CODE;;The maximum depth of each tree. The depth of a tree is the number of
1342::CODE;;edges to go from the root to the deepest leaf.
1343::CODE;;Depth isn't constrained by default.
1344::CODE;;min_samples_leaf : int, default=20
1345::CODE;;The minimum number of samples per leaf. For small datasets with less
1346::CODE;;than a few hundred samples, it is recommended to lower this value
1347::CODE;;since only very shallow trees would be built.
1348::CODE;;l2_regularization : float, default=0
1349::CODE;;The L2 regularization parameter penalizing leaves with small hessians.
1350::CODE;;Use ``0`` for no regularization (default).
1351::CODE;;max_features : float, default=1.0
1352::CODE;;Proportion of randomly chosen features in each and every node split.
1353::CODE;;This is a form of regularization, smaller values make the trees weaker
1354::CODE;;learners and might prevent overfitting.
1355::CODE;;If interaction constraints from `interaction_cst` are present, only allowed
1356::CODE;;features are taken into account for the subsampling.
1357::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.4
1358::CODE;;max_bins : int, default=255
1359::CODE;;The maximum number of bins to use for non-missing values. Before
1360::CODE;;training, each feature of the input array `X` is binned into
1361::CODE;;integer-valued bins, which allows for a much faster training stage.
1362::CODE;;Features with a small number of unique values may use less than
1363::CODE;;``max_bins`` bins. In addition to the ``max_bins`` bins, one more bin
1364::CODE;;is always reserved for missing values. Must be no larger than 255.
1365::CODE;;categorical_features : array-like of {bool, int, str} of shape (n_features) \
1366::CODE;;or shape (n_categorical_features,), default='from_dtype'
1367::CODE;;Indicates the categorical features.
1368::CODE;;- None : no feature will be considered categorical.
1369::CODE;;- boolean array-like : boolean mask indicating categorical features.
1370::CODE;;- integer array-like : integer indices indicating categorical
1371::CODE;;features.
1372::CODE;;- str array-like: names of categorical features (assuming the training
1373::CODE;;data has feature names).
1374::CODE;;- `"from_dtype"`: dataframe columns with dtype "category" are
1375::CODE;;considered to be categorical features. The input must be an object
1376::CODE;;exposing a ``__dataframe__`` method such as pandas or polars
1377::CODE;;DataFrames to use this feature.
1378::CODE;;For each categorical feature, there must be at most `max_bins` unique
1379::CODE;;categories. Negative values for categorical features encoded as numeric
1380::CODE;;dtypes are treated as missing values. All categorical values are
1381::CODE;;converted to floating point numbers. This means that categorical values
1382::CODE;;of 1.0 and 1 are treated as the same category.
1383::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <categorical_support_gbdt>` and
1384::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_gradient_boosting_categorical.py`.
1385::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1386::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.2
1387::CODE;;Added support for feature names.
1388::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.4
1389::CODE;;Added `"from_dtype"` option.
1390::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.6
1391::CODE;;The default value changed from `None` to `"from_dtype"`.
1392::CODE;;monotonic_cst : array-like of int of shape (n_features) or dict, default=None
1393::CODE;;Monotonic constraint to enforce on each feature are specified using the
1394::CODE;;following integer values:
1395::CODE;;- 1: monotonic increase
1396::CODE;;- 0: no constraint
1397::CODE;;- -1: monotonic decrease
1398::CODE;;If a dict with str keys, map feature to monotonic constraints by name.
1399::CODE;;If an array, the features are mapped to constraints by position. See
1400::CODE;;:ref:`monotonic_cst_features_names` for a usage example.
1401::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <monotonic_cst_gbdt>`.
1402::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
1403::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.2
1404::CODE;;Accept dict of constraints with feature names as keys.
1405::CODE;;interaction_cst : {"pairwise", "no_interactions"} or sequence of lists/tuples/sets \
1406::CODE;;of int, default=None
1407::CODE;;Specify interaction constraints, the sets of features which can
1408::CODE;;interact with each other in child node splits.
1409::CODE;;Each item specifies the set of feature indices that are allowed
1410::CODE;;to interact with each other. If there are more features than
1411::CODE;;specified in these constraints, they are treated as if they were
1412::CODE;;specified as an additional set.
1413::CODE;;The strings "pairwise" and "no_interactions" are shorthands for
1414::CODE;;allowing only pairwise or no interactions, respectively.
1415::CODE;;For instance, with 5 features in total, `interaction_cst=[{0, 1}]`
1416::CODE;;is equivalent to `interaction_cst=[{0, 1}, {2, 3, 4}]`,
1417::CODE;;and specifies that each branch of a tree will either only split
1418::CODE;;on features 0 and 1 or only split on features 2, 3 and 4.
1419::CODE;;See :ref:`this example<ice-vs-pdp>` on how to use `interaction_cst`.
1420::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
1421::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
1422::CODE;;When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit
1423::CODE;;and add more estimators to the ensemble. For results to be valid, the
1424::CODE;;estimator should be re-trained on the same data only.
1425::CODE;;See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
1426::CODE;;early_stopping : 'auto' or bool, default='auto'
1427::CODE;;If 'auto', early stopping is enabled if the sample size is larger than
1428::CODE;;10000 or if `X_val` and `y_val` are passed to `fit`. If True, early stopping
1429::CODE;;is enabled, otherwise early stopping is disabled.
1430::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
1431::CODE;;scoring : str or callable or None, default='loss'
1432::CODE;;Scoring method to use for early stopping. Only used if `early_stopping`
1433::CODE;;is enabled. Options:
1434::CODE;;- str: see :ref:`scoring_string_names` for options.
1435::CODE;;- callable: a scorer callable object (e.g., function) with signature
1436::CODE;;``scorer(estimator, X, y)``. See :ref:`scoring_callable` for details.
1437::CODE;;- `None`: the :ref:`coefficient of determination <r2_score>`
1438::CODE;;(:math:`R^2`) is used.
1439::CODE;;- 'loss': early stopping is checked w.r.t the loss value.
1440::CODE;;validation_fraction : int or float or None, default=0.1
1441::CODE;;Proportion (or absolute size) of training data to set aside as
1442::CODE;;validation data for early stopping. If None, early stopping is done on
1443::CODE;;the training data.
1444::CODE;;The value is ignored if either early stopping is not performed, e.g.
1445::CODE;;`early_stopping=False`, or if `X_val` and `y_val` are passed to fit.
1446::CODE;;n_iter_no_change : int, default=10
1447::CODE;;Used to determine when to "early stop". The fitting process is
1448::CODE;;stopped when none of the last ``n_iter_no_change`` scores are better
1449::CODE;;than the ``n_iter_no_change - 1`` -th-to-last one, up to some
1450::CODE;;tolerance. Only used if early stopping is performed.
1451::CODE;;tol : float, default=1e-7
1452::CODE;;The absolute tolerance to use when comparing scores during early
1453::CODE;;stopping. The higher the tolerance, the more likely we are to early
1454::CODE;;stop: higher tolerance means that it will be harder for subsequent
1455::CODE;;iterations to be considered an improvement upon the reference score.
1456::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
1457::CODE;;The verbosity level. If not zero, print some information about the
1458::CODE;;fitting process. ``1`` prints only summary info, ``2`` prints info per
1459::CODE;;iteration.
1460::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
1461::CODE;;Pseudo-random number generator to control the subsampling in the
1462::CODE;;binning process, and the train/validation data split if early stopping
1463::CODE;;is enabled.
1464::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
1465::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
1466::CODE;;Attributes
1467::CODE;;----------
1468::CODE;;do_early_stopping_ : bool
1469::CODE;;Indicates whether early stopping is used during training.

1471::CODE;;The number of iterations as selected by early stopping, depending on
1472::CODE;;the `early_stopping` parameter. Otherwise it corresponds to max_iter.
1473::CODE;;n_trees_per_iteration_ : int
1474::CODE;;The number of tree that are built at each iteration. For regressors,
1475::CODE;;this is always 1.

1477::CODE;;The scores at each iteration on the training data. The first entry
1478::CODE;;is the score of the ensemble before the first iteration. Scores are
1479::CODE;;computed according to the ``scoring`` parameter. If ``scoring`` is
1480::CODE;;not 'loss', scores are computed on a subset of at most 10 000
1481::CODE;;samples. Empty if no early stopping.
1482::CODE;;validation_score_ : ndarray, shape (n_iter_+1,)
1483::CODE;;The scores at each iteration on the held-out validation data. The
1484::CODE;;first entry is the score of the ensemble before the first iteration.
1485::CODE;;Scores are computed according to the ``scoring`` parameter. Empty if
1486::CODE;;no early stopping or if ``validation_fraction`` is None.

1488::CODE;;Boolean mask for the categorical features. ``None`` if there are no
1489::CODE;;categorical features.

1491::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
1492::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1493::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
1494::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
1495::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.

1497::CODE;;See Also
1498::CODE;;--------
1499::CODE;;GradientBoostingRegressor : Exact gradient boosting method that does not
1500::CODE;;scale as good on datasets with a large number of samples.
1501::CODE;;sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeRegressor : A decision tree regressor.
1502::CODE;;RandomForestRegressor : A meta-estimator that fits a number of decision
1503::CODE;;tree regressors on various sub-samples of the dataset and uses
1504::CODE;;averaging to improve the statistical performance and control
1505::CODE;;over-fitting.
1506::CODE;;AdaBoostRegressor : A meta-estimator that begins by fitting a regressor
1507::CODE;;on the original dataset and then fits additional copies of the
1508::CODE;;regressor on the same dataset but where the weights of instances are
1509::CODE;;adjusted according to the error of the current prediction. As such,
1510::CODE;;subsequent regressors focus more on difficult cases.

1593::CODE;;The predicted values.
1601::CODE;;This method allows monitoring (i.e. determine error on testing set)
1602::CODE;;after each stage.
1603::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1604::CODE;;Parameters
1605::CODE;;----------
1606::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
1607::CODE;;The input samples.
1608::CODE;;Yields
1609::CODE;;------
1610::CODE;;y : generator of ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
1611::CODE;;The predicted values of the input samples, for each iteration.
1641::CODE;;This estimator is much faster than
1642::CODE;;:class:`GradientBoostingClassifier<sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier>`
1643::CODE;;for big datasets (n_samples >= 10 000).
1644::CODE;;This estimator has native support for missing values (NaNs). During
1645::CODE;;training, the tree grower learns at each split point whether samples
1646::CODE;;with missing values should go to the left or right child, based on the
1647::CODE;;potential gain. When predicting, samples with missing values are
1648::CODE;;assigned to the left or right child consequently. If no missing values
1649::CODE;;were encountered for a given feature during training, then samples with
1650::CODE;;missing values are mapped to whichever child has the most samples.
1651::CODE;;This implementation is inspired by
1652::CODE;;`LightGBM <https://github.com/Microsoft/LightGBM>`_.
1653::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <histogram_based_gradient_boosting>`.
1654::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
1655::CODE;;Parameters
1656::CODE;;----------
1657::CODE;;loss : {'log_loss'}, default='log_loss'
1658::CODE;;The loss function to use in the boosting process.
1659::CODE;;For binary classification problems, 'log_loss' is also known as logistic loss,
1660::CODE;;binomial deviance or binary crossentropy. Internally, the model fits one tree
1661::CODE;;per boosting iteration and uses the logistic sigmoid function (expit) as
1662::CODE;;inverse link function to compute the predicted positive class probability.
1663::CODE;;For multiclass classification problems, 'log_loss' is also known as multinomial
1664::CODE;;deviance or categorical crossentropy. Internally, the model fits one tree per
1665::CODE;;boosting iteration and per class and uses the softmax function as inverse link
1666::CODE;;function to compute the predicted probabilities of the classes.
1667::CODE;;learning_rate : float, default=0.1
1668::CODE;;The learning rate, also known as *shrinkage*. This is used as a
1669::CODE;;multiplicative factor for the leaves values. Use ``1`` for no
1670::CODE;;shrinkage.
1671::CODE;;max_iter : int, default=100
1672::CODE;;The maximum number of iterations of the boosting process, i.e. the
1673::CODE;;maximum number of trees for binary classification. For multiclass
1674::CODE;;classification, `n_classes` trees per iteration are built.
1675::CODE;;max_leaf_nodes : int or None, default=31
1676::CODE;;The maximum number of leaves for each tree. Must be strictly greater
1677::CODE;;than 1. If None, there is no maximum limit.
1678::CODE;;max_depth : int or None, default=None
1679::CODE;;The maximum depth of each tree. The depth of a tree is the number of
1680::CODE;;edges to go from the root to the deepest leaf.
1681::CODE;;Depth isn't constrained by default.
1682::CODE;;min_samples_leaf : int, default=20
1683::CODE;;The minimum number of samples per leaf. For small datasets with less
1684::CODE;;than a few hundred samples, it is recommended to lower this value
1685::CODE;;since only very shallow trees would be built.
1686::CODE;;l2_regularization : float, default=0
1687::CODE;;The L2 regularization parameter penalizing leaves with small hessians.
1688::CODE;;Use ``0`` for no regularization (default).
1689::CODE;;max_features : float, default=1.0
1690::CODE;;Proportion of randomly chosen features in each and every node split.
1691::CODE;;This is a form of regularization, smaller values make the trees weaker
1692::CODE;;learners and might prevent overfitting.
1693::CODE;;If interaction constraints from `interaction_cst` are present, only allowed
1694::CODE;;features are taken into account for the subsampling.
1695::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.4
1696::CODE;;max_bins : int, default=255
1697::CODE;;The maximum number of bins to use for non-missing values. Before
1698::CODE;;training, each feature of the input array `X` is binned into
1699::CODE;;integer-valued bins, which allows for a much faster training stage.
1700::CODE;;Features with a small number of unique values may use less than
1701::CODE;;``max_bins`` bins. In addition to the ``max_bins`` bins, one more bin
1702::CODE;;is always reserved for missing values. Must be no larger than 255.
1703::CODE;;categorical_features : array-like of {bool, int, str} of shape (n_features) \
1704::CODE;;or shape (n_categorical_features,), default='from_dtype'
1705::CODE;;Indicates the categorical features.
1706::CODE;;- None : no feature will be considered categorical.
1707::CODE;;- boolean array-like : boolean mask indicating categorical features.
1708::CODE;;- integer array-like : integer indices indicating categorical
1709::CODE;;features.
1710::CODE;;- str array-like: names of categorical features (assuming the training
1711::CODE;;data has feature names).
1712::CODE;;- `"from_dtype"`: dataframe columns with dtype "category" are
1713::CODE;;considered to be categorical features. The input must be an object
1714::CODE;;exposing a ``__dataframe__`` method such as pandas or polars
1715::CODE;;DataFrames to use this feature.
1716::CODE;;For each categorical feature, there must be at most `max_bins` unique
1717::CODE;;categories. Negative values for categorical features encoded as numeric
1718::CODE;;dtypes are treated as missing values. All categorical values are
1719::CODE;;converted to floating point numbers. This means that categorical values
1720::CODE;;of 1.0 and 1 are treated as the same category.
1721::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <categorical_support_gbdt>`.
1722::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1723::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.2
1724::CODE;;Added support for feature names.
1725::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.4
1726::CODE;;Added `"from_dtype"` option.
1727::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.6
1728::CODE;;The default value changed from `None` to `"from_dtype"`.
1729::CODE;;monotonic_cst : array-like of int of shape (n_features) or dict, default=None
1730::CODE;;Monotonic constraint to enforce on each feature are specified using the
1731::CODE;;following integer values:
1732::CODE;;- 1: monotonic increase
1733::CODE;;- 0: no constraint
1734::CODE;;- -1: monotonic decrease
1735::CODE;;If a dict with str keys, map feature to monotonic constraints by name.
1736::CODE;;If an array, the features are mapped to constraints by position. See
1737::CODE;;:ref:`monotonic_cst_features_names` for a usage example.
1738::CODE;;The constraints are only valid for binary classifications and hold
1739::CODE;;over the probability of the positive class.
1740::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <monotonic_cst_gbdt>`.
1741::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
1742::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.2
1743::CODE;;Accept dict of constraints with feature names as keys.
1744::CODE;;interaction_cst : {"pairwise", "no_interactions"} or sequence of lists/tuples/sets \
1745::CODE;;of int, default=None
1746::CODE;;Specify interaction constraints, the sets of features which can
1747::CODE;;interact with each other in child node splits.
1748::CODE;;Each item specifies the set of feature indices that are allowed
1749::CODE;;to interact with each other. If there are more features than
1750::CODE;;specified in these constraints, they are treated as if they were
1751::CODE;;specified as an additional set.
1752::CODE;;The strings "pairwise" and "no_interactions" are shorthands for
1753::CODE;;allowing only pairwise or no interactions, respectively.
1754::CODE;;For instance, with 5 features in total, `interaction_cst=[{0, 1}]`
1755::CODE;;is equivalent to `interaction_cst=[{0, 1}, {2, 3, 4}]`,
1756::CODE;;and specifies that each branch of a tree will either only split
1757::CODE;;on features 0 and 1 or only split on features 2, 3 and 4.
1758::CODE;;See :ref:`this example<ice-vs-pdp>` on how to use `interaction_cst`.
1759::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
1760::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
1761::CODE;;When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit
1762::CODE;;and add more estimators to the ensemble. For results to be valid, the
1763::CODE;;estimator should be re-trained on the same data only.
1764::CODE;;See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
1765::CODE;;early_stopping : 'auto' or bool, default='auto'
1766::CODE;;If 'auto', early stopping is enabled if the sample size is larger than
1767::CODE;;10000 or if `X_val` and `y_val` are passed to `fit`. If True, early stopping
1768::CODE;;is enabled, otherwise early stopping is disabled.
1769::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
1770::CODE;;scoring : str or callable or None, default='loss'
1771::CODE;;Scoring method to use for early stopping. Only used if `early_stopping`
1772::CODE;;is enabled. Options:
1773::CODE;;- str: see :ref:`scoring_string_names` for options.
1774::CODE;;- callable: a scorer callable object (e.g., function) with signature
1775::CODE;;``scorer(estimator, X, y)``. See :ref:`scoring_callable` for details.
1776::CODE;;- `None`: :ref:`accuracy <accuracy_score>` is used.
1777::CODE;;- 'loss': early stopping is checked w.r.t the loss value.
1778::CODE;;validation_fraction : int or float or None, default=0.1
1779::CODE;;Proportion (or absolute size) of training data to set aside as
1780::CODE;;validation data for early stopping. If None, early stopping is done on
1781::CODE;;the training data.
1782::CODE;;The value is ignored if either early stopping is not performed, e.g.
1783::CODE;;`early_stopping=False`, or if `X_val` and `y_val` are passed to fit.
1784::CODE;;n_iter_no_change : int, default=10
1785::CODE;;Used to determine when to "early stop". The fitting process is
1786::CODE;;stopped when none of the last ``n_iter_no_change`` scores are better
1787::CODE;;than the ``n_iter_no_change - 1`` -th-to-last one, up to some
1788::CODE;;tolerance. Only used if early stopping is performed.
1789::CODE;;tol : float, default=1e-7
1790::CODE;;The absolute tolerance to use when comparing scores. The higher the
1791::CODE;;tolerance, the more likely we are to early stop: higher tolerance
1792::CODE;;means that it will be harder for subsequent iterations to be
1793::CODE;;considered an improvement upon the reference score.
1794::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
1795::CODE;;The verbosity level. If not zero, print some information about the
1796::CODE;;fitting process. ``1`` prints only summary info, ``2`` prints info per
1797::CODE;;iteration.
1798::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
1799::CODE;;Pseudo-random number generator to control the subsampling in the
1800::CODE;;binning process, and the train/validation data split if early stopping
1801::CODE;;is enabled.
1802::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
1803::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
1804::CODE;;class_weight : dict or 'balanced', default=None
1805::CODE;;Weights associated with classes in the form `{class_label: weight}`.
1806::CODE;;If not given, all classes are supposed to have weight one.
1807::CODE;;The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
1808::CODE;;weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
1809::CODE;;as `n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))`.
1810::CODE;;Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
1811::CODE;;through the fit method) if `sample_weight` is specified.

120::CODE;;Nodes with high gain are higher priority than nodes with low gain.
121::CODE;;heapq.heappush only need the '<' operator.
122::CODE;;heapq.heappop take the smallest item first (smaller is higher
123::CODE;;priority).
124::CODE;;Parameters
125::CODE;;----------
126::CODE;;other_node : TreeNode
127::CODE;;The node to compare with.
132::CODE;;The tree is fitted to predict the values of a Newton-Raphson step. The
133::CODE;;splits are considered in a best-first fashion, and the quality of a
134::CODE;;split is defined in splitting._split_gain.
135::CODE;;Parameters
136::CODE;;----------
137::CODE;;X_binned : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features), dtype=np.uint8
138::CODE;;The binned input samples. Must be Fortran-aligned.
139::CODE;;gradients : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
140::CODE;;The gradients of each training sample. Those are the gradients of the
141::CODE;;loss w.r.t the predictions, evaluated at iteration ``i - 1``.
142::CODE;;hessians : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
143::CODE;;The hessians of each training sample. Those are the hessians of the
144::CODE;;loss w.r.t the predictions, evaluated at iteration ``i - 1``.
145::CODE;;max_leaf_nodes : int, default=None
146::CODE;;The maximum number of leaves for each tree. If None, there is no
147::CODE;;maximum limit.
148::CODE;;max_depth : int, default=None
149::CODE;;The maximum depth of each tree. The depth of a tree is the number of
150::CODE;;edges to go from the root to the deepest leaf.
151::CODE;;Depth isn't constrained by default.
152::CODE;;min_samples_leaf : int, default=20
153::CODE;;The minimum number of samples per leaf.
154::CODE;;min_gain_to_split : float, default=0.
155::CODE;;The minimum gain needed to split a node. Splits with lower gain will
156::CODE;;be ignored.
157::CODE;;min_hessian_to_split : float, default=1e-3
158::CODE;;The minimum sum of hessians needed in each node. Splits that result in
159::CODE;;at least one child having a sum of hessians less than
160::CODE;;``min_hessian_to_split`` are discarded.

163::CODE;;to define the shape of the histograms.

165::CODE;;For each feature, gives the number of bins actually used for
166::CODE;;non-missing values. For features with a lot of unique values, this
167::CODE;;is equal to ``n_bins - 1``. If it's an int, all features are
168::CODE;;considered to have the same number of bins. If None, all features
169::CODE;;are considered to have ``n_bins - 1`` bins.

172::CODE;;If it's a bool, the same value is used for all features.

185::CODE;;Use ``0`` for no regularization (default).
186::CODE;;feature_fraction_per_split : float, default=1
187::CODE;;Proportion of randomly chosen features in each and every node split.
188::CODE;;This is a form of regularization, smaller values make the trees weaker
189::CODE;;learners and might prevent overfitting.
190::CODE;;rng : Generator
191::CODE;;Numpy random Generator used for feature subsampling.
192::CODE;;shrinkage : float, default=1.
193::CODE;;The shrinkage parameter to apply to the leaves values, also known as
194::CODE;;learning rate.
195::CODE;;n_threads : int, default=None
196::CODE;;Number of OpenMP threads to use. `_openmp_effective_n_threads` is called
197::CODE;;to determine the effective number of threads use, which takes cgroups CPU
198::CODE;;quotes into account. See the docstring of `_openmp_effective_n_threads`
199::CODE;;for details.

364::CODE;;for leaf in self.finalized_leaves:

420::CODE;;Also push it in the heap of splittable nodes if gain isn't zero.
421::CODE;;The gain of a node is 0 if either all the leaves are pure
422::CODE;;(best gain = 0), or if no split would satisfy the constraints,
423::CODE;;(min_hessians_to_split, min_gain_to_split, min_samples_leaf)

588::CODE;;Example: Assume constraints [{0, 1}, {1, 2}].
589::CODE;;1 <- Both constraint groups could be applied from now on
590::CODE;;/ \
591::CODE;;1 2 <- Left split still fulfills both constraint groups.
592::CODE;;/ \ / \ Right split at feature 2 has only group {1, 2} from now on.
593::CODE;;LightGBM uses the same logic for overlapping groups. See
594::CODE;;https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM/issues/4481 for details.

790::CODE;;def test_split_interaction_constraints():
878::CODE;;Because we set `n_features = 4` and `feature_fraction_per_split = 0.25`, it means
879::CODE;;that calling `splitter.find_node_split` will be allowed to select a split for a
880::CODE;;single completely random feature at each call. So if we iterate enough, we should
881::CODE;;cover all the allowed features, irrespective of the values of the gradients and
882::CODE;;Hessians of the objective.
1::CODE;;import numpy as np
2::CODE;;import pytest

47::CODE;;Isolation Forest Algorithm.
48::CODE;;Return the anomaly score of each sample using the IsolationForest algorithm
49::CODE;;The IsolationForest 'isolates' observations by randomly selecting a feature
50::CODE;;and then randomly selecting a split value between the maximum and minimum
51::CODE;;values of the selected feature.
52::CODE;;Since recursive partitioning can be represented by a tree structure, the
53::CODE;;number of splittings required to isolate a sample is equivalent to the path
54::CODE;;length from the root node to the terminating node.
55::CODE;;This path length, averaged over a forest of such random trees, is a
56::CODE;;measure of normality and our decision function.
57::CODE;;Random partitioning produces noticeably shorter paths for anomalies.
58::CODE;;Hence, when a forest of random trees collectively produce shorter path
59::CODE;;lengths for particular samples, they are highly likely to be anomalies.
60::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <isolation_forest>`.
61::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
62::CODE;;Parameters
63::CODE;;----------
64::CODE;;n_estimators : int, default=100
65::CODE;;The number of base estimators in the ensemble.
66::CODE;;max_samples : "auto", int or float, default="auto"
67::CODE;;The number of samples to draw from X to train each base estimator.
68::CODE;;- If int, then draw `max_samples` samples.
69::CODE;;- If float, then draw `max_samples * X.shape[0]` samples.
70::CODE;;- If "auto", then `max_samples=min(256, n_samples)`.
71::CODE;;If max_samples is larger than the number of samples provided,
72::CODE;;all samples will be used for all trees (no sampling).
73::CODE;;contamination : 'auto' or float, default='auto'
74::CODE;;The amount of contamination of the data set, i.e. the proportion
75::CODE;;of outliers in the data set. Used when fitting to define the threshold
76::CODE;;on the scores of the samples.
77::CODE;;- If 'auto', the threshold is determined as in the
78::CODE;;original paper.
79::CODE;;- If float, the contamination should be in the range (0, 0.5].
80::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.22
81::CODE;;The default value of ``contamination`` changed from 0.1
82::CODE;;to ``'auto'``.
83::CODE;;max_features : int or float, default=1.0
84::CODE;;The number of features to draw from X to train each base estimator.
85::CODE;;- If int, then draw `max_features` features.
86::CODE;;- If float, then draw `max(1, int(max_features * n_features_in_))` features.
87::CODE;;Note: using a float number less than 1.0 or integer less than number of
88::CODE;;features will enable feature subsampling and leads to a longer runtime.
89::CODE;;bootstrap : bool, default=False
90::CODE;;If True, individual trees are fit on random subsets of the training
91::CODE;;data sampled with replacement. If False, sampling without replacement
92::CODE;;is performed.
93::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
94::CODE;;The number of jobs to run in parallel for :meth:`fit`. ``None`` means 1
95::CODE;;unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context. ``-1`` means using
96::CODE;;all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>` for more details.
97::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
98::CODE;;Controls the pseudo-randomness of the selection of the feature
99::CODE;;and split values for each branching step and each tree in the forest.
100::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
101::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
102::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
103::CODE;;Controls the verbosity of the tree building process.
104::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
105::CODE;;When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit
106::CODE;;and add more estimators to the ensemble, otherwise, just fit a whole
107::CODE;;new forest. See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
108::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
109::CODE;;Attributes
110::CODE;;----------
111::CODE;;estimator_ : :class:`~sklearn.tree.ExtraTreeRegressor` instance
112::CODE;;The child estimator template used to create the collection of
113::CODE;;fitted sub-estimators.
114::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
115::CODE;;`base_estimator_` was renamed to `estimator_`.
116::CODE;;estimators_ : list of ExtraTreeRegressor instances
117::CODE;;The collection of fitted sub-estimators.
118::CODE;;estimators_features_ : list of ndarray
119::CODE;;The subset of drawn features for each base estimator.
120::CODE;;estimators_samples_ : list of ndarray
121::CODE;;The subset of drawn samples (i.e., the in-bag samples) for each base
122::CODE;;estimator.
123::CODE;;max_samples_ : int
124::CODE;;The actual number of samples.
125::CODE;;offset_ : float
126::CODE;;Offset used to define the decision function from the raw scores. We
127::CODE;;have the relation: ``decision_function = score_samples - offset_``.
128::CODE;;``offset_`` is defined as follows. When the contamination parameter is
129::CODE;;set to "auto", the offset is equal to -0.5 as the scores of inliers are
130::CODE;;close to 0 and the scores of outliers are close to -1. When a
131::CODE;;contamination parameter different than "auto" is provided, the offset
132::CODE;;is defined in such a way we obtain the expected number of outliers
133::CODE;;(samples with decision function < 0) in training.
134::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
135::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
136::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
137::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
138::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
139::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
140::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
141::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
142::CODE;;See Also
143::CODE;;--------
144::CODE;;sklearn.covariance.EllipticEnvelope : An object for detecting outliers in a
145::CODE;;Gaussian distributed dataset.
146::CODE;;sklearn.svm.OneClassSVM : Unsupervised Outlier Detection.
147::CODE;;Estimate the support of a high-dimensional distribution.
148::CODE;;The implementation is based on libsvm.
149::CODE;;sklearn.neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor : Unsupervised Outlier Detection
150::CODE;;using Local Outlier Factor (LOF).
151::CODE;;Notes
152::CODE;;-----
153::CODE;;The implementation is based on an ensemble of ExtraTreeRegressor. The
154::CODE;;maximum depth of each tree is set to ``ceil(log_2(n))`` where
155::CODE;;:math:`n` is the number of samples used to build the tree
156::CODE;;(see [1]_ for more details).
157::CODE;;References
158::CODE;;----------
159::CODE;;.. [1] F. T. Liu, K. M. Ting and Z. -H. Zhou.
160::CODE;;:doi:`"Isolation forest." <10.1109/ICDM.2008.17>`
161::CODE;;2008 Eighth IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM),
162::CODE;;2008, pp. 413-422.
163::CODE;;.. [2] F. T. Liu, K. M. Ting and Z. -H. Zhou.
164::CODE;;:doi:`"Isolation-based anomaly detection."
165::CODE;;<10.1145/2133360.2133363>` ACM Transactions on
166::CODE;;Knowledge Discovery from Data (TKDD) 6.1 (2012): 1-39.
167::CODE;;Examples
168::CODE;;--------
169::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
170::CODE;;>>> X = [[-1.1], [0.3], [0.5], [100]]
171::CODE;;>>> clf = IsolationForest(random_state=0).fit(X)
172::CODE;;>>> clf.predict([[0.1], [0], [90]])
173::CODE;;array([ 1, 1, -1])
174::CODE;;For an example of using isolation forest for anomaly detection see
175::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_isolation_forest.py`.

354::CODE;;Average anomaly score of X of the base classifiers.
355::CODE;;The anomaly score of an input sample is computed as
356::CODE;;the mean anomaly score of the trees in the forest.
357::CODE;;The measure of normality of an observation given a tree is the depth
358::CODE;;of the leaf containing this observation, which is equivalent to
359::CODE;;the number of splittings required to isolate this point. In case of
360::CODE;;several observations n_left in the leaf, the average path length of
361::CODE;;a n_left samples isolation tree is added.
362::CODE;;Parameters

444::CODE;;A voting regressor is an ensemble meta-estimator that fits several base
445::CODE;;regressors, each on the whole dataset. Then it averages the individual
446::CODE;;predictions to form a final prediction.
447::CODE;;For a detailed example, refer to
448::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_voting_regressor.py`.
449::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <voting_regressor>`.
450::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
451::CODE;;Parameters
452::CODE;;----------
453::CODE;;estimators : list of (str, estimator) tuples
454::CODE;;Invoking the ``fit`` method on the ``VotingRegressor`` will fit clones
455::CODE;;of those original estimators that will be stored in the class attribute
456::CODE;;``self.estimators_``. An estimator can be set to ``'drop'`` using
457::CODE;;:meth:`set_params`.
458::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.21
459::CODE;;``'drop'`` is accepted. Using None was deprecated in 0.22 and
460::CODE;;support was removed in 0.24.
461::CODE;;weights : array-like of shape (n_regressors,), default=None
462::CODE;;Sequence of weights (`float` or `int`) to weight the occurrences of
463::CODE;;predicted values before averaging. Uses uniform weights if `None`.
464::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
465::CODE;;The number of jobs to run in parallel for ``fit``.
466::CODE;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
467::CODE;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
468::CODE;;for more details.
469::CODE;;verbose : bool, default=False
470::CODE;;If True, the time elapsed while fitting will be printed as it
471::CODE;;is completed.
472::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
473::CODE;;Attributes
474::CODE;;----------
475::CODE;;estimators_ : list of regressors
476::CODE;;The collection of fitted sub-estimators as defined in ``estimators``
477::CODE;;that are not 'drop'.
478::CODE;;named_estimators_ : :class:`~sklearn.utils.Bunch`
479::CODE;;Attribute to access any fitted sub-estimators by name.
480::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
481::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
482::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
483::CODE;;underlying regressor exposes such an attribute when fit.

139::CODE;;sample_weight, estimator_weight, estimator_error = self._boost(
140::CODE;;iboost, X, y, sample_weight, random_state
141::CODE;;)
143::CODE;;if sample_weight is None:
144::CODE;;break
145::CODE;;self.estimator_weights_[iboost] = estimator_weight
146::CODE;;self.estimator_errors_[iboost] = estimator_error
148::CODE;;if estimator_error == 0:
149::CODE;;break

151::CODE;;if not np.isfinite(sample_weight_sum):
152::CODE;;warnings.warn(
153::CODE;;(
154::CODE;;"Sample weights have reached infinite values,"
155::CODE;;f" at iteration {iboost}, causing overflow. "
156::CODE;;"Iterations stopped. Try lowering the learning rate."
157::CODE;;),
158::CODE;;stacklevel=2,
159::CODE;;)
160::CODE;;break
162::CODE;;if sample_weight_sum <= 0:
163::CODE;;break
164::CODE;;if iboost < self.n_estimators - 1:
166::CODE;;sample_weight /= sample_weight_sum
167::CODE;;return self

581::CODE;;This is based eq. (15) of [1] where:
582::CODE;;p(y=c|X) = exp((1 / K-1) f_c(X)) / sum_k(exp((1 / K-1) f_k(X)))

618::CODE;;The predicted class probabilities of an input sample is computed as

622::CODE;;after each iteration of boosting and therefore allows monitoring, such

624::CODE;;each boost.

634::CODE;;outputs is the same of that of the :term:`classes_` attribute.
641::CODE;;The predicted class log-probabilities of an input sample is computed as
642::CODE;;the weighted mean predicted class log-probabilities of the classifiers
643::CODE;;in the ensemble.
644::CODE;;Parameters
645::CODE;;----------
646::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
647::CODE;;The training input samples. Sparse matrix can be CSC, CSR, COO,
648::CODE;;DOK, or LIL. COO, DOK, and LIL are converted to CSR.
649::CODE;;Returns
650::CODE;;-------
651::CODE;;p : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_classes)
652::CODE;;The class probabilities of the input samples. The order of
653::CODE;;outputs is the same of that of the :term:`classes_` attribute.
658::CODE;;An AdaBoost [1] regressor is a meta-estimator that begins by fitting a
659::CODE;;regressor on the original dataset and then fits additional copies of the
660::CODE;;regressor on the same dataset but where the weights of instances are
661::CODE;;adjusted according to the error of the current prediction. As such,
662::CODE;;subsequent regressors focus more on difficult cases.
663::CODE;;This class implements the algorithm known as AdaBoost.R2 [2].
664::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <adaboost>`.
665::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.14
666::CODE;;Parameters
667::CODE;;----------
668::CODE;;estimator : object, default=None
669::CODE;;The base estimator from which the boosted ensemble is built.
670::CODE;;If ``None``, then the base estimator is
671::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeRegressor` initialized with
672::CODE;;`max_depth=3`.
673::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
674::CODE;;`base_estimator` was renamed to `estimator`.
675::CODE;;n_estimators : int, default=50
676::CODE;;The maximum number of estimators at which boosting is terminated.
677::CODE;;In case of perfect fit, the learning procedure is stopped early.
678::CODE;;Values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
679::CODE;;learning_rate : float, default=1.0
680::CODE;;Weight applied to each regressor at each boosting iteration. A higher
681::CODE;;learning rate increases the contribution of each regressor. There is
682::CODE;;a trade-off between the `learning_rate` and `n_estimators` parameters.
683::CODE;;Values must be in the range `(0.0, inf)`.
684::CODE;;loss : {'linear', 'square', 'exponential'}, default='linear'
685::CODE;;The loss function to use when updating the weights after each
686::CODE;;boosting iteration.
687::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
688::CODE;;Controls the random seed given at each `estimator` at each
689::CODE;;boosting iteration.
690::CODE;;Thus, it is only used when `estimator` exposes a `random_state`.
691::CODE;;In addition, it controls the bootstrap of the weights used to train the
692::CODE;;`estimator` at each boosting iteration.
693::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
694::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
695::CODE;;Attributes
696::CODE;;----------
697::CODE;;estimator_ : estimator
698::CODE;;The base estimator from which the ensemble is grown.
699::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
700::CODE;;`base_estimator_` was renamed to `estimator_`.
701::CODE;;estimators_ : list of regressors
702::CODE;;The collection of fitted sub-estimators.
703::CODE;;estimator_weights_ : ndarray of floats
704::CODE;;Weights for each estimator in the boosted ensemble.
705::CODE;;estimator_errors_ : ndarray of floats
706::CODE;;Regression error for each estimator in the boosted ensemble.
707::CODE;;feature_importances_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
708::CODE;;The impurity-based feature importances if supported by the
709::CODE;;``estimator`` (when based on decision trees).
710::CODE;;Warning: impurity-based feature importances can be misleading for
711::CODE;;high cardinality features (many unique values). See
712::CODE;;:func:`sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance` as an alternative.
713::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
714::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
715::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
716::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
717::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
718::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.

771::CODE;;def _boost(self, iboost, X, y, sample_weight, random_state):
803::CODE;;estimator = self._make_estimator(random_state=random_state)
805::CODE;;bootstrap_idx = random_state.choice(
806::CODE;;np.arange(_num_samples(X)),
807::CODE;;size=_num_samples(X),
808::CODE;;replace=True,
809::CODE;;p=sample_weight,
810::CODE;;)
813::CODE;;X_ = _safe_indexing(X, bootstrap_idx)
814::CODE;;y_ = _safe_indexing(y, bootstrap_idx)
815::CODE;;estimator.fit(X_, y_)
816::CODE;;y_predict = estimator.predict(X)
817::CODE;;error_vect = np.abs(y_predict - y)
818::CODE;;sample_mask = sample_weight > 0
819::CODE;;masked_sample_weight = sample_weight[sample_mask]
820::CODE;;masked_error_vector = error_vect[sample_mask]
821::CODE;;error_max = masked_error_vector.max()
822::CODE;;if error_max != 0:
823::CODE;;masked_error_vector /= error_max
824::CODE;;if self.loss == "square":
825::CODE;;masked_error_vector **= 2
826::CODE;;elif self.loss == "exponential":
827::CODE;;masked_error_vector = 1.0 - np.exp(-masked_error_vector)
829::CODE;;estimator_error = (masked_sample_weight * masked_error_vector).sum()
830::CODE;;if estimator_error <= 0:
832::CODE;;return sample_weight, 1.0, 0.0
833::CODE;;elif estimator_error >= 0.5:
835::CODE;;if len(self.estimators_) > 1:
836::CODE;;self.estimators_.pop(-1)
837::CODE;;return None, None, None
838::CODE;;beta = estimator_error / (1.0 - estimator_error)
840::CODE;;estimator_weight = self.learning_rate * np.log(1.0 / beta)
841::CODE;;if not iboost == self.n_estimators - 1:
842::CODE;;sample_weight[sample_mask] *= np.power(
843::CODE;;beta, (1.0 - masked_error_vector) * self.learning_rate
844::CODE;;)
845::CODE;;return sample_weight, estimator_weight, estimator_error
846::CODE;;def _get_median_predict(self, X, limit):
848::CODE;;predictions = np.array([est.predict(X) for est in self.estimators_[:limit]]).T
850::CODE;;sorted_idx = np.argsort(predictions, axis=1)
852::CODE;;weight_cdf = np.cumsum(self.estimator_weights_[sorted_idx], axis=1)
853::CODE;;median_or_above = weight_cdf >= 0.5 * weight_cdf[:, -1][:, np.newaxis]
854::CODE;;median_idx = median_or_above.argmax(axis=1)
855::CODE;;median_estimators = sorted_idx[np.arange(_num_samples(X)), median_idx]
857::CODE;;return predictions[np.arange(_num_samples(X)), median_estimators]

288::CODE;;def test_importances_asymptotic():
292::CODE;;def binomial(k, n):
293::CODE;;return 0 if k < 0 or k > n else comb(int(n), int(k), exact=True)
294::CODE;;def entropy(samples):
295::CODE;;n_samples = len(samples)
296::CODE;;entropy = 0.0
297::CODE;;for count in np.bincount(samples):
298::CODE;;p = 1.0 * count / n_samples
299::CODE;;if p > 0:
300::CODE;;entropy -= p * np.log2(p)
301::CODE;;return entropy
302::CODE;;def mdi_importance(X_m, X, y):
303::CODE;;n_samples, n_features = X.shape
304::CODE;;features = list(range(n_features))
305::CODE;;features.pop(X_m)
306::CODE;;values = [np.unique(X[:, i]) for i in range(n_features)]
307::CODE;;imp = 0.0
308::CODE;;for k in range(n_features):
310::CODE;;coef = 1.0 / (binomial(k, n_features) * (n_features - k))
312::CODE;;for B in combinations(features, k):
314::CODE;;for b in product(*[values[B[j]] for j in range(k)]):
315::CODE;;mask_b = np.ones(n_samples, dtype=bool)
316::CODE;;for j in range(k):
317::CODE;;mask_b &= X[:, B[j]] == b[j]
318::CODE;;X_, y_ = X[mask_b, :], y[mask_b]
319::CODE;;n_samples_b = len(X_)
320::CODE;;if n_samples_b > 0:
321::CODE;;children = []
322::CODE;;for xi in values[X_m]:
323::CODE;;mask_xi = X_[:, X_m] == xi
324::CODE;;children.append(y_[mask_xi])
325::CODE;;imp += (
326::CODE;;coef
328::CODE;;* (
329::CODE;;entropy(y_)
330::CODE;;- sum(
331::CODE;;[
332::CODE;;entropy(c) * len(c) / n_samples_b
333::CODE;;for c in children
334::CODE;;]
335::CODE;;)
336::CODE;;)
337::CODE;;)
338::CODE;;return imp
339::CODE;;data = np.array(
340::CODE;;[
341::CODE;;[0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1],
342::CODE;;[1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 2],
343::CODE;;[1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 3],
344::CODE;;[0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 4],
345::CODE;;[1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 5],
346::CODE;;[1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 6],
347::CODE;;[1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 7],
348::CODE;;[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 8],
349::CODE;;[1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 9],
350::CODE;;[1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0],
351::CODE;;]
352::CODE;;)
353::CODE;;X, y = np.array(data[:, :7], dtype=bool), data[:, 7]
354::CODE;;n_features = X.shape[1]
356::CODE;;true_importances = np.zeros(n_features)
357::CODE;;for i in range(n_features):
358::CODE;;true_importances[i] = mdi_importance(i, X, y)
360::CODE;;clf = ExtraTreesClassifier(
361::CODE;;n_estimators=500, max_features=1, criterion="log_loss", random_state=0
362::CODE;;).fit(X, y)
363::CODE;;importances = (
364::CODE;;sum(
365::CODE;;tree.tree_.compute_feature_importances(normalize=False)
366::CODE;;for tree in clf.estimators_
367::CODE;;)
368::CODE;;/ clf.n_estimators
369::CODE;;)
371::CODE;;assert_almost_equal(entropy(y), sum(importances))
372::CODE;;assert np.abs(true_importances - importances).mean() < 0.01

26::CODE;;'''
27::CODE;;The liac-arff module implements functions to read and write ARFF files in
28::CODE;;Python. It was created in the Connectionist Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
29::CODE;;(LIAC), which takes place at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul
30::CODE;;(UFRGS), in Brazil.
31::CODE;;ARFF (Attribute-Relation File Format) is an file format specially created for
32::CODE;;describe datasets which are commonly used for machine learning experiments and
33::CODE;;software. This file format was created to be used in Weka, the best
34::CODE;;representative software for machine learning automated experiments.
35::CODE;;An ARFF file can be divided into two sections: header and data. The Header
36::CODE;;describes the metadata of the dataset, including a general description of the
37::CODE;;dataset, its name and its attributes. The source below is an example of a
38::CODE;;header section in a XOR dataset::
39::CODE;;%
40::CODE;;% XOR Dataset
41::CODE;;%
42::CODE;;% Created by Renato Pereira
43::CODE;;% rppereira@inf.ufrgs.br
44::CODE;;% http://inf.ufrgs.br/~rppereira
45::CODE;;%
46::CODE;;%
47::CODE;;@RELATION XOR
48::CODE;;@ATTRIBUTE input1 REAL
49::CODE;;@ATTRIBUTE input2 REAL
50::CODE;;@ATTRIBUTE y REAL
51::CODE;;The Data section of an ARFF file describes the observations of the dataset, in
52::CODE;;the case of XOR dataset::
53::CODE;;@DATA
54::CODE;;0.0,0.0,0.0
55::CODE;;0.0,1.0,1.0
56::CODE;;1.0,0.0,1.0
57::CODE;;1.0,1.0,0.0
58::CODE;;%
59::CODE;;%
60::CODE;;%
61::CODE;;Notice that several lines are starting with an ``%`` symbol, denoting a
62::CODE;;comment, thus, lines with ``%`` at the beginning will be ignored, except by the
63::CODE;;description part at the beginning of the file. The declarations ``@RELATION``,
64::CODE;;``@ATTRIBUTE``, and ``@DATA`` are all case insensitive and obligatory.
65::CODE;;For more information and details about the ARFF file description, consult
66::CODE;;http://www.cs.waikato.ac.nz/~ml/weka/arff.html
67::CODE;;ARFF Files in Python
68::CODE;;~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
69::CODE;;This module uses built-ins python objects to represent a deserialized ARFF
70::CODE;;file. A dictionary is used as the container of the data and metadata of ARFF,
71::CODE;;and have the following keys:
72::CODE;;- **description**: (OPTIONAL) a string with the description of the dataset.
73::CODE;;- **relation**: (OBLIGATORY) a string with the name of the dataset.
74::CODE;;- **attributes**: (OBLIGATORY) a list of attributes with the following
75::CODE;;template::
76::CODE;;(attribute_name, attribute_type)
77::CODE;;the attribute_name is a string, and attribute_type must be an string
78::CODE;;or a list of strings.
79::CODE;;- **data**: (OBLIGATORY) a list of data instances. Each data instance must be
80::CODE;;a list with values, depending on the attributes.
81::CODE;;The above keys must follow the case which were described, i.e., the keys are
82::CODE;;case sensitive. The attribute type ``attribute_type`` must be one of these
83::CODE;;strings (they are not case sensitive): ``NUMERIC``, ``INTEGER``, ``REAL`` or
84::CODE;;``STRING``. For nominal attributes, the ``atribute_type`` must be a list of
85::CODE;;strings.
86::CODE;;In this format, the XOR dataset presented above can be represented as a python
87::CODE;;object as::
88::CODE;;xor_dataset = {
89::CODE;;'description': 'XOR Dataset',
90::CODE;;'relation': 'XOR',
91::CODE;;'attributes': [
92::CODE;;('input1', 'REAL'),
93::CODE;;('input2', 'REAL'),
94::CODE;;('y', 'REAL'),
95::CODE;;],
96::CODE;;'data': [
97::CODE;;[0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
98::CODE;;[0.0, 1.0, 1.0],
99::CODE;;[1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
100::CODE;;[1.0, 1.0, 0.0]
101::CODE;;]
102::CODE;;}
103::CODE;;Features
104::CODE;;~~~~~~~~
105::CODE;;This module provides several features, including:
106::CODE;;- Read and write ARFF files using python built-in structures, such dictionaries
107::CODE;;and lists;
108::CODE;;- Supports `scipy.sparse.coo <http://docs.scipy
110::CODE;;and lists of dictionaries as used by SVMLight
111::CODE;;- Supports the following attribute types: NUMERIC, REAL, INTEGER, STRING, and
112::CODE;;NOMINAL;
113::CODE;;- Has an interface similar to other built-in modules such as ``json``, or
114::CODE;;``zipfile``;
115::CODE;;- Supports read and write the descriptions of files;
116::CODE;;- Supports missing values and names with spaces;
117::CODE;;- Supports unicode values and names;
118::CODE;;- Fully compatible with Python 2.7+, Python 3.5+, pypy and pypy3;
119::CODE;;- Under `MIT License <http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT>`_
120::CODE;;'''
121::CODE;;__author__ = 'Renato de Pontes Pereira, Matthias Feurer, Joel Nothman'
122::CODE;;__author_email__ = ('renato.ppontes@gmail.com, '
123::CODE;;'feurerm@informatik.uni-freiburg.de, '
124::CODE;;'joel.nothman@gmail.com')
125::CODE;;__version__ = '2.4.0'
126::CODE;;import re
127::CODE;;import csv
128::CODE;;from typing import TYPE_CHECKING
129::CODE;;from typing import Optional, List, Dict, Any, Iterator, Union, Tuple
131::CODE;;_SIMPLE_TYPES = ['NUMERIC', 'REAL', 'INTEGER', 'STRING']
132::CODE;;_TK_DESCRIPTION = '%'
133::CODE;;_TK_COMMENT = '%'
134::CODE;;_TK_RELATION = '@RELATION'
135::CODE;;_TK_ATTRIBUTE = '@ATTRIBUTE'
136::CODE;;_TK_DATA = '@DATA'
137::CODE;;_RE_RELATION = re.compile(r'^([^\{\}%,\s]*|\".*\"|\'.*\')$', re.UNICODE)
138::CODE;;_RE_ATTRIBUTE = re.compile(r'^(\".*\"|\'.*\'|[^\{\}%,\s]*)\s+(.+)$', re.UNICODE)
139::CODE;;_RE_QUOTE_CHARS = re.compile(r'["\'\\\s%,\000-\031]', re.UNICODE)

14::CODE;;def laplacian(

304::CODE;;def _setdiag_dense(m, d):
305::CODE;;step = len(d) + 1
306::CODE;;m.flat[::step] = d
307::CODE;;def _laplace(m, d):
308::CODE;;return lambda v: v * d[:, np.newaxis] - m @ v
309::CODE;;def _laplace_normed(m, d, nd):
310::CODE;;laplace = _laplace(m, d)
311::CODE;;return lambda v: nd[:, np.newaxis] * laplace(v * nd[:, np.newaxis])
312::CODE;;def _laplace_sym(m, d):
313::CODE;;return (
314::CODE;;lambda v: v * d[:, np.newaxis]
315::CODE;;- m @ v
316::CODE;;- np.transpose(np.conjugate(np.transpose(np.conjugate(v)) @ m))
317::CODE;;)
318::CODE;;def _laplace_normed_sym(m, d, nd):
319::CODE;;laplace_sym = _laplace_sym(m, d)
320::CODE;;return lambda v: nd[:, np.newaxis] * laplace_sym(v * nd[:, np.newaxis])
321::CODE;;def _linearoperator(mv, shape, dtype):

323::CODE;;def _laplacian_sparse_flo(graph, normed, axis, copy, form, dtype, symmetrized):
325::CODE;;del copy
326::CODE;;if dtype is None:
327::CODE;;dtype = graph.dtype
328::CODE;;graph_sum = np.asarray(graph.sum(axis=axis)).ravel()
329::CODE;;graph_diagonal = graph.diagonal()
330::CODE;;diag = graph_sum - graph_diagonal
331::CODE;;if symmetrized:
332::CODE;;graph_sum += np.asarray(graph.sum(axis=1 - axis)).ravel()
333::CODE;;diag = graph_sum - graph_diagonal - graph_diagonal
334::CODE;;if normed:
335::CODE;;isolated_node_mask = diag == 0
336::CODE;;w = np.where(isolated_node_mask, 1, np.sqrt(diag))
337::CODE;;if symmetrized:
338::CODE;;md = _laplace_normed_sym(graph, graph_sum, 1.0 / w)
339::CODE;;else:
340::CODE;;md = _laplace_normed(graph, graph_sum, 1.0 / w)
341::CODE;;if form == "function":
342::CODE;;return md, w.astype(dtype, copy=False)
343::CODE;;elif form == "lo":
344::CODE;;m = _linearoperator(md, shape=graph.shape, dtype=dtype)
345::CODE;;return m, w.astype(dtype, copy=False)
346::CODE;;else:
347::CODE;;raise ValueError(f"Invalid form: {form!r}")
348::CODE;;else:
349::CODE;;if symmetrized:
350::CODE;;md = _laplace_sym(graph, graph_sum)
351::CODE;;else:
352::CODE;;md = _laplace(graph, graph_sum)
353::CODE;;if form == "function":
354::CODE;;return md, diag.astype(dtype, copy=False)

360::CODE;;def _laplacian_sparse(graph, normed, axis, copy, form, dtype, symmetrized):
362::CODE;;del form
363::CODE;;if dtype is None:
364::CODE;;dtype = graph.dtype
365::CODE;;needs_copy = False
366::CODE;;if graph.format in ("lil", "dok"):
367::CODE;;m = graph.tocoo()
368::CODE;;else:
369::CODE;;m = graph
370::CODE;;if copy:
371::CODE;;needs_copy = True
372::CODE;;if symmetrized:
373::CODE;;m += m.T.conj()
374::CODE;;w = np.asarray(m.sum(axis=axis)).ravel() - m.diagonal()
375::CODE;;if normed:
376::CODE;;m = m.tocoo(copy=needs_copy)
377::CODE;;isolated_node_mask = w == 0
378::CODE;;w = np.where(isolated_node_mask, 1, np.sqrt(w))
379::CODE;;m.data /= w[m.row]
380::CODE;;m.data /= w[m.col]
381::CODE;;m.data *= -1
382::CODE;;m.setdiag(1 - isolated_node_mask)
383::CODE;;else:
384::CODE;;if m.format == "dia":
385::CODE;;m = m.copy()
386::CODE;;else:
387::CODE;;m = m.tocoo(copy=needs_copy)
388::CODE;;m.data *= -1
389::CODE;;m.setdiag(w)
390::CODE;;return m.astype(dtype, copy=False), w.astype(dtype)

438::CODE;;m = np.asarray(graph)
439::CODE;;if dtype is None:
440::CODE;;dtype = m.dtype
441::CODE;;if symmetrized:
442::CODE;;m += m.T.conj()
443::CODE;;np.fill_diagonal(m, 0)
444::CODE;;w = m.sum(axis=axis)
445::CODE;;if normed:
446::CODE;;isolated_node_mask = w == 0
447::CODE;;w = np.where(isolated_node_mask, 1, np.sqrt(w))
448::CODE;;m /= w
449::CODE;;m /= w[:, np.newaxis]
450::CODE;;m *= -1
451::CODE;;_setdiag_dense(m, 1 - isolated_node_mask)
452::CODE;;else:
453::CODE;;m *= -1
454::CODE;;_setdiag_dense(m, w)
455::CODE;;return m.astype(dtype, copy=False), w.astype(dtype, copy=False)
