33::CODE;;The one-way ANOVA tests the null hypothesis that 2 or more groups have
34::CODE;;the same population mean. The test is applied to samples from two or
35::CODE;;more groups, possibly with differing sizes.
36::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <univariate_feature_selection>`.
37::CODE;;Parameters
38::CODE;;----------
39::CODE;;*args : {array-like, sparse matrix}
40::CODE;;Sample1, sample2... The sample measurements should be given as
41::CODE;;arguments.
42::CODE;;Returns
43::CODE;;-------
44::CODE;;f_statistic : float
45::CODE;;The computed F-value of the test.
46::CODE;;p_value : float
47::CODE;;The associated p-value from the F-distribution.
48::CODE;;Notes
49::CODE;;-----
50::CODE;;The ANOVA test has important assumptions that must be satisfied in order
51::CODE;;for the associated p-value to be valid.
52::CODE;;1. The samples are independent
53::CODE;;2. Each sample is from a normally distributed population
54::CODE;;3. The population standard deviations of the groups are all equal. This
55::CODE;;property is known as homoscedasticity.
56::CODE;;If these assumptions are not true for a given set of data, it may still be
57::CODE;;possible to use the Kruskal-Wallis H-test (`scipy.stats.kruskal`_) although
58::CODE;;with some loss of power.
59::CODE;;The algorithm is from Heiman[2], pp.394-7.
60::CODE;;See ``scipy.stats.f_oneway`` that should give the same results while
61::CODE;;being less efficient.
62::CODE;;References
63::CODE;;----------
64::CODE;;.. [1] Lowry, Richard. "Concepts and Applications of Inferential
65::CODE;;Statistics". Chapter 14.
66::CODE;;http://vassarstats.net/textbook
67::CODE;;.. [2] Heiman, G.W. Research Methods in Statistics. 2002.
104::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <univariate_feature_selection>`.
105::CODE;;Parameters
106::CODE;;----------
107::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
108::CODE;;The set of regressors that will be tested sequentially.
109::CODE;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
110::CODE;;The target vector.
111::CODE;;Returns
112::CODE;;-------
113::CODE;;f_statistic : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
114::CODE;;F-statistic for each feature.
115::CODE;;p_values : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
116::CODE;;P-values associated with the F-statistic.
117::CODE;;See Also
118::CODE;;--------
119::CODE;;chi2 : Chi-squared stats of non-negative features for classification tasks.
120::CODE;;f_regression : F-value between label/feature for regression tasks.
121::CODE;;Examples
122::CODE;;--------
123::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
124::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.feature_selection import f_classif
125::CODE;;>>> X, y = make_classification(
126::CODE;;... n_samples=100, n_features=10, n_informative=2, n_clusters_per_class=1,
127::CODE;;... shuffle=False, random_state=42
128::CODE;;... )
129::CODE;;>>> f_statistic, p_values = f_classif(X, y)
130::CODE;;>>> f_statistic
131::CODE;;array([2.21e+02, 7.02e-01, 1.70e+00, 9.31e-01,
132::CODE;;5.41e+00, 3.25e-01, 4.71e-02, 5.72e-01,
133::CODE;;7.54e-01, 8.90e-02])
134::CODE;;>>> p_values
135::CODE;;array([7.14e-27, 4.04e-01, 1.96e-01, 3.37e-01,
136::CODE;;2.21e-02, 5.70e-01, 8.29e-01, 4.51e-01,
137::CODE;;3.87e-01, 7.66e-01])
144::CODE;;Version from https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/2525 with additional
145::CODE;;optimizations.
166::CODE;;This score can be used to select the `n_features` features with the
167::CODE;;highest values for the test chi-squared statistic from X, which must
168::CODE;;contain only **non-negative integer feature values** such as booleans or frequencies
169::CODE;;(e.g., term counts in document classification), relative to the classes.
170::CODE;;If some of your features are continuous, you need to bin them, for
171::CODE;;example by using :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.KBinsDiscretizer`.
172::CODE;;Recall that the chi-square test measures dependence between stochastic
173::CODE;;variables, so using this function "weeds out" the features that are the
174::CODE;;most likely to be independent of class and therefore irrelevant for
175::CODE;;classification.
176::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <univariate_feature_selection>`.
177::CODE;;Parameters
178::CODE;;----------
179::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
180::CODE;;Sample vectors.
181::CODE;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
182::CODE;;Target vector (class labels).
183::CODE;;Returns
184::CODE;;-------
185::CODE;;chi2 : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
186::CODE;;Chi2 statistics for each feature.
187::CODE;;p_values : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
188::CODE;;P-values for each feature.
189::CODE;;See Also
190::CODE;;--------
191::CODE;;f_classif : ANOVA F-value between label/feature for classification tasks.
192::CODE;;f_regression : F-value between label/feature for regression tasks.
193::CODE;;Notes
194::CODE;;-----
195::CODE;;Complexity of this algorithm is O(n_classes * n_features).
196::CODE;;Examples
197::CODE;;--------
198::CODE;;>>> import numpy as np
199::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.feature_selection import chi2
200::CODE;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 1, 3],
201::CODE;;... [0, 1, 5],
202::CODE;;... [5, 4, 1],
203::CODE;;... [6, 6, 2],
204::CODE;;... [1, 4, 0],
205::CODE;;... [0, 0, 0]])
206::CODE;;>>> y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2])
207::CODE;;>>> chi2_stats, p_values = chi2(X, y)
208::CODE;;>>> chi2_stats
209::CODE;;array([15.3, 6.5 , 8.9])
210::CODE;;>>> p_values
211::CODE;;array([0.000456, 0.0387, 0.0116 ])
248::CODE;;Pearson's r is also known as the Pearson correlation coefficient.
249::CODE;;Linear model for testing the individual effect of each of many regressors.
250::CODE;;This is a scoring function to be used in a feature selection procedure, not
251::CODE;;a free standing feature selection procedure.
252::CODE;;The cross correlation between each regressor and the target is computed
253::CODE;;as::
254::CODE;;E[(X[:, i] - mean(X[:, i])) * (y - mean(y))] / (std(X[:, i]) * std(y))
255::CODE;;For more on usage see the :ref:`User Guide <univariate_feature_selection>`.
256::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
257::CODE;;Parameters
258::CODE;;----------
259::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
260::CODE;;The data matrix.
261::CODE;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
262::CODE;;The target vector.
263::CODE;;center : bool, default=True
264::CODE;;Whether or not to center the data matrix `X` and the target vector `y`.
265::CODE;;By default, `X` and `y` will be centered.
266::CODE;;force_finite : bool, default=True
267::CODE;;Whether or not to force the Pearson's R correlation to be finite.
268::CODE;;In the particular case where some features in `X` or the target `y`
269::CODE;;are constant, the Pearson's R correlation is not defined. When
270::CODE;;`force_finite=False`, a correlation of `np.nan` is returned to
271::CODE;;acknowledge this case. When `force_finite=True`, this value will be
272::CODE;;forced to a minimal correlation of `0.0`.
273::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
274::CODE;;Returns
275::CODE;;-------
276::CODE;;correlation_coefficient : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
277::CODE;;Pearson's R correlation coefficients of features.
278::CODE;;See Also
279::CODE;;--------
280::CODE;;f_regression: Univariate linear regression tests returning f-statistic
281::CODE;;and p-values.
282::CODE;;mutual_info_regression: Mutual information for a continuous target.
283::CODE;;f_classif: ANOVA F-value between label/feature for classification tasks.
284::CODE;;chi2: Chi-squared stats of non-negative features for classification tasks.
285::CODE;;Examples
286::CODE;;--------
287::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
288::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.feature_selection import r_regression
289::CODE;;>>> X, y = make_regression(
290::CODE;;... n_samples=50, n_features=3, n_informative=1, noise=1e-4, random_state=42
291::CODE;;... )
292::CODE;;>>> r_regression(X, y)
293::CODE;;array([-0.157, 1. , -0.229])
334::CODE;;Quick linear model for testing the effect of a single regressor,
335::CODE;;sequentially for many regressors.
336::CODE;;This is done in 2 steps:
337::CODE;;1. The cross correlation between each regressor and the target is computed
338::CODE;;using :func:`r_regression` as::
339::CODE;;E[(X[:, i] - mean(X[:, i])) * (y - mean(y))] / (std(X[:, i]) * std(y))
340::CODE;;2. It is converted to an F score and then to a p-value.
341::CODE;;:func:`f_regression` is derived from :func:`r_regression` and will rank
342::CODE;;features in the same order if all the features are positively correlated
343::CODE;;with the target.
344::CODE;;Note however that contrary to :func:`f_regression`, :func:`r_regression`
345::CODE;;values lie in [-1, 1] and can thus be negative. :func:`f_regression` is
346::CODE;;therefore recommended as a feature selection criterion to identify
347::CODE;;potentially predictive feature for a downstream classifier, irrespective of
348::CODE;;the sign of the association with the target variable.
349::CODE;;Furthermore :func:`f_regression` returns p-values while
350::CODE;;:func:`r_regression` does not.
351::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <univariate_feature_selection>`.
352::CODE;;Parameters
353::CODE;;----------
354::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
355::CODE;;The data matrix.
356::CODE;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
357::CODE;;The target vector.
358::CODE;;center : bool, default=True
359::CODE;;Whether or not to center the data matrix `X` and the target vector `y`.
360::CODE;;By default, `X` and `y` will be centered.
361::CODE;;force_finite : bool, default=True
362::CODE;;Whether or not to force the F-statistics and associated p-values to
363::CODE;;be finite. There are two cases where the F-statistic is expected to not
364::CODE;;be finite:
365::CODE;;- when the target `y` or some features in `X` are constant. In this
366::CODE;;case, the Pearson's R correlation is not defined leading to obtain
367::CODE;;`np.nan` values in the F-statistic and p-value. When
368::CODE;;`force_finite=True`, the F-statistic is set to `0.0` and the
369::CODE;;associated p-value is set to `1.0`.
370::CODE;;- when a feature in `X` is perfectly correlated (or
371::CODE;;anti-correlated) with the target `y`. In this case, the F-statistic
372::CODE;;is expected to be `np.inf`. When `force_finite=True`, the F-statistic
373::CODE;;is set to `np.finfo(dtype).max` and the associated p-value is set to
374::CODE;;`0.0`.
375::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
376::CODE;;Returns
377::CODE;;-------
378::CODE;;f_statistic : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
379::CODE;;F-statistic for each feature.
380::CODE;;p_values : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
381::CODE;;P-values associated with the F-statistic.
382::CODE;;See Also
383::CODE;;--------
384::CODE;;r_regression: Pearson's R between label/feature for regression tasks.
385::CODE;;f_classif: ANOVA F-value between label/feature for classification tasks.
386::CODE;;chi2: Chi-squared stats of non-negative features for classification tasks.
387::CODE;;SelectKBest: Select features based on the k highest scores.
388::CODE;;SelectFpr: Select features based on a false positive rate test.
389::CODE;;SelectFdr: Select features based on an estimated false discovery rate.
390::CODE;;SelectFwe: Select features based on family-wise error rate.
391::CODE;;SelectPercentile: Select features based on percentile of the highest
392::CODE;;scores.
393::CODE;;Examples
394::CODE;;--------
395::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
396::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.feature_selection import f_regression
397::CODE;;>>> X, y = make_regression(
398::CODE;;... n_samples=50, n_features=3, n_informative=1, noise=1e-4, random_state=42
399::CODE;;... )
400::CODE;;>>> f_statistic, p_values = f_regression(X, y)
401::CODE;;>>> f_statistic
402::CODE;;array([1.21, 2.67e13, 2.66])
403::CODE;;>>> p_values
404::CODE;;array([0.276, 1.54e-283, 0.11])

96::CODE;;compare_arr = np.array([self.variances_, peak_to_peaks])
97::CODE;;self.variances_ = np.nanmin(compare_arr, axis=0)
98::CODE;;if np.all(~np.isfinite(self.variances_) | (self.variances_ <= self.threshold)):
99::CODE;;msg = "No feature in X meets the variance threshold {0:.5f}"
100::CODE;;if X.shape[0] == 1:
101::CODE;;msg += " (X contains only one sample)"
102::CODE;;raise ValueError(msg.format(self.threshold))
103::CODE;;return self
104::CODE;;def _get_support_mask(self):
105::CODE;;check_is_fitted(self)
106::CODE;;return self.variances_ > self.threshold

109::CODE;;tags.input_tags.allow_nan = True

16::CODE;;y = np.array([1, 0, 0, 0, 1])
17::CODE;;H_x = H_y = -(3 / 5) * np.log(3 / 5) - (2 / 5) * np.log(2 / 5)
18::CODE;;H_xy = -1 / 5 * np.log(1 / 5) - 2 / 5 * np.log(2 / 5) - 2 / 5 * np.log(2 / 5)

21::CODE;;def test_compute_mi_cc(global_dtype):
25::CODE;;mean = np.zeros(2)
27::CODE;;sigma_1 = 1
28::CODE;;sigma_2 = 10
29::CODE;;corr = 0.5
30::CODE;;cov = np.array(
31::CODE;;[
32::CODE;;[sigma_1**2, corr * sigma_1 * sigma_2],
33::CODE;;[corr * sigma_1 * sigma_2, sigma_2**2],
34::CODE;;]
35::CODE;;)
37::CODE;;I_theory = np.log(sigma_1) + np.log(sigma_2) - 0.5 * np.log(np.linalg.det(cov))
38::CODE;;rng = check_random_state(0)
39::CODE;;Z = rng.multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=1000).astype(global_dtype, copy=False)
40::CODE;;x, y = Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1]
43::CODE;;for n_neighbors in [3, 5, 7]:
44::CODE;;I_computed = _compute_mi(
45::CODE;;x, y, x_discrete=False, y_discrete=False, n_neighbors=n_neighbors
46::CODE;;)
47::CODE;;assert_allclose(I_computed, I_theory, rtol=1e-1)
48::CODE;;def test_compute_mi_cd(global_dtype):
61::CODE;;n_samples = 1000
62::CODE;;rng = check_random_state(0)
63::CODE;;for p in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]:
64::CODE;;x = rng.uniform(size=n_samples) > p
65::CODE;;y = np.empty(n_samples, global_dtype)
66::CODE;;mask = x == 0
67::CODE;;y[mask] = rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=np.sum(mask))
68::CODE;;y[~mask] = rng.uniform(0, 2, size=np.sum(~mask))
69::CODE;;I_theory = -0.5 * (
70::CODE;;(1 - p) * np.log(0.5 * (1 - p)) + p * np.log(0.5 * p) + np.log(0.5)
71::CODE;;) - np.log(2)
73::CODE;;for n_neighbors in [3, 5, 7]:
74::CODE;;I_computed = _compute_mi(
75::CODE;;x, y, x_discrete=True, y_discrete=False, n_neighbors=n_neighbors
76::CODE;;)
77::CODE;;assert_allclose(I_computed, I_theory, rtol=1e-1)

170::CODE;;def test_frozen_params():
31::CODE;;The implementation is based on Algorithm 3.1, 3.2, and 5.1 from [RW2006]_.
32::CODE;;Internally, the Laplace approximation is used for approximating the
33::CODE;;non-Gaussian posterior by a Gaussian.
34::CODE;;Currently, the implementation is restricted to using the logistic link
35::CODE;;function.
36::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
37::CODE;;Parameters
38::CODE;;----------
39::CODE;;kernel : kernel instance, default=None
40::CODE;;The kernel specifying the covariance function of the GP. If None is
41::CODE;;passed, the kernel "1.0 * RBF(1.0)" is used as default. Note that
42::CODE;;the kernel's hyperparameters are optimized during fitting.
43::CODE;;optimizer : 'fmin_l_bfgs_b' or callable, default='fmin_l_bfgs_b'
44::CODE;;Can either be one of the internally supported optimizers for optimizing
45::CODE;;the kernel's parameters, specified by a string, or an externally
46::CODE;;defined optimizer passed as a callable. If a callable is passed, it
47::CODE;;must have the signature::
48::CODE;;def optimizer(obj_func, initial_theta, bounds):
56::CODE;;....
59::CODE;;return theta_opt, func_min
60::CODE;;Per default, the 'L-BFGS-B' algorithm from scipy.optimize.minimize
61::CODE;;is used. If None is passed, the kernel's parameters are kept fixed.
62::CODE;;Available internal optimizers are::
63::CODE;;'fmin_l_bfgs_b'
64::CODE;;n_restarts_optimizer : int, default=0
65::CODE;;The number of restarts of the optimizer for finding the kernel's
66::CODE;;parameters which maximize the log-marginal likelihood. The first run
67::CODE;;of the optimizer is performed from the kernel's initial parameters,
68::CODE;;the remaining ones (if any) from thetas sampled log-uniform randomly
69::CODE;;from the space of allowed theta-values. If greater than 0, all bounds
70::CODE;;must be finite. Note that n_restarts_optimizer=0 implies that one
71::CODE;;run is performed.
72::CODE;;max_iter_predict : int, default=100
73::CODE;;The maximum number of iterations in Newton's method for approximating
74::CODE;;the posterior during predict. Smaller values will reduce computation
75::CODE;;time at the cost of worse results.
76::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
77::CODE;;If warm-starts are enabled, the solution of the last Newton iteration
78::CODE;;on the Laplace approximation of the posterior mode is used as
79::CODE;;initialization for the next call of _posterior_mode(). This can speed
80::CODE;;up convergence when _posterior_mode is called several times on similar
81::CODE;;problems as in hyperparameter optimization. See :term:`the Glossary
82::CODE;;<warm_start>`.
83::CODE;;copy_X_train : bool, default=True
84::CODE;;If True, a persistent copy of the training data is stored in the
85::CODE;;object. Otherwise, just a reference to the training data is stored,
86::CODE;;which might cause predictions to change if the data is modified
87::CODE;;externally.
88::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
89::CODE;;Determines random number generation used to initialize the centers.
90::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
91::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
92::CODE;;Attributes
93::CODE;;----------
94::CODE;;X_train_ : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features) or list of object
95::CODE;;Feature vectors or other representations of training data (also
96::CODE;;required for prediction).
97::CODE;;y_train_ : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
98::CODE;;Target values in training data (also required for prediction)
99::CODE;;classes_ : array-like of shape (n_classes,)
100::CODE;;Unique class labels.
101::CODE;;kernel_ : kernl instance
102::CODE;;The kernel used for prediction. The structure of the kernel is the
103::CODE;;same as the one passed as parameter but with optimized hyperparameters
104::CODE;;L_ : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
105::CODE;;Lower-triangular Cholesky decomposition of the kernel in X_train_
106::CODE;;pi_ : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
107::CODE;;The probabilities of the positive class for the training points
108::CODE;;X_train_
109::CODE;;W_sr_ : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
110::CODE;;Square root of W, the Hessian of log-likelihood of the latent function
111::CODE;;values for the observed labels. Since W is diagonal, only the diagonal
112::CODE;;of sqrt(W) is stored.
113::CODE;;log_marginal_likelihood_value_ : float
114::CODE;;The log-marginal-likelihood of ``self.kernel_.theta``
115::CODE;;References
116::CODE;;----------
117::CODE;;.. [RW2006] `Carl E. Rasmussen and Christopher K.I. Williams,
118::CODE;;"Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning",
119::CODE;;MIT Press 2006 <https://www.gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW.pdf>`_
141::CODE;;Parameters
142::CODE;;----------
143::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features) or list of object
144::CODE;;Feature vectors or other representations of training data.
145::CODE;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
146::CODE;;Target values, must be binary.
147::CODE;;Returns
148::CODE;;-------
149::CODE;;self : returns an instance of self.
225::CODE;;Parameters
226::CODE;;----------
227::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features) or list of object
228::CODE;;Query points where the GP is evaluated for classification.
229::CODE;;Returns
230::CODE;;-------
231::CODE;;C : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
232::CODE;;Predicted target values for X, values are from ``classes_``
243::CODE;;Parameters
244::CODE;;----------
245::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features) or list of object
246::CODE;;Query points where the GP is evaluated for classification.
247::CODE;;Returns
248::CODE;;-------
249::CODE;;C : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_classes)
250::CODE;;Returns the probability of the samples for each class in
251::CODE;;the model. The columns correspond to the classes in sorted
252::CODE;;order, as they appear in the attribute ``classes_``.
278::CODE;;Parameters
279::CODE;;----------
280::CODE;;theta : array-like of shape (n_kernel_params,), default=None
281::CODE;;Kernel hyperparameters for which the log-marginal likelihood is
282::CODE;;evaluated. If None, the precomputed log_marginal_likelihood
283::CODE;;of ``self.kernel_.theta`` is returned.
284::CODE;;eval_gradient : bool, default=False
285::CODE;;If True, the gradient of the log-marginal likelihood with respect
286::CODE;;to the kernel hyperparameters at position theta is returned
287::CODE;;additionally. If True, theta must not be None.
288::CODE;;clone_kernel : bool, default=True
289::CODE;;If True, the kernel attribute is copied. If False, the kernel
290::CODE;;attribute is modified, but may result in a performance improvement.
291::CODE;;Returns
292::CODE;;-------
293::CODE;;log_likelihood : float
294::CODE;;Log-marginal likelihood of theta for training data.
295::CODE;;log_likelihood_gradient : ndarray of shape (n_kernel_params,), \
296::CODE;;optional
297::CODE;;Gradient of the log-marginal likelihood with respect to the kernel
298::CODE;;hyperparameters at position theta.
299::CODE;;Only returned when `eval_gradient` is True.
340::CODE;;Based on algorithm 3.2 of [RW2006]_, this function returns the latent
341::CODE;;mean (Line 4) and variance (Line 6) of the Gaussian process
342::CODE;;classification model.
343::CODE;;Note that this function is only supported for binary classification.
344::CODE;;Parameters
345::CODE;;----------
346::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features) or list of object
347::CODE;;Query points where the GP is evaluated for classification.
348::CODE;;Returns
349::CODE;;-------
350::CODE;;latent_mean : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
351::CODE;;Mean of the latent function values at the query points.
352::CODE;;latent_var : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
353::CODE;;Variance of the latent function values at the query points.
365::CODE;;This approximates the posterior of the latent function values for given
366::CODE;;inputs and target observations with a Gaussian approximation and uses
367::CODE;;Newton's iteration to find the mode of this approximation.
429::CODE;;The implementation is based on Algorithm 3.1, 3.2, and 5.1 from [RW2006]_.
430::CODE;;Internally, the Laplace approximation is used for approximating the
431::CODE;;non-Gaussian posterior by a Gaussian.
432::CODE;;Currently, the implementation is restricted to using the logistic link
433::CODE;;function. For multi-class classification, several binary one-versus rest
434::CODE;;classifiers are fitted. Note that this class thus does not implement
435::CODE;;a true multi-class Laplace approximation.
436::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gaussian_process>`.
437::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
438::CODE;;Parameters
439::CODE;;----------
440::CODE;;kernel : kernel instance, default=None
441::CODE;;The kernel specifying the covariance function of the GP. If None is
442::CODE;;passed, the kernel "1.0 * RBF(1.0)" is used as default. Note that
443::CODE;;the kernel's hyperparameters are optimized during fitting. Also kernel
444::CODE;;cannot be a `CompoundKernel`.
445::CODE;;optimizer : 'fmin_l_bfgs_b', callable or None, default='fmin_l_bfgs_b'
446::CODE;;Can either be one of the internally supported optimizers for optimizing
447::CODE;;the kernel's parameters, specified by a string, or an externally
448::CODE;;defined optimizer passed as a callable. If a callable is passed, it
449::CODE;;must have the signature::
450::CODE;;def optimizer(obj_func, initial_theta, bounds):
458::CODE;;....
461::CODE;;return theta_opt, func_min
462::CODE;;Per default, the 'L-BFGS-B' algorithm from scipy.optimize.minimize
463::CODE;;is used. If None is passed, the kernel's parameters are kept fixed.
464::CODE;;Available internal optimizers are::
465::CODE;;'fmin_l_bfgs_b'
466::CODE;;n_restarts_optimizer : int, default=0
467::CODE;;The number of restarts of the optimizer for finding the kernel's
468::CODE;;parameters which maximize the log-marginal likelihood. The first run
469::CODE;;of the optimizer is performed from the kernel's initial parameters,
470::CODE;;the remaining ones (if any) from thetas sampled log-uniform randomly
471::CODE;;from the space of allowed theta-values. If greater than 0, all bounds
472::CODE;;must be finite. Note that n_restarts_optimizer=0 implies that one
473::CODE;;run is performed.
474::CODE;;max_iter_predict : int, default=100
475::CODE;;The maximum number of iterations in Newton's method for approximating
476::CODE;;the posterior during predict. Smaller values will reduce computation
477::CODE;;time at the cost of worse results.
478::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
479::CODE;;If warm-starts are enabled, the solution of the last Newton iteration
480::CODE;;on the Laplace approximation of the posterior mode is used as
481::CODE;;initialization for the next call of _posterior_mode(). This can speed
482::CODE;;up convergence when _posterior_mode is called several times on similar
483::CODE;;problems as in hyperparameter optimization. See :term:`the Glossary
484::CODE;;<warm_start>`.
485::CODE;;copy_X_train : bool, default=True
486::CODE;;If True, a persistent copy of the training data is stored in the
487::CODE;;object. Otherwise, just a reference to the training data is stored,
488::CODE;;which might cause predictions to change if the data is modified
489::CODE;;externally.
490::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
491::CODE;;Determines random number generation used to initialize the centers.
492::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
493::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
494::CODE;;multi_class : {'one_vs_rest', 'one_vs_one'}, default='one_vs_rest'
495::CODE;;Specifies how multi-class classification problems are handled.
496::CODE;;Supported are 'one_vs_rest' and 'one_vs_one'. In 'one_vs_rest',
497::CODE;;one binary Gaussian process classifier is fitted for each class, which
498::CODE;;is trained to separate this class from the rest. In 'one_vs_one', one
499::CODE;;binary Gaussian process classifier is fitted for each pair of classes,
500::CODE;;which is trained to separate these two classes. The predictions of
501::CODE;;these binary predictors are combined into multi-class predictions.
502::CODE;;Note that 'one_vs_one' does not support predicting probability
503::CODE;;estimates.
504::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None

27::CODE;;The implementation is based on Algorithm 2.1 of [RW2006]_.
28::CODE;;In addition to standard scikit-learn estimator API,
29::CODE;;:class:`GaussianProcessRegressor`:
30::CODE;;* allows prediction without prior fitting (based on the GP prior)
31::CODE;;* provides an additional method `sample_y(X)`, which evaluates samples
32::CODE;;drawn from the GPR (prior or posterior) at given inputs
33::CODE;;* exposes a method `log_marginal_likelihood(theta)`, which can be used
34::CODE;;externally for other ways of selecting hyperparameters, e.g., via
35::CODE;;Markov chain Monte Carlo.
36::CODE;;To learn the difference between a point-estimate approach vs. a more
37::CODE;;Bayesian modelling approach, refer to the example entitled
38::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_gaussian_process_plot_compare_gpr_krr.py`.
39::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gaussian_process>`.
40::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
41::CODE;;Parameters
42::CODE;;----------
43::CODE;;kernel : kernel instance, default=None
44::CODE;;The kernel specifying the covariance function of the GP. If None is
45::CODE;;passed, the kernel ``ConstantKernel(1.0, constant_value_bounds="fixed")
46::CODE;;* RBF(1.0, length_scale_bounds="fixed")`` is used as default. Note that
47::CODE;;the kernel hyperparameters are optimized during fitting unless the
48::CODE;;bounds are marked as "fixed".
49::CODE;;alpha : float or ndarray of shape (n_samples,), default=1e-10
50::CODE;;Value added to the diagonal of the kernel matrix during fitting.
51::CODE;;This can prevent a potential numerical issue during fitting, by
52::CODE;;ensuring that the calculated values form a positive definite matrix.
53::CODE;;It can also be interpreted as the variance of additional Gaussian
54::CODE;;measurement noise on the training observations. Note that this is
55::CODE;;different from using a `WhiteKernel`. If an array is passed, it must
56::CODE;;have the same number of entries as the data used for fitting and is
57::CODE;;used as datapoint-dependent noise level. Allowing to specify the
58::CODE;;noise level directly as a parameter is mainly for convenience and
59::CODE;;for consistency with :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge`.
60::CODE;;For an example illustrating how the alpha parameter controls
61::CODE;;the noise variance in Gaussian Process Regression, see
62::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_gaussian_process_plot_gpr_noisy_targets.py`.
63::CODE;;optimizer : "fmin_l_bfgs_b", callable or None, default="fmin_l_bfgs_b"
64::CODE;;Can either be one of the internally supported optimizers for optimizing
65::CODE;;the kernel's parameters, specified by a string, or an externally
66::CODE;;defined optimizer passed as a callable. If a callable is passed, it
67::CODE;;must have the signature::
68::CODE;;def optimizer(obj_func, initial_theta, bounds):
76::CODE;;....
79::CODE;;return theta_opt, func_min
80::CODE;;Per default, the L-BFGS-B algorithm from `scipy.optimize.minimize`
81::CODE;;is used. If None is passed, the kernel's parameters are kept fixed.
82::CODE;;Available internal optimizers are: `{'fmin_l_bfgs_b'}`.
83::CODE;;n_restarts_optimizer : int, default=0
84::CODE;;The number of restarts of the optimizer for finding the kernel's
85::CODE;;parameters which maximize the log-marginal likelihood. The first run
86::CODE;;of the optimizer is performed from the kernel's initial parameters,
87::CODE;;the remaining ones (if any) from thetas sampled log-uniform randomly
88::CODE;;from the space of allowed theta-values. If greater than 0, all bounds
89::CODE;;must be finite. Note that `n_restarts_optimizer == 0` implies that one
90::CODE;;run is performed.
91::CODE;;normalize_y : bool, default=False
92::CODE;;Whether or not to normalize the target values `y` by removing the mean
93::CODE;;and scaling to unit-variance. This is recommended for cases where
94::CODE;;zero-mean, unit-variance priors are used. Note that, in this
95::CODE;;implementation, the normalisation is reversed before the GP predictions
96::CODE;;are reported.
97::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.23
98::CODE;;copy_X_train : bool, default=True
99::CODE;;If True, a persistent copy of the training data is stored in the
100::CODE;;object. Otherwise, just a reference to the training data is stored,
101::CODE;;which might cause predictions to change if the data is modified
102::CODE;;externally.
103::CODE;;n_targets : int, default=None
104::CODE;;The number of dimensions of the target values. Used to decide the number
105::CODE;;of outputs when sampling from the prior distributions (i.e. calling
106::CODE;;:meth:`sample_y` before :meth:`fit`). This parameter is ignored once
107::CODE;;:meth:`fit` has been called.
108::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
109::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
110::CODE;;Determines random number generation used to initialize the centers.
111::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
112::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.

115::CODE;;X_train_ : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features) or list of object

117::CODE;;required for prediction).
118::CODE;;y_train_ : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_targets)

1672::CODE;;Parameters
1673::CODE;;----------
1674::CODE;;X : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_features)
1675::CODE;;Left argument of the returned kernel k(X, Y)
1676::CODE;;Y : ndarray of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features), default=None
1677::CODE;;Right argument of the returned kernel k(X, Y). If None, k(X, X)
1678::CODE;;if evaluated instead.
1679::CODE;;eval_gradient : bool, default=False
1680::CODE;;Determines whether the gradient with respect to the log of
1681::CODE;;the kernel hyperparameter is computed.
1682::CODE;;Only supported when Y is None.
1683::CODE;;Returns
1684::CODE;;-------
1685::CODE;;K : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_samples_Y)
1686::CODE;;Kernel k(X, Y)
1687::CODE;;K_gradient : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_samples_X, n_dims), \
1688::CODE;;optional
1689::CODE;;The gradient of the kernel k(X, X) with respect to the log of the
1690::CODE;;hyperparameter of the kernel. Only returned when `eval_gradient`
1691::CODE;;is True.
1731::CODE;;The DotProduct kernel is non-stationary and can be obtained from linear
1732::CODE;;regression by putting :math:`N(0, 1)` priors on the coefficients
1733::CODE;;of :math:`x_d (d = 1, . . . , D)` and a prior of :math:`N(0, \sigma_0^2)`
1734::CODE;;on the bias. The DotProduct kernel is invariant to a rotation of
1735::CODE;;the coordinates about the origin, but not translations.
1736::CODE;;It is parameterized by a parameter sigma_0 :math:`\sigma`
1737::CODE;;which controls the inhomogenity of the kernel. For :math:`\sigma_0^2 =0`,
1738::CODE;;the kernel is called the homogeneous linear kernel, otherwise
1739::CODE;;it is inhomogeneous. The kernel is given by
1740::CODE;;.. math::
1741::CODE;;k(x_i, x_j) = \sigma_0 ^ 2 + x_i \cdot x_j
1742::CODE;;The DotProduct kernel is commonly combined with exponentiation.
1743::CODE;;See [1]_, Chapter 4, Section 4.2, for further details regarding the
1744::CODE;;DotProduct kernel.
1745::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gp_kernels>`.
1746::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1747::CODE;;Parameters
1748::CODE;;----------
1749::CODE;;sigma_0 : float >= 0, default=1.0
1750::CODE;;Parameter controlling the inhomogenity of the kernel. If sigma_0=0,
1751::CODE;;the kernel is homogeneous.
1752::CODE;;sigma_0_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1753::CODE;;The lower and upper bound on 'sigma_0'.
1754::CODE;;If set to "fixed", 'sigma_0' cannot be changed during
1755::CODE;;hyperparameter tuning.
1756::CODE;;References
1757::CODE;;----------
1758::CODE;;.. [1] `Carl Edward Rasmussen, Christopher K. I. Williams (2006).
1759::CODE;;"Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning". The MIT Press.
1760::CODE;;<http://www.gaussianprocess.org/gpml/>`_
1761::CODE;;Examples
1762::CODE;;--------
1763::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman2
1764::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
1765::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import DotProduct, WhiteKernel
1766::CODE;;>>> X, y = make_friedman2(n_samples=500, noise=0, random_state=0)
1767::CODE;;>>> kernel = DotProduct() + WhiteKernel()
1768::CODE;;>>> gpr = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=kernel,
1769::CODE;;... random_state=0).fit(X, y)
1770::CODE;;>>> gpr.score(X, y)
1771::CODE;;0.3680
1772::CODE;;>>> gpr.predict(X[:2,:], return_std=True)
1773::CODE;;(array([653.0, 592.1]), array([316.6, 316.6]))

1841::CODE;;def _approx_fprime(xk, f, epsilon, args=()):
1842::CODE;;f0 = f(*((xk,) + args))
1843::CODE;;grad = np.zeros((f0.shape[0], f0.shape[1], len(xk)), float)
1844::CODE;;ei = np.zeros((len(xk),), float)
1845::CODE;;for k in range(len(xk)):
1846::CODE;;ei[k] = 1.0
1847::CODE;;d = epsilon * ei
1848::CODE;;grad[:, :, k] = (f(*((xk + d,) + args)) - f0) / d[k]
1849::CODE;;ei[k] = 0.0
1850::CODE;;return grad

460::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("na, allow_nan", [(-1, False), (np.nan, True)])
461::CODE;;def test_knn_tags(na, allow_nan):
462::CODE;;knn = KNNImputer(missing_values=na)
463::CODE;;assert knn.__sklearn_tags__().input_tags.allow_nan == allow_nan
39::CODE;;The grid is a cartesian product between the columns of ``values``. The
40::CODE;;ith column of ``values`` consists in ``grid_resolution`` equally-spaced
41::CODE;;points between the percentiles of the jth column of X.
42::CODE;;If ``grid_resolution`` is bigger than the number of unique values in the
43::CODE;;j-th column of X or if the feature is a categorical feature (by inspecting
44::CODE;;`is_categorical`) , then those unique values will be used instead.
45::CODE;;Parameters
46::CODE;;----------
47::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_target_features)
48::CODE;;The data.
49::CODE;;percentiles : tuple of float
50::CODE;;The percentiles which are used to construct the extreme values of
51::CODE;;the grid. Must be in [0, 1].
52::CODE;;is_categorical : list of bool
53::CODE;;For each feature, tells whether it is categorical or not. If a feature
54::CODE;;is categorical, then the values used will be the unique ones
55::CODE;;(i.e. categories) instead of the percentiles.
56::CODE;;grid_resolution : int
57::CODE;;The number of equally spaced points to be placed on the grid for each
58::CODE;;feature.
59::CODE;;custom_values: dict
60::CODE;;Mapping from column index of X to an array-like of values where
61::CODE;;the partial dependence should be calculated for that feature
62::CODE;;Returns
63::CODE;;-------
64::CODE;;grid : ndarray of shape (n_points, n_target_features)
65::CODE;;A value for each feature at each point in the grid. ``n_points`` is
66::CODE;;always ``<= grid_resolution ** X.shape[1]``.
67::CODE;;values : list of 1d ndarrays
68::CODE;;The values with which the grid has been created. The size of each
69::CODE;;array ``values[j]`` is either ``grid_resolution``, the number of
70::CODE;;unique values in ``X[:, j]``, if j is not in ``custom_range``.
71::CODE;;If j is in ``custom_range``, then it is the length of ``custom_range[j]``.
141::CODE;;The recursion method is in particular enabled for tree-based estimators.
142::CODE;;For each `grid` value, a weighted tree traversal is performed: if a split node
143::CODE;;involves an input feature of interest, the corresponding left or right branch
144::CODE;;is followed; otherwise both branches are followed, each branch being weighted
145::CODE;;by the fraction of training samples that entered that branch. Finally, the
146::CODE;;partial dependence is given by a weighted average of all the visited leaves
147::CODE;;values.
148::CODE;;This method is more efficient in terms of speed than the `'brute'` method
149::CODE;;(:func:`~sklearn.inspection._partial_dependence._partial_dependence_brute`).
150::CODE;;However, here, the partial dependence computation is done explicitly with the
151::CODE;;`X` used during training of `est`.
152::CODE;;Parameters
153::CODE;;----------
154::CODE;;est : BaseEstimator
155::CODE;;A fitted estimator object implementing :term:`predict` or
156::CODE;;:term:`decision_function`. Multioutput-multiclass classifiers are not
157::CODE;;supported. Note that `'recursion'` is only supported for some tree-based
158::CODE;;estimators (namely
159::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier`,
160::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`,
161::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier`,
162::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`,
163::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeRegressor`,
164::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor`,
165::CODE;;).
166::CODE;;grid : array-like of shape (n_points, n_target_features)
167::CODE;;The grid of feature values for which the partial dependence is calculated.
168::CODE;;Note that `n_points` is the number of points in the grid and `n_target_features`
169::CODE;;is the number of features you are doing partial dependence at.
170::CODE;;features : array-like of {int, str}
171::CODE;;The feature (e.g. `[0]`) or pair of interacting features
172::CODE;;(e.g. `[(0, 1)]`) for which the partial dependency should be computed.
173::CODE;;Returns
174::CODE;;-------
175::CODE;;averaged_predictions : array-like of shape (n_targets, n_points)
176::CODE;;The averaged predictions for the given `grid` of features values.
177::CODE;;Note that `n_targets` is the number of targets (e.g. 1 for binary
178::CODE;;classification, `n_tasks` for multi-output regression, and `n_classes` for
179::CODE;;multiclass classification) and `n_points` is the number of points in the `grid`.
191::CODE;;The brute method explicitly averages the predictions of an estimator over a
192::CODE;;grid of feature values.
193::CODE;;For each `grid` value, all the samples from `X` have their variables of
194::CODE;;interest replaced by that specific `grid` value. The predictions are then made
195::CODE;;and averaged across the samples.
196::CODE;;This method is slower than the `'recursion'`
197::CODE;;(:func:`~sklearn.inspection._partial_dependence._partial_dependence_recursion`)
198::CODE;;version for estimators with this second option. However, with the `'brute'`
199::CODE;;force method, the average will be done with the given `X` and not the `X`
200::CODE;;used during training, as it is done in the `'recursion'` version. Therefore
201::CODE;;the average can always accept `sample_weight` (even when the estimator was
202::CODE;;fitted without).
203::CODE;;Parameters
204::CODE;;----------
205::CODE;;est : BaseEstimator
206::CODE;;A fitted estimator object implementing :term:`predict`,
207::CODE;;:term:`predict_proba`, or :term:`decision_function`.
208::CODE;;Multioutput-multiclass classifiers are not supported.
209::CODE;;grid : array-like of shape (n_points, n_target_features)
210::CODE;;The grid of feature values for which the partial dependence is calculated.
211::CODE;;Note that `n_points` is the number of points in the grid and `n_target_features`
212::CODE;;is the number of features you are doing partial dependence at.
213::CODE;;features : array-like of {int, str}
214::CODE;;The feature (e.g. `[0]`) or pair of interacting features
215::CODE;;(e.g. `[(0, 1)]`) for which the partial dependency should be computed.
216::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
217::CODE;;`X` is used to generate values for the complement features. That is, for
218::CODE;;each value in `grid`, the method will average the prediction of each
219::CODE;;sample from `X` having that grid value for `features`.
220::CODE;;response_method : {'auto', 'predict_proba', 'decision_function'}, \
221::CODE;;default='auto'
222::CODE;;Specifies whether to use :term:`predict_proba` or
223::CODE;;:term:`decision_function` as the target response. For regressors
224::CODE;;this parameter is ignored and the response is always the output of
225::CODE;;:term:`predict`. By default, :term:`predict_proba` is tried first
226::CODE;;and we revert to :term:`decision_function` if it doesn't exist.
227::CODE;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
228::CODE;;Sample weights are used to calculate weighted means when averaging the
229::CODE;;model output. If `None`, then samples are equally weighted. Note that
230::CODE;;`sample_weight` does not change the individual predictions.
231::CODE;;Returns
232::CODE;;-------
233::CODE;;averaged_predictions : array-like of shape (n_targets, n_points)
234::CODE;;The averaged predictions for the given `grid` of features values.
235::CODE;;Note that `n_targets` is the number of targets (e.g. 1 for binary
236::CODE;;classification, `n_tasks` for multi-output regression, and `n_classes` for
237::CODE;;multiclass classification) and `n_points` is the number of points in the `grid`.
238::CODE;;predictions : array-like
239::CODE;;The predictions for the given `grid` of features values over the samples
240::CODE;;from `X`. For non-multioutput regression and binary classification the
241::CODE;;shape is `(n_instances, n_points)` and for multi-output regression and
242::CODE;;multiclass classification the shape is `(n_targets, n_instances, n_points)`,
243::CODE;;where `n_targets` is the number of targets (`n_tasks` for multi-output
244::CODE;;regression, and `n_classes` for multiclass classification), `n_instances`
245::CODE;;is the number of instances in `X`, and `n_points` is the number of points
246::CODE;;in the `grid`.
331::CODE;;Partial dependence of a feature (or a set of features) corresponds to
332::CODE;;the average response of an estimator for each possible value of the
333::CODE;;feature.
334::CODE;;Read more in
335::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_inspection_plot_partial_dependence.py`
336::CODE;;and the :ref:`User Guide <partial_dependence>`.
337::CODE;;.. warning::
338::CODE;;For :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier` and
339::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`, the
340::CODE;;`'recursion'` method (used by default) will not account for the `init`
341::CODE;;predictor of the boosting process. In practice, this will produce
342::CODE;;the same values as `'brute'` up to a constant offset in the target
343::CODE;;response, provided that `init` is a constant estimator (which is the
344::CODE;;default). However, if `init` is not a constant estimator, the
345::CODE;;partial dependence values are incorrect for `'recursion'` because the
346::CODE;;offset will be sample-dependent. It is preferable to use the `'brute'`
347::CODE;;method. Note that this only applies to
348::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier` and
349::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`, not to
350::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier` and
351::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`.
352::CODE;;Parameters
353::CODE;;----------
354::CODE;;estimator : BaseEstimator
355::CODE;;A fitted estimator object implementing :term:`predict`,
356::CODE;;:term:`predict_proba`, or :term:`decision_function`.
357::CODE;;Multioutput-multiclass classifiers are not supported.
358::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix or dataframe} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
359::CODE;;``X`` is used to generate a grid of values for the target
360::CODE;;``features`` (where the partial dependence will be evaluated), and
361::CODE;;also to generate values for the complement features when the
362::CODE;;`method` is 'brute'.
363::CODE;;features : array-like of {int, str, bool} or int or str
364::CODE;;The feature (e.g. `[0]`) or pair of interacting features
365::CODE;;(e.g. `[(0, 1)]`) for which the partial dependency should be computed.
366::CODE;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
367::CODE;;Sample weights are used to calculate weighted means when averaging the
368::CODE;;model output. If `None`, then samples are equally weighted. If
369::CODE;;`sample_weight` is not `None`, then `method` will be set to `'brute'`.
370::CODE;;Note that `sample_weight` is ignored for `kind='individual'`.
371::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
372::CODE;;categorical_features : array-like of shape (n_features,) or shape \
373::CODE;;(n_categorical_features,), dtype={bool, int, str}, default=None
374::CODE;;Indicates the categorical features.
375::CODE;;- `None`: no feature will be considered categorical;
376::CODE;;- boolean array-like: boolean mask of shape `(n_features,)`
377::CODE;;indicating which features are categorical. Thus, this array has
378::CODE;;the same shape has `X.shape[1]`;
379::CODE;;- integer or string array-like: integer indices or strings
380::CODE;;indicating categorical features.
381::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
382::CODE;;feature_names : array-like of shape (n_features,), dtype=str, default=None
383::CODE;;Name of each feature; `feature_names[i]` holds the name of the feature
384::CODE;;with index `i`.
385::CODE;;By default, the name of the feature corresponds to their numerical
386::CODE;;index for NumPy array and their column name for pandas dataframe.
387::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
388::CODE;;response_method : {'auto', 'predict_proba', 'decision_function'}, \
389::CODE;;default='auto'
390::CODE;;Specifies whether to use :term:`predict_proba` or
391::CODE;;:term:`decision_function` as the target response. For regressors
392::CODE;;this parameter is ignored and the response is always the output of
393::CODE;;:term:`predict`. By default, :term:`predict_proba` is tried first
394::CODE;;and we revert to :term:`decision_function` if it doesn't exist. If
395::CODE;;``method`` is 'recursion', the response is always the output of
396::CODE;;:term:`decision_function`.
397::CODE;;percentiles : tuple of float, default=(0.05, 0.95)
398::CODE;;The lower and upper percentile used to create the extreme values
399::CODE;;for the grid. Must be in [0, 1].
400::CODE;;This parameter is overridden by `custom_values` if that parameter is set.
401::CODE;;grid_resolution : int, default=100
402::CODE;;The number of equally spaced points on the grid, for each target
403::CODE;;feature.
404::CODE;;This parameter is overridden by `custom_values` if that parameter is set.
405::CODE;;custom_values : dict
406::CODE;;A dictionary mapping the index of an element of `features` to an array
407::CODE;;of values where the partial dependence should be calculated
408::CODE;;for that feature. Setting a range of values for a feature overrides
409::CODE;;`grid_resolution` and `percentiles`.
410::CODE;;See :ref:`how to use partial_dependence
411::CODE;;<plt_partial_dependence_custom_values>` for an example of how this parameter can
412::CODE;;be used.
413::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.7
414::CODE;;method : {'auto', 'recursion', 'brute'}, default='auto'
415::CODE;;The method used to calculate the averaged predictions:
416::CODE;;- `'recursion'` is only supported for some tree-based estimators
417::CODE;;(namely
418::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier`,
419::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`,
420::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier`,
421::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`,
422::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeRegressor`,
423::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor`,
424::CODE;;) when `kind='average'`.
425::CODE;;This is more efficient in terms of speed.
426::CODE;;With this method, the target response of a
427::CODE;;classifier is always the decision function, not the predicted
428::CODE;;probabilities. Since the `'recursion'` method implicitly computes
429::CODE;;the average of the Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) by
430::CODE;;design, it is not compatible with ICE and thus `kind` must be
431::CODE;;`'average'`.
432::CODE;;- `'brute'` is supported for any estimator, but is more
433::CODE;;computationally intensive.
434::CODE;;- `'auto'`: the `'recursion'` is used for estimators that support it,
435::CODE;;and `'brute'` is used otherwise. If `sample_weight` is not `None`,
436::CODE;;then `'brute'` is used regardless of the estimator.
437::CODE;;Please see :ref:`this note <pdp_method_differences>` for
438::CODE;;differences between the `'brute'` and `'recursion'` method.
439::CODE;;kind : {'average', 'individual', 'both'}, default='average'
440::CODE;;Whether to return the partial dependence averaged across all the
441::CODE;;samples in the dataset or one value per sample or both.
442::CODE;;See Returns below.
443::CODE;;Note that the fast `method='recursion'` option is only available for
444::CODE;;`kind='average'` and `sample_weights=None`. Computing individual
445::CODE;;dependencies and doing weighted averages requires using the slower
446::CODE;;`method='brute'`.
447::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
448::CODE;;Returns
449::CODE;;-------
450::CODE;;predictions : :class:`~sklearn.utils.Bunch`
451::CODE;;Dictionary-like object, with the following attributes.
452::CODE;;individual : ndarray of shape (n_outputs, n_instances, \
453::CODE;;len(values[0]), len(values[1]), ...)
454::CODE;;The predictions for all the points in the grid for all
455::CODE;;samples in X. This is also known as Individual
456::CODE;;Conditional Expectation (ICE).
457::CODE;;Only available when `kind='individual'` or `kind='both'`.
458::CODE;;average : ndarray of shape (n_outputs, len(values[0]), \
459::CODE;;len(values[1]), ...)
460::CODE;;The predictions for all the points in the grid, averaged
461::CODE;;over all samples in X (or over the training data if
462::CODE;;`method` is 'recursion').
463::CODE;;Only available when `kind='average'` or `kind='both'`.
464::CODE;;grid_values : seq of 1d ndarrays
465::CODE;;The values with which the grid has been created. The generated
466::CODE;;grid is a cartesian product of the arrays in `grid_values` where
467::CODE;;`len(grid_values) == len(features)`. The size of each array
468::CODE;;`grid_values[j]` is either `grid_resolution`, or the number of
469::CODE;;unique values in `X[:, j]`, whichever is smaller.
470::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
471::CODE;;`n_outputs` corresponds to the number of classes in a multi-class
472::CODE;;setting, or to the number of tasks for multi-output regression.
473::CODE;;For classical regression and binary classification `n_outputs==1`.
474::CODE;;`n_values_feature_j` corresponds to the size `grid_values[j]`.
475::CODE;;See Also
476::CODE;;--------
477::CODE;;PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator : Plot Partial Dependence.
478::CODE;;PartialDependenceDisplay : Partial Dependence visualization.
479::CODE;;Examples
480::CODE;;--------
481::CODE;;>>> X = [[0, 0, 2], [1, 0, 0]]
482::CODE;;>>> y = [0, 1]
483::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
484::CODE;;>>> gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X, y)
485::CODE;;>>> partial_dependence(gb, features=[0], X=X, percentiles=(0, 1),
487::CODE;;(array([[-4.52, 4.52]]), [array([ 0., 1.])])

33::CODE;;Implements Tensor Sketch, which approximates the feature map
34::CODE;;of the polynomial kernel::
35::CODE;;K(X, Y) = (gamma * <X, Y> + coef0)^degree
36::CODE;;by efficiently computing a Count Sketch of the outer product of a
37::CODE;;vector with itself using Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT). Read more in the
38::CODE;;:ref:`User Guide <polynomial_kernel_approx>`.
39::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
40::CODE;;Parameters
41::CODE;;----------
42::CODE;;gamma : float, default=1.0
43::CODE;;Parameter of the polynomial kernel whose feature map
44::CODE;;will be approximated.
45::CODE;;degree : int, default=2
46::CODE;;Degree of the polynomial kernel whose feature map
47::CODE;;will be approximated.
48::CODE;;coef0 : int, default=0
49::CODE;;Constant term of the polynomial kernel whose feature map
50::CODE;;will be approximated.
51::CODE;;n_components : int, default=100
52::CODE;;Dimensionality of the output feature space. Usually, `n_components`
53::CODE;;should be greater than the number of features in input samples in
54::CODE;;order to achieve good performance. The optimal score / run time
55::CODE;;balance is typically achieved around `n_components` = 10 * `n_features`,
56::CODE;;but this depends on the specific dataset being used.
57::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
58::CODE;;Determines random number generation for indexHash and bitHash
59::CODE;;initialization. Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple
60::CODE;;function calls. See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
61::CODE;;Attributes
62::CODE;;----------
63::CODE;;indexHash_ : ndarray of shape (degree, n_features), dtype=int64
64::CODE;;Array of indexes in range [0, n_components) used to represent
65::CODE;;the 2-wise independent hash functions for Count Sketch computation.
66::CODE;;bitHash_ : ndarray of shape (degree, n_features), dtype=float32
67::CODE;;Array with random entries in {+1, -1}, used to represent
68::CODE;;the 2-wise independent hash functions for Count Sketch computation.
69::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
70::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
71::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
72::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
73::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
74::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
75::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
76::CODE;;See Also
77::CODE;;--------
78::CODE;;AdditiveChi2Sampler : Approximate feature map for additive chi2 kernel.
79::CODE;;Nystroem : Approximate a kernel map using a subset of the training data.
80::CODE;;RBFSampler : Approximate a RBF kernel feature map using random Fourier
81::CODE;;features.
82::CODE;;SkewedChi2Sampler : Approximate feature map for "skewed chi-squared" kernel.
83::CODE;;sklearn.metrics.pairwise.kernel_metrics : List of built-in kernels.

471::CODE;;Uses sampling the fourier transform of the kernel characteristic
472::CODE;;at regular intervals.
473::CODE;;Since the kernel that is to be approximated is additive, the components of
474::CODE;;the input vectors can be treated separately. Each entry in the original
475::CODE;;space is transformed into 2*sample_steps-1 features, where sample_steps is
476::CODE;;a parameter of the method. Typical values of sample_steps include 1, 2 and
477::CODE;;3.
478::CODE;;Optimal choices for the sampling interval for certain data ranges can be
479::CODE;;computed (see the reference). The default values should be reasonable.
480::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <additive_chi_kernel_approx>`.
481::CODE;;Parameters
482::CODE;;----------
483::CODE;;sample_steps : int, default=2
484::CODE;;Gives the number of (complex) sampling points.

678::CODE;;Constructs an approximate feature map for an arbitrary kernel

853::CODE;;Computes an approximate feature map using the kernel
854::CODE;;between some training points and X.

860::CODE;;-------
861::CODE;;X_transformed : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components)
862::CODE;;Transformed data.
17::CODE;;Kernel ridge regression (KRR) combines ridge regression (linear least
18::CODE;;squares with l2-norm regularization) with the kernel trick. It thus
19::CODE;;learns a linear function in the space induced by the respective kernel and
20::CODE;;the data. For non-linear kernels, this corresponds to a non-linear
21::CODE;;function in the original space.
22::CODE;;The form of the model learned by KRR is identical to support vector
23::CODE;;regression (SVR). However, different loss functions are used: KRR uses
24::CODE;;squared error loss while support vector regression uses epsilon-insensitive
25::CODE;;loss, both combined with l2 regularization. In contrast to SVR, fitting a
26::CODE;;KRR model can be done in closed-form and is typically faster for
27::CODE;;medium-sized datasets. On the other hand, the learned model is non-sparse
28::CODE;;and thus slower than SVR, which learns a sparse model for epsilon > 0, at
29::CODE;;prediction-time.
30::CODE;;This estimator has built-in support for multi-variate regression
31::CODE;;(i.e., when y is a 2d-array of shape [n_samples, n_targets]).
32::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <kernel_ridge>`.
33::CODE;;Parameters
34::CODE;;----------
35::CODE;;alpha : float or array-like of shape (n_targets,), default=1.0
36::CODE;;Regularization strength; must be a positive float. Regularization
37::CODE;;improves the conditioning of the problem and reduces the variance of
38::CODE;;the estimates. Larger values specify stronger regularization.
39::CODE;;Alpha corresponds to ``1 / (2C)`` in other linear models such as
40::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` or
41::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC`. If an array is passed, penalties are
42::CODE;;assumed to be specific to the targets. Hence they must correspond in
43::CODE;;number. See :ref:`ridge_regression` for formula.
44::CODE;;kernel : str or callable, default="linear"
45::CODE;;Kernel mapping used internally. This parameter is directly passed to
46::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise.pairwise_kernels`.
47::CODE;;If `kernel` is a string, it must be one of the metrics
48::CODE;;in `pairwise.PAIRWISE_KERNEL_FUNCTIONS` or "precomputed".
49::CODE;;If `kernel` is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a kernel matrix.
50::CODE;;Alternatively, if `kernel` is a callable function, it is called on
51::CODE;;each pair of instances (rows) and the resulting value recorded. The
52::CODE;;callable should take two rows from X as input and return the
53::CODE;;corresponding kernel value as a single number. This means that
54::CODE;;callables from :mod:`sklearn.metrics.pairwise` are not allowed, as
55::CODE;;they operate on matrices, not single samples. Use the string
56::CODE;;identifying the kernel instead.
57::CODE;;gamma : float, default=None
58::CODE;;Gamma parameter for the RBF, laplacian, polynomial, exponential chi2
59::CODE;;and sigmoid kernels. Interpretation of the default value is left to
60::CODE;;the kernel; see the documentation for sklearn.metrics.pairwise.
61::CODE;;Ignored by other kernels.
62::CODE;;degree : float, default=3
63::CODE;;Degree of the polynomial kernel. Ignored by other kernels.
64::CODE;;coef0 : float, default=1
65::CODE;;Zero coefficient for polynomial and sigmoid kernels.
66::CODE;;Ignored by other kernels.
67::CODE;;kernel_params : dict, default=None
68::CODE;;Additional parameters (keyword arguments) for kernel function passed
69::CODE;;as callable object.
70::CODE;;Attributes
71::CODE;;----------
72::CODE;;dual_coef_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_targets)
73::CODE;;Representation of weight vector(s) in kernel space
74::CODE;;X_fit_ : {ndarray, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
75::CODE;;Training data, which is also required for prediction. If
76::CODE;;kernel == "precomputed" this is instead the precomputed
77::CODE;;training matrix, of shape (n_samples, n_samples).
78::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
79::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
80::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
81::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
82::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
83::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
84::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
85::CODE;;See Also

384::CODE;;Ordinary least squares Linear Regression.
385::CODE;;LinearRegression fits a linear model with coefficients w = (w1, ..., wp)
386::CODE;;to minimize the residual sum of squares between the observed targets in
387::CODE;;the dataset, and the targets predicted by the linear approximation.
388::CODE;;Parameters
389::CODE;;----------
390::CODE;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
391::CODE;;Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set
392::CODE;;to False, no intercept will be used in calculations
393::CODE;;(i.e. data is expected to be centered).
394::CODE;;copy_X : bool, default=True
395::CODE;;If True, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten.
396::CODE;;tol : float, default=1e-6
397::CODE;;The precision of the solution (`coef_`) is determined by `tol` which
398::CODE;;specifies a different convergence criterion for the `lsqr` solver.
399::CODE;;`tol` is set as `atol` and `btol` of :func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr` when
400::CODE;;fitting on sparse training data. This parameter has no effect when fitting
401::CODE;;on dense data.
402::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.7
403::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
404::CODE;;The number of jobs to use for the computation. This will only provide
405::CODE;;speedup in case of sufficiently large problems, that is if firstly
406::CODE;;`n_targets > 1` and secondly `X` is sparse or if `positive` is set
407::CODE;;to `True`. ``None`` means 1 unless in a
408::CODE;;:obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context. ``-1`` means using all
409::CODE;;processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>` for more details.
410::CODE;;positive : bool, default=False
411::CODE;;When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive. This
412::CODE;;option is only supported for dense arrays.
413::CODE;;For a comparison between a linear regression model with positive constraints
414::CODE;;on the regression coefficients and a linear regression without such constraints,
415::CODE;;see :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_nnls.py`.
416::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
417::CODE;;Attributes
418::CODE;;----------
419::CODE;;coef_ : array of shape (n_features, ) or (n_targets, n_features)
420::CODE;;Estimated coefficients for the linear regression problem.
421::CODE;;If multiple targets are passed during the fit (y 2D), this
422::CODE;;is a 2D array of shape (n_targets, n_features), while if only
423::CODE;;one target is passed, this is a 1D array of length n_features.
424::CODE;;rank_ : int
425::CODE;;Rank of matrix `X`. Only available when `X` is dense.
426::CODE;;singular_ : array of shape (min(X, y),)
427::CODE;;Singular values of `X`. Only available when `X` is dense.
428::CODE;;intercept_ : float or array of shape (n_targets,)
429::CODE;;Independent term in the linear model. Set to 0.0 if
430::CODE;;`fit_intercept = False`.
431::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
432::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
433::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
434::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
435::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
436::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
437::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
438::CODE;;See Also
439::CODE;;--------
440::CODE;;Ridge : Ridge regression addresses some of the
441::CODE;;problems of Ordinary Least Squares by imposing a penalty on the
442::CODE;;size of the coefficients with l2 regularization.
443::CODE;;Lasso : The Lasso is a linear model that estimates
444::CODE;;sparse coefficients with l1 regularization.
445::CODE;;ElasticNet : Elastic-Net is a linear regression
446::CODE;;model trained with both l1 and l2 -norm regularization of the
447::CODE;;coefficients.
448::CODE;;Notes
449::CODE;;-----
450::CODE;;From the implementation point of view, this is just plain Ordinary
451::CODE;;Least Squares (:func:`scipy.linalg.lstsq`) or Non Negative Least Squares
452::CODE;;(:func:`scipy.optimize.nnls`) wrapped as a predictor object.

333::CODE;;self, X, y, n_samples, n_features, XT_y, U, Vh, eigen_vals_, alpha_, lambda_
334::CODE;;):
340::CODE;;if n_samples > n_features:

342::CODE;;[Vh.T, Vh / (eigen_vals_ + lambda_ / alpha_)[:, np.newaxis], XT_y]
343::CODE;;)

352::CODE;;def _log_marginal_likelihood(

354::CODE;;):
384::CODE;;Fit the weights of a regression model, using an ARD prior. The weights of
385::CODE;;the regression model are assumed to be in Gaussian distributions.
386::CODE;;Also estimate the parameters lambda (precisions of the distributions of the
387::CODE;;weights) and alpha (precision of the distribution of the noise).
388::CODE;;The estimation is done by an iterative procedures (Evidence Maximization)
389::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <bayesian_regression>`.
390::CODE;;Parameters
391::CODE;;----------
392::CODE;;max_iter : int, default=300
393::CODE;;Maximum number of iterations.
394::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.3
395::CODE;;tol : float, default=1e-3
396::CODE;;Stop the algorithm if w has converged.
397::CODE;;alpha_1 : float, default=1e-6
398::CODE;;Hyper-parameter : shape parameter for the Gamma distribution prior
399::CODE;;over the alpha parameter.
400::CODE;;alpha_2 : float, default=1e-6
401::CODE;;Hyper-parameter : inverse scale parameter (rate parameter) for the
402::CODE;;Gamma distribution prior over the alpha parameter.
403::CODE;;lambda_1 : float, default=1e-6
404::CODE;;Hyper-parameter : shape parameter for the Gamma distribution prior
405::CODE;;over the lambda parameter.
406::CODE;;lambda_2 : float, default=1e-6
407::CODE;;Hyper-parameter : inverse scale parameter (rate parameter) for the
408::CODE;;Gamma distribution prior over the lambda parameter.
409::CODE;;compute_score : bool, default=False
410::CODE;;If True, compute the objective function at each step of the model.
411::CODE;;threshold_lambda : float, default=10 000
412::CODE;;Threshold for removing (pruning) weights with high precision from
413::CODE;;the computation.
414::CODE;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
415::CODE;;Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set
416::CODE;;to false, no intercept will be used in calculations
417::CODE;;(i.e. data is expected to be centered).
418::CODE;;copy_X : bool, default=True
419::CODE;;If True, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten.
420::CODE;;verbose : bool, default=False
421::CODE;;Verbose mode when fitting the model.
422::CODE;;Attributes
423::CODE;;----------
424::CODE;;coef_ : array-like of shape (n_features,)
425::CODE;;Coefficients of the regression model (mean of distribution)
426::CODE;;alpha_ : float
427::CODE;;estimated precision of the noise.
428::CODE;;lambda_ : array-like of shape (n_features,)
429::CODE;;estimated precisions of the weights.
430::CODE;;sigma_ : array-like of shape (n_features, n_features)
431::CODE;;estimated variance-covariance matrix of the weights
432::CODE;;scores_ : float
433::CODE;;if computed, value of the objective function (to be maximized)
434::CODE;;n_iter_ : int
435::CODE;;The actual number of iterations to reach the stopping criterion.
436::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
437::CODE;;intercept_ : float
438::CODE;;Independent term in decision function. Set to 0.0 if
439::CODE;;``fit_intercept = False``.
440::CODE;;X_offset_ : float
441::CODE;;If `fit_intercept=True`, offset subtracted for centering data to a
442::CODE;;zero mean. Set to np.zeros(n_features) otherwise.
443::CODE;;X_scale_ : float
444::CODE;;Set to np.ones(n_features).
445::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
446::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
447::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
448::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
449::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
450::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
451::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
452::CODE;;See Also
453::CODE;;--------
454::CODE;;BayesianRidge : Bayesian ridge regression.
455::CODE;;References
456::CODE;;----------
457::CODE;;D. J. C. MacKay, Bayesian nonlinear modeling for the prediction
458::CODE;;competition, ASHRAE Transactions, 1994.
459::CODE;;R. Salakhutdinov, Lecture notes on Statistical Machine Learning,
461::CODE;;Their beta is our ``self.alpha_``
462::CODE;;Their alpha is our ``self.lambda_``
463::CODE;;ARD is a little different than the slide: only dimensions/features for
464::CODE;;which ``self.lambda_ < self.threshold_lambda`` are kept and the rest are
465::CODE;;discarded.
466::CODE;;Examples
467::CODE;;--------
468::CODE;;>>> from sklearn import linear_model
469::CODE;;>>> clf = linear_model.ARDRegression()
470::CODE;;>>> clf.fit([[0,0], [1, 1], [2, 2]], [0, 1, 2])
471::CODE;;ARDRegression()
472::CODE;;>>> clf.predict([[1, 1]])
473::CODE;;array([1.])
474::CODE;;- :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_ard.py` demonstrates ARD
475::CODE;;Regression.
476::CODE;;- :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_lasso_and_elasticnet.py`
477::CODE;;showcases ARD Regression alongside Lasso and Elastic-Net for sparse,
478::CODE;;correlated signals, in the presence of noise.
522::CODE;;Iterative procedure to maximize the evidence
523::CODE;;Parameters
524::CODE;;----------
525::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
526::CODE;;Training vector, where `n_samples` is the number of samples and
527::CODE;;`n_features` is the number of features.
528::CODE;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
529::CODE;;Target values (integers). Will be cast to X's dtype if necessary.
530::CODE;;Returns
531::CODE;;-------
532::CODE;;self : object
533::CODE;;Fitted estimator.
653::CODE;;In addition to the mean of the predictive distribution, also its
654::CODE;;standard deviation can be returned.
655::CODE;;Parameters
656::CODE;;----------
657::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
658::CODE;;Samples.

81::CODE;;def _alpha_grid(
82::CODE;;X,
83::CODE;;y,
84::CODE;;Xy=None,
85::CODE;;l1_ratio=1.0,
86::CODE;;fit_intercept=True,
87::CODE;;eps=1e-3,
88::CODE;;n_alphas=100,
89::CODE;;sample_weight=None,
90::CODE;;):
123::CODE;;if l1_ratio == 0:
124::CODE;;raise ValueError(

127::CODE;;"your estimator with the appropriate `alphas=` "

130::CODE;;if Xy is not None:
131::CODE;;Xyw = Xy
132::CODE;;else:

135::CODE;;y = y - np.average(y, axis=0, weights=sample_weight)
136::CODE;;if sparse.issparse(X):
137::CODE;;X_mean, _ = mean_variance_axis(X, axis=0, weights=sample_weight)
138::CODE;;else:
139::CODE;;X_mean = np.average(X, axis=0, weights=sample_weight)
140::CODE;;if sample_weight is None:

142::CODE;;else:

165::CODE;;return np.full(n_alphas, np.finfo(np.float64).resolution)
