65::CODE;;def _generalized_average(U, V, average_method):
93::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <contingency_matrix>`.
94::CODE;;Parameters
95::CODE;;----------
96::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
97::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
98::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
99::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
100::CODE;;eps : float, default=None
101::CODE;;If a float, that value is added to all values in the contingency
102::CODE;;matrix. This helps to stop NaN propagation.
103::CODE;;If ``None``, nothing is adjusted.
104::CODE;;sparse : bool, default=False
105::CODE;;If `True`, return a sparse CSR contingency matrix. If `eps` is not
106::CODE;;`None` and `sparse` is `True` will raise ValueError.
107::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
108::CODE;;dtype : numeric type, default=np.int64
109::CODE;;Output dtype. Ignored if `eps` is not `None`.
110::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
111::CODE;;Returns
112::CODE;;-------
113::CODE;;contingency : {array-like, sparse}, shape=[n_classes_true, n_classes_pred]
114::CODE;;Matrix :math:`C` such that :math:`C_{i, j}` is the number of samples in
115::CODE;;true class :math:`i` and in predicted class :math:`j`. If
116::CODE;;``eps is None``, the dtype of this array will be integer unless set
117::CODE;;otherwise with the ``dtype`` argument. If ``eps`` is given, the dtype
118::CODE;;will be float.
119::CODE;;Will be a ``sklearn.sparse.csr_matrix`` if ``sparse=True``.
120::CODE;;Examples
121::CODE;;--------
122::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import contingency_matrix
123::CODE;;>>> labels_true = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
124::CODE;;>>> labels_pred = [1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 2]
125::CODE;;>>> contingency_matrix(labels_true, labels_pred)
126::CODE;;array([[1, 1, 0],
127::CODE;;[0, 1, 1],
128::CODE;;[1, 0, 1]])
163::CODE;;The pair confusion matrix :math:`C` computes a 2 by 2 similarity matrix
164::CODE;;between two clusterings by considering all pairs of samples and counting
165::CODE;;pairs that are assigned into the same or into different clusters under
166::CODE;;the true and predicted clusterings [1]_.
167::CODE;;Considering a pair of samples that is clustered together a positive pair,
168::CODE;;then as in binary classification the count of true negatives is
169::CODE;;:math:`C_{00}`, false negatives is :math:`C_{10}`, true positives is
170::CODE;;:math:`C_{11}` and false positives is :math:`C_{01}`.
171::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <pair_confusion_matrix>`.
172::CODE;;Parameters
173::CODE;;----------
174::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=integral
175::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
176::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=integral
177::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
178::CODE;;Returns
179::CODE;;-------
180::CODE;;C : ndarray of shape (2, 2), dtype=np.int64
181::CODE;;The contingency matrix.
182::CODE;;See Also
183::CODE;;--------
184::CODE;;sklearn.metrics.rand_score : Rand Score.
185::CODE;;sklearn.metrics.adjusted_rand_score : Adjusted Rand Score.
186::CODE;;sklearn.metrics.adjusted_mutual_info_score : Adjusted Mutual Information.
187::CODE;;References
188::CODE;;----------
189::CODE;;.. [1] :doi:`Hubert, L., Arabie, P. "Comparing partitions."
190::CODE;;Journal of Classification 2, 193–218 (1985).
191::CODE;;<10.1007/BF01908075>`
192::CODE;;Examples
193::CODE;;--------
194::CODE;;Perfectly matching labelings have all non-zero entries on the
195::CODE;;diagonal regardless of actual label values:
196::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import pair_confusion_matrix
197::CODE;;>>> pair_confusion_matrix([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
198::CODE;;array([[8, 0],
199::CODE;;[0, 4]]...
200::CODE;;Labelings that assign all classes members to the same clusters
201::CODE;;are complete but may be not always pure, hence penalized, and
202::CODE;;have some off-diagonal non-zero entries:
203::CODE;;>>> pair_confusion_matrix([0, 0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 1, 1])
204::CODE;;array([[8, 2],
205::CODE;;[0, 2]]...
206::CODE;;Note that the matrix is not symmetric.
232::CODE;;The Rand Index computes a similarity measure between two clusterings
233::CODE;;by considering all pairs of samples and counting pairs that are
234::CODE;;assigned in the same or different clusters in the predicted and
235::CODE;;true clusterings [1]_ [2]_.
236::CODE;;The raw RI score [3]_ is:
237::CODE;;.. code-block:: text
238::CODE;;RI = (number of agreeing pairs) / (number of pairs)
239::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <rand_score>`.
240::CODE;;Parameters
241::CODE;;----------
242::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=integral
243::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
244::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=integral
245::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
246::CODE;;Returns
247::CODE;;-------
248::CODE;;RI : float
249::CODE;;Similarity score between 0.0 and 1.0, inclusive, 1.0 stands for
250::CODE;;perfect match.
251::CODE;;See Also
252::CODE;;--------
253::CODE;;adjusted_rand_score: Adjusted Rand Score.
254::CODE;;adjusted_mutual_info_score: Adjusted Mutual Information.
255::CODE;;References
256::CODE;;----------
257::CODE;;.. [1] :doi:`Hubert, L., Arabie, P. "Comparing partitions."
258::CODE;;Journal of Classification 2, 193–218 (1985).
259::CODE;;<10.1007/BF01908075>`.
260::CODE;;.. [2] `Wikipedia: Simple Matching Coefficient
261::CODE;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_matching_coefficient>`_
262::CODE;;.. [3] `Wikipedia: Rand Index <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rand_index>`_
263::CODE;;Examples
264::CODE;;--------
265::CODE;;Perfectly matching labelings have a score of 1 even
266::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import rand_score
267::CODE;;>>> rand_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
268::CODE;;1.0
269::CODE;;Labelings that assign all classes members to the same clusters
270::CODE;;are complete but may not always be pure, hence penalized:
271::CODE;;>>> rand_score([0, 0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 1, 1])
272::CODE;;0.83
292::CODE;;The Rand Index computes a similarity measure between two clusterings
293::CODE;;by considering all pairs of samples and counting pairs that are
294::CODE;;assigned in the same or different clusters in the predicted and
295::CODE;;true clusterings.
296::CODE;;The raw RI score is then "adjusted for chance" into the ARI score
297::CODE;;using the following scheme::
298::CODE;;ARI = (RI - Expected_RI) / (max(RI) - Expected_RI)
299::CODE;;The adjusted Rand index is thus ensured to have a value close to
300::CODE;;0.0 for random labeling independently of the number of clusters and
301::CODE;;samples and exactly 1.0 when the clusterings are identical (up to
302::CODE;;a permutation). The adjusted Rand index is bounded below by -0.5 for
303::CODE;;especially discordant clusterings.
304::CODE;;ARI is a symmetric measure::
305::CODE;;adjusted_rand_score(a, b) == adjusted_rand_score(b, a)
306::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <adjusted_rand_score>`.
307::CODE;;Parameters
308::CODE;;----------
309::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=int
310::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
311::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=int
312::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
313::CODE;;Returns
314::CODE;;-------
315::CODE;;ARI : float
316::CODE;;Similarity score between -0.5 and 1.0. Random labelings have an ARI
317::CODE;;close to 0.0. 1.0 stands for perfect match.
318::CODE;;See Also
319::CODE;;--------
320::CODE;;adjusted_mutual_info_score : Adjusted Mutual Information.
321::CODE;;References
322::CODE;;----------
323::CODE;;.. [Hubert1985] L. Hubert and P. Arabie, Comparing Partitions,
324::CODE;;Journal of Classification 1985
325::CODE;;https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2FBF01908075
326::CODE;;.. [Steinley2004] D. Steinley, Properties of the Hubert-Arabie
327::CODE;;adjusted Rand index, Psychological Methods 2004
329::CODE;;.. [Chacon] :doi:`Minimum adjusted Rand index for two clusterings of a given size,
330::CODE;;2022, J. E. Chacón and A. I. Rastrojo <10.1007/s11634-022-00491-w>`
331::CODE;;Examples
332::CODE;;--------
333::CODE;;Perfectly matching labelings have a score of 1 even
334::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import adjusted_rand_score
335::CODE;;>>> adjusted_rand_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1])
336::CODE;;1.0
337::CODE;;>>> adjusted_rand_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
338::CODE;;1.0
339::CODE;;Labelings that assign all classes members to the same clusters
340::CODE;;are complete but may not always be pure, hence penalized::
341::CODE;;>>> adjusted_rand_score([0, 0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 1, 1])
342::CODE;;0.57
343::CODE;;ARI is symmetric, so labelings that have pure clusters with members
344::CODE;;coming from the same classes but unnecessary splits are penalized::
345::CODE;;>>> adjusted_rand_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 2])
346::CODE;;0.57
347::CODE;;If classes members are completely split across different clusters, the
348::CODE;;assignment is totally incomplete, hence the ARI is very low::
349::CODE;;>>> adjusted_rand_score([0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3])
350::CODE;;0.0
351::CODE;;ARI may take a negative value for especially discordant labelings that
352::CODE;;are a worse choice than the expected value of random labels::
353::CODE;;>>> adjusted_rand_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0, 1])
354::CODE;;-0.5
355::CODE;;See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_adjusted_for_chance_measures.py`
356::CODE;;for a more detailed example.
375::CODE;;Those metrics are based on normalized conditional entropy measures of
376::CODE;;the clustering labeling to evaluate given the knowledge of a Ground
377::CODE;;Truth class labels of the same samples.
378::CODE;;A clustering result satisfies homogeneity if all of its clusters
379::CODE;;contain only data points which are members of a single class.
380::CODE;;A clustering result satisfies completeness if all the data points
381::CODE;;that are members of a given class are elements of the same cluster.
382::CODE;;Both scores have positive values between 0.0 and 1.0, larger values
383::CODE;;being desirable.
384::CODE;;Those 3 metrics are independent of the absolute values of the labels:
385::CODE;;a permutation of the class or cluster label values won't change the
386::CODE;;score values in any way.
387::CODE;;V-Measure is furthermore symmetric: swapping ``labels_true`` and
388::CODE;;``label_pred`` will give the same score. This does not hold for
389::CODE;;homogeneity and completeness. V-Measure is identical to
390::CODE;;:func:`normalized_mutual_info_score` with the arithmetic averaging
391::CODE;;method.
392::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <homogeneity_completeness>`.
393::CODE;;Parameters
394::CODE;;----------
395::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
396::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
397::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
398::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
399::CODE;;beta : float, default=1.0
400::CODE;;Ratio of weight attributed to ``homogeneity`` vs ``completeness``.
401::CODE;;If ``beta`` is greater than 1, ``completeness`` is weighted more
402::CODE;;strongly in the calculation. If ``beta`` is less than 1,
403::CODE;;``homogeneity`` is weighted more strongly.
404::CODE;;Returns
405::CODE;;-------
406::CODE;;homogeneity : float
407::CODE;;Score between 0.0 and 1.0. 1.0 stands for perfectly homogeneous labeling.
408::CODE;;completeness : float
409::CODE;;Score between 0.0 and 1.0. 1.0 stands for perfectly complete labeling.
410::CODE;;v_measure : float
411::CODE;;Harmonic mean of the first two.
412::CODE;;See Also
413::CODE;;--------
414::CODE;;homogeneity_score : Homogeneity metric of cluster labeling.
415::CODE;;completeness_score : Completeness metric of cluster labeling.
416::CODE;;v_measure_score : V-Measure (NMI with arithmetic mean option).
417::CODE;;Examples
418::CODE;;--------
419::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics import homogeneity_completeness_v_measure
420::CODE;;>>> y_true, y_pred = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2], [0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2]
421::CODE;;>>> homogeneity_completeness_v_measure(y_true, y_pred)
422::CODE;;(0.71, 0.771, 0.74)
452::CODE;;A clustering result satisfies homogeneity if all of its clusters
453::CODE;;contain only data points which are members of a single class.
454::CODE;;This metric is independent of the absolute values of the labels:
455::CODE;;a permutation of the class or cluster label values won't change the
456::CODE;;score value in any way.
457::CODE;;This metric is not symmetric: switching ``label_true`` with ``label_pred``
458::CODE;;will return the :func:`completeness_score` which will be different in
459::CODE;;general.
460::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <homogeneity_completeness>`.
461::CODE;;Parameters
462::CODE;;----------
463::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
464::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
465::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
466::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
467::CODE;;Returns
468::CODE;;-------
469::CODE;;homogeneity : float
470::CODE;;Score between 0.0 and 1.0. 1.0 stands for perfectly homogeneous labeling.
471::CODE;;See Also
472::CODE;;--------
473::CODE;;completeness_score : Completeness metric of cluster labeling.
474::CODE;;v_measure_score : V-Measure (NMI with arithmetic mean option).
475::CODE;;References
476::CODE;;----------
477::CODE;;.. [1] `Andrew Rosenberg and Julia Hirschberg, 2007. V-Measure: A
478::CODE;;conditional entropy-based external cluster evaluation measure
479::CODE;;<https://aclweb.org/anthology/D/D07/D07-1043.pdf>`_
480::CODE;;Examples
481::CODE;;--------
482::CODE;;Perfect labelings are homogeneous::
483::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import homogeneity_score
484::CODE;;>>> homogeneity_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
485::CODE;;1.0
486::CODE;;Non-perfect labelings that further split classes into more clusters can be
487::CODE;;perfectly homogeneous::
488::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % homogeneity_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 2]))
489::CODE;;1.000000
490::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % homogeneity_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 2, 3]))
491::CODE;;1.000000
492::CODE;;Clusters that include samples from different classes do not make for an
493::CODE;;homogeneous labeling::
494::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % homogeneity_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0, 1]))
495::CODE;;0.0...
496::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % homogeneity_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 0]))
497::CODE;;0.0...
509::CODE;;A clustering result satisfies completeness if all the data points
510::CODE;;that are members of a given class are elements of the same cluster.
511::CODE;;This metric is independent of the absolute values of the labels:
512::CODE;;a permutation of the class or cluster label values won't change the
513::CODE;;score value in any way.
514::CODE;;This metric is not symmetric: switching ``label_true`` with ``label_pred``
515::CODE;;will return the :func:`homogeneity_score` which will be different in
516::CODE;;general.
517::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <homogeneity_completeness>`.
518::CODE;;Parameters
519::CODE;;----------
520::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
521::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
522::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
523::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
524::CODE;;Returns
525::CODE;;-------
526::CODE;;completeness : float
527::CODE;;Score between 0.0 and 1.0. 1.0 stands for perfectly complete labeling.
528::CODE;;See Also
529::CODE;;--------
530::CODE;;homogeneity_score : Homogeneity metric of cluster labeling.
531::CODE;;v_measure_score : V-Measure (NMI with arithmetic mean option).
532::CODE;;References
533::CODE;;----------
534::CODE;;.. [1] `Andrew Rosenberg and Julia Hirschberg, 2007. V-Measure: A
535::CODE;;conditional entropy-based external cluster evaluation measure
536::CODE;;<https://aclweb.org/anthology/D/D07/D07-1043.pdf>`_
537::CODE;;Examples
538::CODE;;--------
539::CODE;;Perfect labelings are complete::
540::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import completeness_score
541::CODE;;>>> completeness_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
542::CODE;;1.0
543::CODE;;Non-perfect labelings that assign all classes members to the same clusters
544::CODE;;are still complete::
545::CODE;;>>> print(completeness_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 0]))
546::CODE;;1.0
547::CODE;;>>> print(completeness_score([0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 1, 1]))
548::CODE;;0.999
549::CODE;;If classes members are split across different clusters, the
550::CODE;;assignment cannot be complete::
551::CODE;;>>> print(completeness_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0, 1]))
552::CODE;;0.0
553::CODE;;>>> print(completeness_score([0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3]))
554::CODE;;0.0
567::CODE;;This score is identical to :func:`normalized_mutual_info_score` with
568::CODE;;the ``'arithmetic'`` option for averaging.
569::CODE;;The V-measure is the harmonic mean between homogeneity and completeness::
570::CODE;;v = (1 + beta) * homogeneity * completeness
571::CODE;;/ (beta * homogeneity + completeness)
572::CODE;;This metric is independent of the absolute values of the labels:
573::CODE;;a permutation of the class or cluster label values won't change the
574::CODE;;score value in any way.
575::CODE;;This metric is furthermore symmetric: switching ``label_true`` with
576::CODE;;``label_pred`` will return the same score value. This can be useful to
577::CODE;;measure the agreement of two independent label assignments strategies
578::CODE;;on the same dataset when the real ground truth is not known.
579::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <homogeneity_completeness>`.
580::CODE;;Parameters
581::CODE;;----------
582::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
583::CODE;;Ground truth class labels to be used as a reference.
584::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
585::CODE;;Cluster labels to evaluate.
586::CODE;;beta : float, default=1.0
587::CODE;;Ratio of weight attributed to ``homogeneity`` vs ``completeness``.
588::CODE;;If ``beta`` is greater than 1, ``completeness`` is weighted more
589::CODE;;strongly in the calculation. If ``beta`` is less than 1,
590::CODE;;``homogeneity`` is weighted more strongly.
591::CODE;;Returns
592::CODE;;-------
593::CODE;;v_measure : float
594::CODE;;Score between 0.0 and 1.0. 1.0 stands for perfectly complete labeling.
595::CODE;;See Also
596::CODE;;--------
597::CODE;;homogeneity_score : Homogeneity metric of cluster labeling.
598::CODE;;completeness_score : Completeness metric of cluster labeling.
599::CODE;;normalized_mutual_info_score : Normalized Mutual Information.
600::CODE;;References
601::CODE;;----------
602::CODE;;.. [1] `Andrew Rosenberg and Julia Hirschberg, 2007. V-Measure: A
603::CODE;;conditional entropy-based external cluster evaluation measure
604::CODE;;<https://aclweb.org/anthology/D/D07/D07-1043.pdf>`_
605::CODE;;Examples
606::CODE;;--------
607::CODE;;Perfect labelings are both homogeneous and complete, hence have score 1.0::
608::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import v_measure_score
609::CODE;;>>> v_measure_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1])
610::CODE;;1.0
611::CODE;;>>> v_measure_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
612::CODE;;1.0
613::CODE;;Labelings that assign all classes members to the same clusters
614::CODE;;are complete but not homogeneous, hence penalized::
615::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % v_measure_score([0, 0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 1, 1]))
616::CODE;;0.8
617::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % v_measure_score([0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 1, 1]))
618::CODE;;0.67
619::CODE;;Labelings that have pure clusters with members coming from the same
620::CODE;;classes are homogeneous but un-necessary splits harm completeness
621::CODE;;and thus penalize V-measure as well::
622::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % v_measure_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 2]))
623::CODE;;0.8
624::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % v_measure_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 2, 3]))
625::CODE;;0.67
626::CODE;;If classes members are completely split across different clusters,
627::CODE;;the assignment is totally incomplete, hence the V-Measure is null::
628::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % v_measure_score([0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3]))
629::CODE;;0.0
630::CODE;;Clusters that include samples from totally different classes totally
631::CODE;;destroy the homogeneity of the labeling, hence::
632::CODE;;>>> print("%.6f" % v_measure_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 0]))
633::CODE;;0.0
646::CODE;;The Mutual Information is a measure of the similarity between two labels
647::CODE;;of the same data. Where :math:`|U_i|` is the number of the samples
648::CODE;;in cluster :math:`U_i` and :math:`|V_j|` is the number of the
649::CODE;;samples in cluster :math:`V_j`, the Mutual Information
650::CODE;;between clusterings :math:`U` and :math:`V` is given as:
651::CODE;;.. math::
652::CODE;;MI(U,V)=\\sum_{i=1}^{|U|} \\sum_{j=1}^{|V|} \\frac{|U_i\\cap V_j|}{N}
653::CODE;;\\log\\frac{N|U_i \\cap V_j|}{|U_i||V_j|}
654::CODE;;This metric is independent of the absolute values of the labels:
655::CODE;;a permutation of the class or cluster label values won't change the
656::CODE;;score value in any way.
657::CODE;;This metric is furthermore symmetric: switching :math:`U` (i.e
658::CODE;;``label_true``) with :math:`V` (i.e. ``label_pred``) will return the
659::CODE;;same score value. This can be useful to measure the agreement of two
660::CODE;;independent label assignments strategies on the same dataset when the
661::CODE;;real ground truth is not known.
662::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <mutual_info_score>`.
663::CODE;;Parameters
664::CODE;;----------
665::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=integral
666::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets, called :math:`U` in
667::CODE;;the above formula.
668::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=integral
669::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets, called :math:`V` in
670::CODE;;the above formula.
671::CODE;;contingency : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape \
672::CODE;;(n_classes_true, n_classes_pred), default=None
673::CODE;;A contingency matrix given by the
674::CODE;;:func:`~sklearn.metrics.cluster.contingency_matrix` function. If value
675::CODE;;is ``None``, it will be computed, otherwise the given value is used,
676::CODE;;with ``labels_true`` and ``labels_pred`` ignored.
677::CODE;;Returns
678::CODE;;-------
679::CODE;;mi : float
680::CODE;;Mutual information, a non-negative value, measured in nats using the
681::CODE;;natural logarithm.
682::CODE;;See Also
683::CODE;;--------
684::CODE;;adjusted_mutual_info_score : Adjusted against chance Mutual Information.
685::CODE;;normalized_mutual_info_score : Normalized Mutual Information.
686::CODE;;Notes
687::CODE;;-----
688::CODE;;The logarithm used is the natural logarithm (base-e).
689::CODE;;Examples
690::CODE;;--------
691::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics import mutual_info_score
692::CODE;;>>> labels_true = [0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0]
693::CODE;;>>> labels_pred = [0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1]
694::CODE;;>>> mutual_info_score(labels_true, labels_pred)
695::CODE;;0.0566
745::CODE;;Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI) is an adjustment of the Mutual
746::CODE;;Information (MI) score to account for chance. It accounts for the fact that
747::CODE;;the MI is generally higher for two clusterings with a larger number of
748::CODE;;clusters, regardless of whether there is actually more information shared.
749::CODE;;For two clusterings :math:`U` and :math:`V`, the AMI is given as::
750::CODE;;AMI(U, V) = [MI(U, V) - E(MI(U, V))] / [avg(H(U), H(V)) - E(MI(U, V))]
751::CODE;;This metric is independent of the absolute values of the labels:
752::CODE;;a permutation of the class or cluster label values won't change the
753::CODE;;score value in any way.
754::CODE;;This metric is furthermore symmetric: switching :math:`U` (``label_true``)
755::CODE;;with :math:`V` (``labels_pred``) will return the same score value. This can
756::CODE;;be useful to measure the agreement of two independent label assignments
757::CODE;;strategies on the same dataset when the real ground truth is not known.
758::CODE;;Be mindful that this function is an order of magnitude slower than other
759::CODE;;metrics, such as the Adjusted Rand Index.
760::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <mutual_info_score>`.
761::CODE;;Parameters
762::CODE;;----------
763::CODE;;labels_true : int array-like of shape (n_samples,)
764::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets, called :math:`U` in
765::CODE;;the above formula.
766::CODE;;labels_pred : int array-like of shape (n_samples,)
767::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets, called :math:`V` in
768::CODE;;the above formula.
769::CODE;;average_method : {'min', 'geometric', 'arithmetic', 'max'}, default='arithmetic'
770::CODE;;How to compute the normalizer in the denominator.
771::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
772::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.22
773::CODE;;The default value of ``average_method`` changed from 'max' to
774::CODE;;'arithmetic'.
775::CODE;;Returns
776::CODE;;-------
777::CODE;;ami: float (upperlimited by 1.0)
778::CODE;;The AMI returns a value of 1 when the two partitions are identical
779::CODE;;(ie perfectly matched). Random partitions (independent labellings) have
780::CODE;;an expected AMI around 0 on average hence can be negative. The value is
781::CODE;;in adjusted nats (based on the natural logarithm).
782::CODE;;See Also
783::CODE;;--------
784::CODE;;adjusted_rand_score : Adjusted Rand Index.
785::CODE;;mutual_info_score : Mutual Information (not adjusted for chance).
786::CODE;;References
787::CODE;;----------
788::CODE;;.. [1] `Vinh, Epps, and Bailey, (2010). Information Theoretic Measures for
789::CODE;;Clusterings Comparison: Variants, Properties, Normalization and
790::CODE;;Correction for Chance, JMLR
791::CODE;;<http://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume11/vinh10a/vinh10a.pdf>`_
792::CODE;;.. [2] `Wikipedia entry for the Adjusted Mutual Information
793::CODE;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjusted_Mutual_Information>`_
794::CODE;;Examples
795::CODE;;--------
796::CODE;;Perfect labelings are both homogeneous and complete, hence have
797::CODE;;score 1.0::
798::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import adjusted_mutual_info_score
799::CODE;;>>> adjusted_mutual_info_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1])
800::CODE;;1.0
801::CODE;;>>> adjusted_mutual_info_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
802::CODE;;1.0
803::CODE;;If classes members are completely split across different clusters,
804::CODE;;the assignment is totally in-complete, hence the AMI is null::
805::CODE;;>>> adjusted_mutual_info_score([0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3])
806::CODE;;0.0
859::CODE;;Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) is a normalization of the Mutual
860::CODE;;Information (MI) score to scale the results between 0 (no mutual
861::CODE;;information) and 1 (perfect correlation). In this function, mutual
862::CODE;;information is normalized by some generalized mean of ``H(labels_true)``
863::CODE;;and ``H(labels_pred))``, defined by the `average_method`.
864::CODE;;This measure is not adjusted for chance. Therefore
865::CODE;;:func:`adjusted_mutual_info_score` might be preferred.
866::CODE;;This metric is independent of the absolute values of the labels:
867::CODE;;a permutation of the class or cluster label values won't change the
868::CODE;;score value in any way.
869::CODE;;This metric is furthermore symmetric: switching ``label_true`` with
870::CODE;;``label_pred`` will return the same score value. This can be useful to
871::CODE;;measure the agreement of two independent label assignments strategies
872::CODE;;on the same dataset when the real ground truth is not known.
873::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <mutual_info_score>`.
874::CODE;;Parameters
875::CODE;;----------
876::CODE;;labels_true : int array-like of shape (n_samples,)
877::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets.
878::CODE;;labels_pred : int array-like of shape (n_samples,)
879::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets.
880::CODE;;average_method : {'min', 'geometric', 'arithmetic', 'max'}, default='arithmetic'
881::CODE;;How to compute the normalizer in the denominator.
882::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
883::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.22
884::CODE;;The default value of ``average_method`` changed from 'geometric' to
885::CODE;;'arithmetic'.
886::CODE;;Returns
887::CODE;;-------
888::CODE;;nmi : float
889::CODE;;Score between 0.0 and 1.0 in normalized nats (based on the natural
890::CODE;;logarithm). 1.0 stands for perfectly complete labeling.
891::CODE;;See Also
892::CODE;;--------
893::CODE;;v_measure_score : V-Measure (NMI with arithmetic mean option).
894::CODE;;adjusted_rand_score : Adjusted Rand Index.
895::CODE;;adjusted_mutual_info_score : Adjusted Mutual Information (adjusted
896::CODE;;against chance).
897::CODE;;Examples
898::CODE;;--------
899::CODE;;Perfect labelings are both homogeneous and complete, hence have
900::CODE;;score 1.0::
901::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import normalized_mutual_info_score
902::CODE;;>>> normalized_mutual_info_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1])
903::CODE;;1.0
904::CODE;;>>> normalized_mutual_info_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
905::CODE;;1.0
906::CODE;;If classes members are completely split across different clusters,
907::CODE;;the assignment is totally in-complete, hence the NMI is null::
908::CODE;;>>> normalized_mutual_info_score([0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3])
909::CODE;;0.0
945::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
946::CODE;;The Fowlkes-Mallows index (FMI) is defined as the geometric mean of
947::CODE;;the precision and recall::
948::CODE;;FMI = TP / sqrt((TP + FP) * (TP + FN))
949::CODE;;Where ``TP`` is the number of **True Positive** (i.e. the number of pairs of
950::CODE;;points that belong to the same cluster in both ``labels_true`` and
951::CODE;;``labels_pred``), ``FP`` is the number of **False Positive** (i.e. the
952::CODE;;number of pairs of points that belong to the same cluster in
953::CODE;;``labels_pred`` but not in ``labels_true``) and ``FN`` is the number of
954::CODE;;**False Negative** (i.e. the number of pairs of points that belong to the
955::CODE;;same cluster in ``labels_true`` but not in ``labels_pred``).
956::CODE;;The score ranges from 0 to 1. A high value indicates a good similarity
957::CODE;;between two clusters.
958::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <fowlkes_mallows_scores>`.
959::CODE;;Parameters
960::CODE;;----------
961::CODE;;labels_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=int
962::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets.
963::CODE;;labels_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples,), dtype=int
964::CODE;;A clustering of the data into disjoint subsets.
965::CODE;;sparse : bool, default=False
966::CODE;;Compute contingency matrix internally with sparse matrix.
967::CODE;;.. deprecated:: 1.7
968::CODE;;The ``sparse`` parameter is deprecated and will be removed in 1.9. It has
969::CODE;;no effect.
970::CODE;;Returns
971::CODE;;-------
972::CODE;;score : float
973::CODE;;The resulting Fowlkes-Mallows score.
974::CODE;;References
975::CODE;;----------
976::CODE;;.. [1] `E. B. Fowkles and C. L. Mallows, 1983. "A method for comparing two
977::CODE;;hierarchical clusterings". Journal of the American Statistical
978::CODE;;Association
979::CODE;;<https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1983.10478008>`_
980::CODE;;.. [2] `Wikipedia entry for the Fowlkes-Mallows Index
981::CODE;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowlkes-Mallows_index>`_
982::CODE;;Examples
983::CODE;;--------
984::CODE;;Perfect labelings are both homogeneous and complete, hence have
985::CODE;;score 1.0::
986::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.cluster import fowlkes_mallows_score
987::CODE;;>>> fowlkes_mallows_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1])
988::CODE;;1.0
989::CODE;;>>> fowlkes_mallows_score([0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0, 0])
990::CODE;;1.0
991::CODE;;If classes members are completely split across different clusters,
992::CODE;;the assignment is totally random, hence the FMI is null::
993::CODE;;>>> fowlkes_mallows_score([0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3])
994::CODE;;0.0

26::CODE;;Parameters

29::CODE;;Number of labels.
30::CODE;;n_samples : int
31::CODE;;Number of samples.
52::CODE;;The Silhouette Coefficient is calculated using the mean intra-cluster
53::CODE;;distance (``a``) and the mean nearest-cluster distance (``b``) for each
54::CODE;;sample. The Silhouette Coefficient for a sample is ``(b - a) / max(a,
55::CODE;;b)``. To clarify, ``b`` is the distance between a sample and the nearest
56::CODE;;cluster that the sample is not a part of.
57::CODE;;Note that Silhouette Coefficient is only defined if number of labels
58::CODE;;is ``2 <= n_labels <= n_samples - 1``.
59::CODE;;This function returns the mean Silhouette Coefficient over all samples.
60::CODE;;To obtain the values for each sample, use :func:`silhouette_samples`.
61::CODE;;The best value is 1 and the worst value is -1. Values near 0 indicate
62::CODE;;overlapping clusters. Negative values generally indicate that a sample has
63::CODE;;been assigned to the wrong cluster, as a different cluster is more similar.
64::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <silhouette_coefficient>`.
65::CODE;;Parameters
66::CODE;;----------
67::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_a, n_samples_a) if metric == \
68::CODE;;"precomputed" or (n_samples_a, n_features) otherwise
69::CODE;;An array of pairwise distances between samples, or a feature array.
70::CODE;;labels : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
71::CODE;;Predicted labels for each sample.
72::CODE;;metric : str or callable, default='euclidean'
73::CODE;;The metric to use when calculating distance between instances in a
74::CODE;;feature array. If metric is a string, it must be one of the options
75::CODE;;allowed by :func:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances`. If ``X`` is
76::CODE;;the distance array itself, use ``metric="precomputed"``.
77::CODE;;sample_size : int, default=None
78::CODE;;The size of the sample to use when computing the Silhouette Coefficient
79::CODE;;on a random subset of the data.
80::CODE;;If ``sample_size is None``, no sampling is used.
81::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
82::CODE;;Determines random number generation for selecting a subset of samples.
83::CODE;;Used when ``sample_size is not None``.
84::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
85::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
86::CODE;;**kwds : optional keyword parameters
87::CODE;;Any further parameters are passed directly to the distance function.
88::CODE;;If using a scipy.spatial.distance metric, the parameters are still
89::CODE;;metric dependent. See the scipy docs for usage examples.
90::CODE;;Returns
91::CODE;;-------
92::CODE;;silhouette : float
93::CODE;;Mean Silhouette Coefficient for all samples.
94::CODE;;References
95::CODE;;----------
96::CODE;;.. [1] `Peter J. Rousseeuw (1987). "Silhouettes: a Graphical Aid to the
97::CODE;;Interpretation and Validation of Cluster Analysis". Computational

180::CODE;;The Silhouette Coefficient is a measure of how well samples are clustered
181::CODE;;with samples that are similar to themselves. Clustering models with a high
182::CODE;;Silhouette Coefficient are said to be dense, where samples in the same
183::CODE;;cluster are similar to each other, and well separated, where samples in
184::CODE;;different clusters are not very similar to each other.
185::CODE;;The Silhouette Coefficient is calculated using the mean intra-cluster
186::CODE;;distance (``a``) and the mean nearest-cluster distance (``b``) for each
187::CODE;;sample. The Silhouette Coefficient for a sample is ``(b - a) / max(a,
188::CODE;;b)``.
189::CODE;;Note that Silhouette Coefficient is only defined if number of labels
190::CODE;;is 2 ``<= n_labels <= n_samples - 1``.
191::CODE;;This function returns the Silhouette Coefficient for each sample.
192::CODE;;The best value is 1 and the worst value is -1. Values near 0 indicate
193::CODE;;overlapping clusters.
194::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <silhouette_coefficient>`.
195::CODE;;Parameters

200::CODE;;a sparse matrix is provided, CSR format should be favoured avoiding

344::CODE;;The score is defined as the average similarity measure of each cluster with
345::CODE;;its most similar cluster, where similarity is the ratio of within-cluster
346::CODE;;distances to between-cluster distances. Thus, clusters which are farther
347::CODE;;apart and less dispersed will result in a better score.
348::CODE;;The minimum score is zero, with lower values indicating better clustering.
349::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <davies-bouldin_index>`.

212::CODE;;@validate_params(
213::CODE;;{
214::CODE;;"X": ["array-like", "sparse matrix"],
215::CODE;;"Y": ["array-like", "sparse matrix", None],
216::CODE;;"Y_norm_squared": ["array-like", None],

222::CODE;;def euclidean_distances(
223::CODE;;X, Y=None, *, Y_norm_squared=None, squared=False, X_norm_squared=None
224::CODE;;):
284::CODE;;xp, _ = get_namespace(X, Y)
285::CODE;;X, Y = check_pairwise_arrays(X, Y)
286::CODE;;if X_norm_squared is not None:
287::CODE;;X_norm_squared = check_array(X_norm_squared, ensure_2d=False)
288::CODE;;original_shape = X_norm_squared.shape
289::CODE;;if X_norm_squared.shape == (X.shape[0],):
290::CODE;;X_norm_squared = xp.reshape(X_norm_squared, (-1, 1))
291::CODE;;if X_norm_squared.shape == (1, X.shape[0]):
292::CODE;;X_norm_squared = X_norm_squared.T
293::CODE;;if X_norm_squared.shape != (X.shape[0], 1):
294::CODE;;raise ValueError(
295::CODE;;f"Incompatible dimensions for X of shape {X.shape} and "
296::CODE;;f"X_norm_squared of shape {original_shape}."
297::CODE;;)
298::CODE;;if Y_norm_squared is not None:
299::CODE;;Y_norm_squared = check_array(Y_norm_squared, ensure_2d=False)
300::CODE;;original_shape = Y_norm_squared.shape
301::CODE;;if Y_norm_squared.shape == (Y.shape[0],):
302::CODE;;Y_norm_squared = xp.reshape(Y_norm_squared, (1, -1))
303::CODE;;if Y_norm_squared.shape == (Y.shape[0], 1):
304::CODE;;Y_norm_squared = Y_norm_squared.T
305::CODE;;if Y_norm_squared.shape != (1, Y.shape[0]):
306::CODE;;raise ValueError(
307::CODE;;f"Incompatible dimensions for Y of shape {Y.shape} and "
308::CODE;;f"Y_norm_squared of shape {original_shape}."
309::CODE;;)
310::CODE;;return _euclidean_distances(X, Y, X_norm_squared, Y_norm_squared, squared)
311::CODE;;def _euclidean_distances(X, Y, X_norm_squared=None, Y_norm_squared=None, squared=False):
318::CODE;;xp, _, device_ = get_namespace_and_device(X, Y)
319::CODE;;if X_norm_squared is not None and X_norm_squared.dtype != xp.float32:
320::CODE;;XX = xp.reshape(X_norm_squared, (-1, 1))
321::CODE;;elif X.dtype != xp.float32:
322::CODE;;XX = row_norms(X, squared=True)[:, None]
323::CODE;;else:
324::CODE;;XX = None
325::CODE;;if Y is X:
326::CODE;;YY = None if XX is None else XX.T
327::CODE;;else:
328::CODE;;if Y_norm_squared is not None and Y_norm_squared.dtype != xp.float32:
329::CODE;;YY = xp.reshape(Y_norm_squared, (1, -1))
330::CODE;;elif Y.dtype != xp.float32:
331::CODE;;YY = row_norms(Y, squared=True)[None, :]
332::CODE;;else:
333::CODE;;YY = None
334::CODE;;if X.dtype == xp.float32 or Y.dtype == xp.float32:
337::CODE;;distances = _euclidean_distances_upcast(X, XX, Y, YY)
338::CODE;;else:
340::CODE;;distances = -2 * safe_sparse_dot(X, Y.T, dense_output=True)
341::CODE;;distances += XX
342::CODE;;distances += YY
343::CODE;;xp_zero = xp.asarray(0, device=device_, dtype=distances.dtype)
344::CODE;;distances = _modify_in_place_if_numpy(
345::CODE;;xp, xp.maximum, distances, xp_zero, out=distances
346::CODE;;)
349::CODE;;if X is Y:
350::CODE;;_fill_diagonal(distances, 0, xp=xp)
351::CODE;;if squared:
352::CODE;;return distances
353::CODE;;distances = _modify_in_place_if_numpy(xp, xp.sqrt, distances, out=distances)
354::CODE;;return distances
355::CODE;;@validate_params(
356::CODE;;{
357::CODE;;"X": ["array-like"],
358::CODE;;"Y": ["array-like", None],
359::CODE;;"squared": ["boolean"],
360::CODE;;"missing_values": [MissingValues(numeric_only=True)],
361::CODE;;"copy": ["boolean"],
362::CODE;;},
363::CODE;;prefer_skip_nested_validation=True,
364::CODE;;)
365::CODE;;def nan_euclidean_distances(
366::CODE;;X, Y=None, *, squared=False, missing_values=np.nan, copy=True
367::CODE;;):
426::CODE;;ensure_all_finite = "allow-nan" if is_scalar_nan(missing_values) else True
427::CODE;;X, Y = check_pairwise_arrays(
428::CODE;;X, Y, accept_sparse=False, ensure_all_finite=ensure_all_finite, copy=copy
429::CODE;;)
431::CODE;;missing_X = _get_mask(X, missing_values)
433::CODE;;missing_Y = missing_X if Y is X else _get_mask(Y, missing_values)
435::CODE;;X[missing_X] = 0
436::CODE;;Y[missing_Y] = 0
437::CODE;;distances = euclidean_distances(X, Y, squared=True)
439::CODE;;XX = X * X
440::CODE;;YY = Y * Y
441::CODE;;distances -= np.dot(XX, missing_Y.T)
442::CODE;;distances -= np.dot(missing_X, YY.T)
443::CODE;;np.clip(distances, 0, None, out=distances)
444::CODE;;if X is Y:
447::CODE;;np.fill_diagonal(distances, 0.0)
448::CODE;;present_X = 1 - missing_X
449::CODE;;present_Y = present_X if Y is X else ~missing_Y
450::CODE;;present_count = np.dot(present_X, present_Y.T)
451::CODE;;distances[present_count == 0] = np.nan
453::CODE;;np.maximum(1, present_count, out=present_count)
454::CODE;;distances /= present_count
455::CODE;;distances *= X.shape[1]
456::CODE;;if not squared:
457::CODE;;np.sqrt(distances, out=distances)
458::CODE;;return distances
459::CODE;;def _euclidean_distances_upcast(X, XX=None, Y=None, YY=None, batch_size=None):
466::CODE;;xp, _, device_ = get_namespace_and_device(X, Y)
467::CODE;;n_samples_X = X.shape[0]
468::CODE;;n_samples_Y = Y.shape[0]
469::CODE;;n_features = X.shape[1]
470::CODE;;distances = xp.empty((n_samples_X, n_samples_Y), dtype=xp.float32, device=device_)
471::CODE;;if batch_size is None:
472::CODE;;x_density = X.nnz / np.prod(X.shape) if issparse(X) else 1
473::CODE;;y_density = Y.nnz / np.prod(Y.shape) if issparse(Y) else 1
476::CODE;;maxmem = max(
477::CODE;;(
478::CODE;;(x_density * n_samples_X + y_density * n_samples_Y) * n_features
479::CODE;;+ (x_density * n_samples_X * y_density * n_samples_Y)
480::CODE;;)
481::CODE;;/ 10,
482::CODE;;10 * 2**17,
483::CODE;;)
490::CODE;;tmp = (x_density + y_density) * n_features
491::CODE;;batch_size = (-tmp + math.sqrt(tmp**2 + 4 * maxmem)) / 2
492::CODE;;batch_size = max(int(batch_size), 1)
493::CODE;;x_batches = gen_batches(n_samples_X, batch_size)
494::CODE;;xp_max_float = _max_precision_float_dtype(xp=xp, device=device_)
495::CODE;;for i, x_slice in enumerate(x_batches):
496::CODE;;X_chunk = xp.astype(X[x_slice, :], xp_max_float)
497::CODE;;if XX is None:
498::CODE;;XX_chunk = row_norms(X_chunk, squared=True)[:, None]
499::CODE;;else:
500::CODE;;XX_chunk = XX[x_slice]
501::CODE;;y_batches = gen_batches(n_samples_Y, batch_size)
502::CODE;;for j, y_slice in enumerate(y_batches):
503::CODE;;if X is Y and j < i:
506::CODE;;d = distances[y_slice, x_slice].T
507::CODE;;else:
508::CODE;;Y_chunk = xp.astype(Y[y_slice, :], xp_max_float)
509::CODE;;if YY is None:
510::CODE;;YY_chunk = row_norms(Y_chunk, squared=True)[None, :]
511::CODE;;else:
512::CODE;;YY_chunk = YY[:, y_slice]
513::CODE;;d = -2 * safe_sparse_dot(X_chunk, Y_chunk.T, dense_output=True)
514::CODE;;d += XX_chunk
515::CODE;;d += YY_chunk
516::CODE;;distances[x_slice, y_slice] = xp.astype(d, xp.float32, copy=False)
517::CODE;;return distances
518::CODE;;def _argmin_min_reduce(dist, start):
522::CODE;;indices = dist.argmin(axis=1)
523::CODE;;values = dist[np.arange(dist.shape[0]), indices]
524::CODE;;return indices, values

580::CODE;;def pairwise_distances_argmin_min(

223::CODE;;def test_haversine_metric(X, Y, csr_container):
225::CODE;;X = np.asarray(X[:, :2])
226::CODE;;Y = np.asarray(Y[:, :2])
227::CODE;;X_csr, Y_csr = csr_container(X), csr_container(Y)
230::CODE;;def haversine_slow(x1, x2):
231::CODE;;return 2 * np.arcsin(
232::CODE;;np.sqrt(
233::CODE;;np.sin(0.5 * (x1[0] - x2[0])) ** 2
234::CODE;;+ np.cos(x1[0]) * np.cos(x2[0]) * np.sin(0.5 * (x1[1] - x2[1])) ** 2
235::CODE;;)
236::CODE;;)
237::CODE;;D_reference = np.zeros((X_csr.shape[0], Y_csr.shape[0]))
238::CODE;;for i, xi in enumerate(X):
239::CODE;;for j, yj in enumerate(Y):
240::CODE;;D_reference[i, j] = haversine_slow(xi, yj)
241::CODE;;haversine = DistanceMetric.get_metric("haversine", X.dtype)
242::CODE;;D_sklearn = haversine.pairwise(X, Y)
243::CODE;;assert_allclose(
244::CODE;;haversine.dist_to_rdist(D_sklearn), np.sin(0.5 * D_reference) ** 2, rtol=1e-6
245::CODE;;)
246::CODE;;assert_allclose(D_sklearn, D_reference)
247::CODE;;D_sklearn = haversine.pairwise(X_csr, Y_csr)
248::CODE;;assert D_sklearn.flags.c_contiguous
249::CODE;;assert_allclose(D_sklearn, D_reference)

1102::CODE;;def test_haversine_distances():
1104::CODE;;def slow_haversine_distances(x, y):
1105::CODE;;diff_lat = y[0] - x[0]
1106::CODE;;diff_lon = y[1] - x[1]
1107::CODE;;a = np.sin(diff_lat / 2) ** 2 + (
1108::CODE;;np.cos(x[0]) * np.cos(y[0]) * np.sin(diff_lon / 2) ** 2
1109::CODE;;)
1110::CODE;;c = 2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(a))
1111::CODE;;return c
1112::CODE;;rng = np.random.RandomState(0)

1117::CODE;;assert_allclose(D1, D2)

38::CODE;;def _get_metric_params_list(metric: str, n_features: int, seed: int = 1):
66::CODE;;This does not check if there are missing neighbors in either result set.
67::CODE;;Missingness is handled by assert_no_missing_neighbors.
99::CODE;;Any neighbor index with a distance below the precision threshold should
100::CODE;;match one in the other result set. We ignore the last few neighbors beyond
101::CODE;;the threshold as those can typically be missing due to rounding errors.
102::CODE;;For radius queries, the threshold is just the radius minus the expected
103::CODE;;precision level.
104::CODE;;For k-NN queries, it is the maximum distance to the k-th neighbor minus the
105::CODE;;expected precision level.
130::CODE;;This function asserts that the results of argkmin queries are valid up to:
131::CODE;;- rounding error tolerance on distance values;
132::CODE;;- permutations of indices for distances values that differ up to the
133::CODE;;expected precision level.
134::CODE;;Furthermore, the distances must be sorted.
135::CODE;;To be used for testing neighbors queries on float32 datasets: we accept
136::CODE;;neighbors rank swaps only if they are caused by small rounding errors on
137::CODE;;the distance computations.
221::CODE;;- relative and absolute tolerance on computed distance values
222::CODE;;- permutations of indices for distances values that differ up to
223::CODE;;a precision level
224::CODE;;- missing or extra last elements if their distance is
225::CODE;;close to the radius
226::CODE;;To be used for testing neighbors queries on float32 datasets: we
227::CODE;;accept neighbors rank swaps only if they are caused by small
228::CODE;;rounding errors on the distance computations.
229::CODE;;Input arrays must be sorted w.r.t distances.

73::CODE;;X = np.c_[X, rng.randn(n_samples, 200 * n_features)]
75::CODE;;clf = LogisticRegression(random_state=0)
76::CODE;;y_score = clf.fit(X[:half], y[:half]).predict_proba(X[half:])
77::CODE;;if binary:
80::CODE;;y_score = y_score[:, 1]
81::CODE;;y_pred = clf.predict(X[half:])
82::CODE;;y_true = y[half:]
83::CODE;;return y_true, y_pred, y_score
86::CODE;;def _auc(y_true, y_score):
89::CODE;;pos_label = np.unique(y_true)[1]
92::CODE;;pos = y_score[y_true == pos_label]
93::CODE;;neg = y_score[y_true != pos_label]
94::CODE;;diff_matrix = pos.reshape(1, -1) - neg.reshape(-1, 1)
95::CODE;;n_correct = np.sum(diff_matrix > 0)
96::CODE;;return n_correct / float(len(pos) * len(neg))
97::CODE;;def _average_precision(y_true, y_score):
105::CODE;;pos_label = np.unique(y_true)[1]
106::CODE;;n_pos = np.sum(y_true == pos_label)
107::CODE;;order = np.argsort(y_score)[::-1]
108::CODE;;y_score = y_score[order]
109::CODE;;y_true = y_true[order]
110::CODE;;score = 0
111::CODE;;for i in range(len(y_score)):
112::CODE;;if y_true[i] == pos_label:
115::CODE;;prec = 0
116::CODE;;for j in range(0, i + 1):
117::CODE;;if y_true[j] == pos_label:
118::CODE;;prec += 1.0
119::CODE;;prec /= i + 1.0
120::CODE;;score += prec
121::CODE;;return score / n_pos
122::CODE;;def _average_precision_slow(y_true, y_score):
131::CODE;;precision, recall, threshold = precision_recall_curve(y_true, y_score)
132::CODE;;precision = list(reversed(precision))
133::CODE;;recall = list(reversed(recall))
134::CODE;;average_precision = 0
135::CODE;;for i in range(1, len(precision)):
136::CODE;;average_precision += precision[i] * (recall[i] - recall[i - 1])
137::CODE;;return average_precision
138::CODE;;def _partial_roc_auc_score(y_true, y_predict, max_fpr):
142::CODE;;def _partial_roc(y_true, y_predict, max_fpr):
143::CODE;;fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_true, y_predict)
144::CODE;;new_fpr = fpr[fpr <= max_fpr]
145::CODE;;new_fpr = np.append(new_fpr, max_fpr)
146::CODE;;new_tpr = tpr[fpr <= max_fpr]
147::CODE;;idx_out = np.argmax(fpr > max_fpr)
148::CODE;;idx_in = idx_out - 1
149::CODE;;x_interp = [fpr[idx_in], fpr[idx_out]]
150::CODE;;y_interp = [tpr[idx_in], tpr[idx_out]]
151::CODE;;new_tpr = np.append(new_tpr, np.interp(max_fpr, x_interp, y_interp))
152::CODE;;return (new_fpr, new_tpr)
153::CODE;;new_fpr, new_tpr = _partial_roc(y_true, y_predict, max_fpr)
154::CODE;;partial_auc = auc(new_fpr, new_tpr)
156::CODE;;fpr1 = 0
157::CODE;;fpr2 = max_fpr
158::CODE;;min_area = 0.5 * (fpr2 - fpr1) * (fpr2 + fpr1)
159::CODE;;max_area = fpr2 - fpr1
160::CODE;;return 0.5 * (1 + (partial_auc - min_area) / (max_area - min_area))

35::CODE;;Parameters
36::CODE;;----------

45::CODE;;------
46::CODE;;log_wishart_norm : array-like of shape (n_components,)
47::CODE;;The log normalization of the Wishart distribution.
60::CODE;;This class allows to infer an approximate posterior distribution over the
61::CODE;;parameters of a Gaussian mixture distribution. The effective number of
62::CODE;;components can be inferred from the data.
63::CODE;;This class implements two types of prior for the weights distribution: a
64::CODE;;finite mixture model with Dirichlet distribution and an infinite mixture
65::CODE;;model with the Dirichlet Process. In practice Dirichlet Process inference
66::CODE;;algorithm is approximated and uses a truncated distribution with a fixed
67::CODE;;maximum number of components (called the Stick-breaking representation).
68::CODE;;The number of components actually used almost always depends on the data.
69::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
70::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <bgmm>`.
71::CODE;;Parameters
72::CODE;;----------
73::CODE;;n_components : int, default=1
74::CODE;;The number of mixture components. Depending on the data and the value
75::CODE;;of the `weight_concentration_prior` the model can decide to not use
76::CODE;;all the components by setting some component `weights_` to values very
77::CODE;;close to zero. The number of effective components is therefore smaller
78::CODE;;than n_components.
79::CODE;;covariance_type : {'full', 'tied', 'diag', 'spherical'}, default='full'
80::CODE;;String describing the type of covariance parameters to use.
81::CODE;;Must be one of:
82::CODE;;- 'full' (each component has its own general covariance matrix),
83::CODE;;- 'tied' (all components share the same general covariance matrix),
84::CODE;;- 'diag' (each component has its own diagonal covariance matrix),
85::CODE;;- 'spherical' (each component has its own single variance).
86::CODE;;tol : float, default=1e-3
87::CODE;;The convergence threshold. EM iterations will stop when the
88::CODE;;lower bound average gain on the likelihood (of the training data with
89::CODE;;respect to the model) is below this threshold.
90::CODE;;reg_covar : float, default=1e-6
91::CODE;;Non-negative regularization added to the diagonal of covariance.
92::CODE;;Allows to assure that the covariance matrices are all positive.
93::CODE;;max_iter : int, default=100
94::CODE;;The number of EM iterations to perform.
95::CODE;;n_init : int, default=1
96::CODE;;The number of initializations to perform. The result with the highest
97::CODE;;lower bound value on the likelihood is kept.
98::CODE;;init_params : {'kmeans', 'k-means++', 'random', 'random_from_data'}, \
99::CODE;;default='kmeans'
100::CODE;;The method used to initialize the weights, the means and the
101::CODE;;covariances. String must be one of:
102::CODE;;- 'kmeans': responsibilities are initialized using kmeans.
103::CODE;;- 'k-means++': use the k-means++ method to initialize.
104::CODE;;- 'random': responsibilities are initialized randomly.
105::CODE;;- 'random_from_data': initial means are randomly selected data points.
106::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: v1.1
107::CODE;;`init_params` now accepts 'random_from_data' and 'k-means++' as
108::CODE;;initialization methods.
109::CODE;;weight_concentration_prior_type : {'dirichlet_process', 'dirichlet_distribution'}, \
110::CODE;;default='dirichlet_process'
111::CODE;;String describing the type of the weight concentration prior.
112::CODE;;weight_concentration_prior : float or None, default=None
113::CODE;;The dirichlet concentration of each component on the weight
114::CODE;;distribution (Dirichlet). This is commonly called gamma in the
115::CODE;;literature. The higher concentration puts more mass in
116::CODE;;the center and will lead to more components being active, while a lower
117::CODE;;concentration parameter will lead to more mass at the edge of the
118::CODE;;mixture weights simplex. The value of the parameter must be greater
119::CODE;;than 0. If it is None, it's set to ``1. / n_components``.
120::CODE;;mean_precision_prior : float or None, default=None
121::CODE;;The precision prior on the mean distribution (Gaussian).
122::CODE;;Controls the extent of where means can be placed. Larger
123::CODE;;values concentrate the cluster means around `mean_prior`.
124::CODE;;The value of the parameter must be greater than 0.
125::CODE;;If it is None, it is set to 1.
126::CODE;;mean_prior : array-like, shape (n_features,), default=None
127::CODE;;The prior on the mean distribution (Gaussian).
128::CODE;;If it is None, it is set to the mean of X.
129::CODE;;degrees_of_freedom_prior : float or None, default=None
130::CODE;;The prior of the number of degrees of freedom on the covariance
131::CODE;;distributions (Wishart). If it is None, it's set to `n_features`.
132::CODE;;covariance_prior : float or array-like, default=None
133::CODE;;The prior on the covariance distribution (Wishart).
134::CODE;;If it is None, the emiprical covariance prior is initialized using the
135::CODE;;covariance of X. The shape depends on `covariance_type`::
136::CODE;;(n_features, n_features) if 'full',
137::CODE;;(n_features, n_features) if 'tied',
138::CODE;;(n_features) if 'diag',
139::CODE;;float if 'spherical'
140::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
141::CODE;;Controls the random seed given to the method chosen to initialize the
142::CODE;;parameters (see `init_params`).
143::CODE;;In addition, it controls the generation of random samples from the
144::CODE;;fitted distribution (see the method `sample`).
145::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
146::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
147::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
148::CODE;;If 'warm_start' is True, the solution of the last fitting is used as
149::CODE;;initialization for the next call of fit(). This can speed up
150::CODE;;convergence when fit is called several times on similar problems.
151::CODE;;See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
152::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
153::CODE;;Enable verbose output. If 1 then it prints the current
154::CODE;;initialization and each iteration step. If greater than 1 then
155::CODE;;it prints also the log probability and the time needed
156::CODE;;for each step.
157::CODE;;verbose_interval : int, default=10
158::CODE;;Number of iteration done before the next print.
159::CODE;;Attributes
160::CODE;;----------
161::CODE;;weights_ : array-like of shape (n_components,)
162::CODE;;The weights of each mixture components.
163::CODE;;means_ : array-like of shape (n_components, n_features)
164::CODE;;The mean of each mixture component.
165::CODE;;covariances_ : array-like
166::CODE;;The covariance of each mixture component.
167::CODE;;The shape depends on `covariance_type`::
168::CODE;;(n_components,) if 'spherical',
169::CODE;;(n_features, n_features) if 'tied',
170::CODE;;(n_components, n_features) if 'diag',
171::CODE;;(n_components, n_features, n_features) if 'full'
172::CODE;;precisions_ : array-like
173::CODE;;The precision matrices for each component in the mixture. A precision
174::CODE;;matrix is the inverse of a covariance matrix. A covariance matrix is
175::CODE;;symmetric positive definite so the mixture of Gaussian can be
176::CODE;;equivalently parameterized by the precision matrices. Storing the
177::CODE;;precision matrices instead of the covariance matrices makes it more
178::CODE;;efficient to compute the log-likelihood of new samples at test time.
179::CODE;;The shape depends on ``covariance_type``::
180::CODE;;(n_components,) if 'spherical',
181::CODE;;(n_features, n_features) if 'tied',
182::CODE;;(n_components, n_features) if 'diag',
183::CODE;;(n_components, n_features, n_features) if 'full'
184::CODE;;precisions_cholesky_ : array-like
185::CODE;;The Cholesky decomposition of the precision matrices of each mixture
186::CODE;;component. A precision matrix is the inverse of a covariance matrix.
187::CODE;;A covariance matrix is symmetric positive definite so the mixture of
188::CODE;;Gaussian can be equivalently parameterized by the precision matrices.
189::CODE;;Storing the precision matrices instead of the covariance matrices makes
190::CODE;;it more efficient to compute the log-likelihood of new samples at test
191::CODE;;time. The shape depends on ``covariance_type``::
192::CODE;;(n_components,) if 'spherical',
193::CODE;;(n_features, n_features) if 'tied',
194::CODE;;(n_components, n_features) if 'diag',
195::CODE;;(n_components, n_features, n_features) if 'full'
196::CODE;;converged_ : bool
197::CODE;;True when convergence of the best fit of inference was reached, False otherwise.
198::CODE;;n_iter_ : int
199::CODE;;Number of step used by the best fit of inference to reach the
200::CODE;;convergence.
201::CODE;;lower_bound_ : float
202::CODE;;Lower bound value on the model evidence (of the training data) of the
203::CODE;;best fit of inference.
204::CODE;;lower_bounds_ : array-like of shape (`n_iter_`,)
205::CODE;;The list of lower bound values on the model evidence from each iteration
206::CODE;;of the best fit of inference.
207::CODE;;weight_concentration_prior_ : tuple or float
208::CODE;;The dirichlet concentration of each component on the weight
209::CODE;;distribution (Dirichlet). The type depends on
210::CODE;;``weight_concentration_prior_type``::
211::CODE;;(float, float) if 'dirichlet_process' (Beta parameters),
212::CODE;;float if 'dirichlet_distribution' (Dirichlet parameters).
213::CODE;;The higher concentration puts more mass in
214::CODE;;the center and will lead to more components being active, while a lower
215::CODE;;concentration parameter will lead to more mass at the edge of the
216::CODE;;simplex.
217::CODE;;weight_concentration_ : array-like of shape (n_components,)
218::CODE;;The dirichlet concentration of each component on the weight
219::CODE;;distribution (Dirichlet).
220::CODE;;mean_precision_prior_ : float
221::CODE;;The precision prior on the mean distribution (Gaussian).
222::CODE;;Controls the extent of where means can be placed.
223::CODE;;Larger values concentrate the cluster means around `mean_prior`.
224::CODE;;If mean_precision_prior is set to None, `mean_precision_prior_` is set
225::CODE;;to 1.
226::CODE;;mean_precision_ : array-like of shape (n_components,)
227::CODE;;The precision of each components on the mean distribution (Gaussian).
228::CODE;;mean_prior_ : array-like of shape (n_features,)
229::CODE;;The prior on the mean distribution (Gaussian).
230::CODE;;degrees_of_freedom_prior_ : float
231::CODE;;The prior of the number of degrees of freedom on the covariance
232::CODE;;distributions (Wishart).
233::CODE;;degrees_of_freedom_ : array-like of shape (n_components,)
234::CODE;;The number of degrees of freedom of each components in the model.
235::CODE;;covariance_prior_ : float or array-like
236::CODE;;The prior on the covariance distribution (Wishart).
237::CODE;;The shape depends on `covariance_type`::
238::CODE;;(n_features, n_features) if 'full',
239::CODE;;(n_features, n_features) if 'tied',
240::CODE;;(n_features) if 'diag',
241::CODE;;float if 'spherical'
242::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
243::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
244::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
245::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
246::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
247::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.

153::CODE;;covariances[k, :, :] = ((resp[:, k] * diff.T) @ diff) / nk[k]
154::CODE;;_add_to_diagonal(covariances[k, :, :], reg_covar, xp)
155::CODE;;return covariances
156::CODE;;def _estimate_gaussian_covariances_tied(resp, X, nk, means, reg_covar, xp=None):
170::CODE;;xp, _ = get_namespace(X, means, xp=xp)
171::CODE;;avg_X2 = X.T @ X
172::CODE;;avg_means2 = nk * means.T @ means
173::CODE;;covariance = avg_X2 - avg_means2
174::CODE;;covariance /= xp.sum(nk)
175::CODE;;_add_to_diagonal(covariance, reg_covar, xp)
176::CODE;;return covariance
177::CODE;;def _estimate_gaussian_covariances_diag(resp, X, nk, means, reg_covar, xp=None):
191::CODE;;xp, _ = get_namespace(X, xp=xp)
192::CODE;;avg_X2 = (resp.T @ (X * X)) / nk[:, xp.newaxis]
193::CODE;;avg_means2 = means**2
194::CODE;;return avg_X2 - avg_means2 + reg_covar
195::CODE;;def _estimate_gaussian_covariances_spherical(resp, X, nk, means, reg_covar, xp=None):
209::CODE;;xp, _ = get_namespace(X)
210::CODE;;return xp.mean(
211::CODE;;_estimate_gaussian_covariances_diag(resp, X, nk, means, reg_covar, xp=xp),
212::CODE;;axis=1,
213::CODE;;)
214::CODE;;def _estimate_gaussian_parameters(X, resp, reg_covar, covariance_type, xp=None):
236::CODE;;xp, _ = get_namespace(X, xp=xp)
237::CODE;;nk = xp.sum(resp, axis=0) + 10 * xp.finfo(resp.dtype).eps
238::CODE;;means = (resp.T @ X) / nk[:, xp.newaxis]
239::CODE;;covariances = {
240::CODE;;"full": _estimate_gaussian_covariances_full,
241::CODE;;"tied": _estimate_gaussian_covariances_tied,
242::CODE;;"diag": _estimate_gaussian_covariances_diag,

246::CODE;;def _compute_precision_cholesky(covariances, covariance_type, xp=None):
261::CODE;;xp, _, device_ = get_namespace_and_device(covariances, xp=xp)
262::CODE;;estimate_precision_error_message = (
263::CODE;;"Fitting the mixture model failed because some components have "
264::CODE;;"ill-defined empirical covariance (for instance caused by singleton "
265::CODE;;"or collapsed samples). Try to decrease the number of components, "
266::CODE;;"increase reg_covar, or scale the input data."
267::CODE;;)
268::CODE;;dtype = covariances.dtype
269::CODE;;if dtype == xp.float32:
270::CODE;;estimate_precision_error_message += (
271::CODE;;" The numerical accuracy can also be improved by passing float64"
272::CODE;;" data instead of float32."
273::CODE;;)
274::CODE;;if covariance_type == "full":
275::CODE;;n_components, n_features, _ = covariances.shape
276::CODE;;precisions_chol = xp.empty(
277::CODE;;(n_components, n_features, n_features), device=device_, dtype=dtype
278::CODE;;)
279::CODE;;for k in range(covariances.shape[0]):
280::CODE;;covariance = covariances[k, :, :]
281::CODE;;try:
282::CODE;;cov_chol = _cholesky(covariance, xp)
284::CODE;;except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
285::CODE;;raise ValueError(estimate_precision_error_message)
286::CODE;;precisions_chol[k, :, :] = _linalg_solve(
287::CODE;;cov_chol, xp.eye(n_features, dtype=dtype, device=device_), xp
288::CODE;;).T
289::CODE;;elif covariance_type == "tied":
290::CODE;;_, n_features = covariances.shape
291::CODE;;try:
292::CODE;;cov_chol = _cholesky(covariances, xp)
294::CODE;;except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
295::CODE;;raise ValueError(estimate_precision_error_message)
296::CODE;;precisions_chol = _linalg_solve(
297::CODE;;cov_chol, xp.eye(n_features, dtype=dtype, device=device_), xp
298::CODE;;).T
299::CODE;;else:
300::CODE;;if xp.any(covariances <= 0.0):
301::CODE;;raise ValueError(estimate_precision_error_message)
302::CODE;;precisions_chol = 1.0 / xp.sqrt(covariances)
303::CODE;;return precisions_chol
304::CODE;;def _flipudlr(array, xp=None):
310::CODE;;As implemented in :func:`_compute_precision_cholesky`, the `precisions_cholesky_` is
311::CODE;;an upper-triangular matrix for each Gaussian component, which can be expressed as
312::CODE;;the $UU^T$ factorization of the precision matrix for each Gaussian component, where
313::CODE;;$U$ is an upper-triangular matrix.
314::CODE;;In order to use the Cholesky decomposition to get $UU^T$, the precision matrix
315::CODE;;$\Lambda$ needs to be permutated such that its rows and columns are reversed, which
316::CODE;;can be done by applying a similarity transformation with an exchange matrix $J$,
317::CODE;;where the 1 elements reside on the anti-diagonal and all other elements are 0. In
318::CODE;;particular, the Cholesky decomposition of the transformed precision matrix is
319::CODE;;$J\Lambda J=LL^T$, where $L$ is a lower-triangular matrix. Because $\Lambda=UU^T$
320::CODE;;and $J=J^{-1}=J^T$, the `precisions_cholesky_` for each Gaussian component can be
321::CODE;;expressed as $JLJ$.
323::CODE;;Parameters
324::CODE;;----------
325::CODE;;precisions : array-like
326::CODE;;The precision matrix of the current components.
327::CODE;;The shape depends on the covariance_type.
328::CODE;;covariance_type : {'full', 'tied', 'diag', 'spherical'}
329::CODE;;The type of precision matrices.
330::CODE;;Returns
331::CODE;;-------
332::CODE;;precisions_cholesky : array-like
333::CODE;;The Cholesky decomposition of sample precisions of the current
334::CODE;;components. The shape depends on the covariance_type.
356::CODE;;Parameters
357::CODE;;----------
358::CODE;;matrix_chol : array-like
359::CODE;;Cholesky decompositions of the matrices.
360::CODE;;'full' : shape of (n_components, n_features, n_features)
361::CODE;;'tied' : shape of (n_features, n_features)
362::CODE;;'diag' : shape of (n_components, n_features)
363::CODE;;'spherical' : shape of (n_components,)
364::CODE;;covariance_type : {'full', 'tied', 'diag', 'spherical'}
365::CODE;;n_features : int
366::CODE;;Number of features.
367::CODE;;Returns
368::CODE;;-------
369::CODE;;log_det_precision_chol : array-like of shape (n_components,)
370::CODE;;The determinant of the precision matrix for each component.
388::CODE;;Parameters
389::CODE;;----------
390::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)

392::CODE;;precisions_chol : array-like

394::CODE;;'full' : shape of (n_components, n_features, n_features)
395::CODE;;'tied' : shape of (n_features, n_features)

397::CODE;;'spherical' : shape of (n_components,)

46::CODE;;COVARIANCE_TYPE = ["full", "tied", "diag", "spherical"]
47::CODE;;def generate_data(
48::CODE;;n_samples, n_features, weights, means, precisions, covariance_type, dtype=np.float64
49::CODE;;):
50::CODE;;rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
51::CODE;;X = []
52::CODE;;if covariance_type == "spherical":
53::CODE;;for _, (w, m, c) in enumerate(zip(weights, means, precisions["spherical"])):
54::CODE;;X.append(
55::CODE;;rng.multivariate_normal(
56::CODE;;m, c * np.eye(n_features), int(np.round(w * n_samples))
57::CODE;;).astype(dtype)
58::CODE;;)
59::CODE;;if covariance_type == "diag":
60::CODE;;for _, (w, m, c) in enumerate(zip(weights, means, precisions["diag"])):
61::CODE;;X.append(
62::CODE;;rng.multivariate_normal(
63::CODE;;m, np.diag(c), int(np.round(w * n_samples))
64::CODE;;).astype(dtype)
65::CODE;;)
66::CODE;;if covariance_type == "tied":
67::CODE;;for _, (w, m) in enumerate(zip(weights, means)):
68::CODE;;X.append(
69::CODE;;rng.multivariate_normal(
70::CODE;;m, precisions["tied"], int(np.round(w * n_samples))
71::CODE;;).astype(dtype)
72::CODE;;)
73::CODE;;if covariance_type == "full":
74::CODE;;for _, (w, m, c) in enumerate(zip(weights, means, precisions["full"])):
75::CODE;;X.append(
76::CODE;;rng.multivariate_normal(m, c, int(np.round(w * n_samples))).astype(
77::CODE;;dtype
78::CODE;;)
79::CODE;;)
80::CODE;;X = np.vstack(X)
81::CODE;;return X
82::CODE;;class RandomData:
83::CODE;;def __init__(
84::CODE;;self,
85::CODE;;rng,
86::CODE;;n_samples=200,
87::CODE;;n_components=2,
88::CODE;;n_features=2,
89::CODE;;scale=50,
90::CODE;;dtype=np.float64,
91::CODE;;):
92::CODE;;self.n_samples = n_samples
93::CODE;;self.n_components = n_components
94::CODE;;self.n_features = n_features
95::CODE;;self.weights = rng.rand(n_components).astype(dtype)
96::CODE;;self.weights = self.weights.astype(dtype) / self.weights.sum()
97::CODE;;self.means = rng.rand(n_components, n_features).astype(dtype) * scale
98::CODE;;self.covariances = {
99::CODE;;"spherical": 0.5 + rng.rand(n_components).astype(dtype),
100::CODE;;"diag": (0.5 + rng.rand(n_components, n_features).astype(dtype)) ** 2,
101::CODE;;"tied": make_spd_matrix(n_features, random_state=rng).astype(dtype),
102::CODE;;"full": np.array(
103::CODE;;[
104::CODE;;make_spd_matrix(n_features, random_state=rng).astype(dtype) * 0.5
105::CODE;;for _ in range(n_components)
106::CODE;;]
107::CODE;;),
108::CODE;;}
109::CODE;;self.precisions = {
110::CODE;;"spherical": 1.0 / self.covariances["spherical"],
111::CODE;;"diag": 1.0 / self.covariances["diag"],
112::CODE;;"tied": linalg.inv(self.covariances["tied"]),
113::CODE;;"full": np.array(
114::CODE;;[linalg.inv(covariance) for covariance in self.covariances["full"]]
115::CODE;;),
116::CODE;;}
117::CODE;;self.X = dict(
118::CODE;;zip(
119::CODE;;COVARIANCE_TYPE,
120::CODE;;[
121::CODE;;generate_data(
122::CODE;;n_samples,
123::CODE;;n_features,
124::CODE;;self.weights,
125::CODE;;self.means,
126::CODE;;self.covariances,
127::CODE;;covar_type,
128::CODE;;dtype=dtype,
129::CODE;;)
130::CODE;;for covar_type in COVARIANCE_TYPE
131::CODE;;],
132::CODE;;)
133::CODE;;)
134::CODE;;self.Y = np.hstack(
135::CODE;;[
136::CODE;;np.full(int(np.round(w * n_samples)), k, dtype=int)
137::CODE;;for k, w in enumerate(self.weights)
138::CODE;;]
139::CODE;;)

680::CODE;;def test_gaussian_mixture_aic_bic():
682::CODE;;rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
683::CODE;;n_samples, n_features, n_components = 50, 3, 2
684::CODE;;X = rng.randn(n_samples, n_features)
686::CODE;;sgh = 0.5 * (
687::CODE;;fast_logdet(np.cov(X.T, bias=1)) + n_features * (1 + np.log(2 * np.pi))
688::CODE;;)
689::CODE;;for cv_type in COVARIANCE_TYPE:
690::CODE;;g = GaussianMixture(
691::CODE;;n_components=n_components,
692::CODE;;covariance_type=cv_type,
693::CODE;;random_state=rng,
694::CODE;;max_iter=200,
695::CODE;;)
696::CODE;;g.fit(X)
697::CODE;;aic = 2 * n_samples * sgh + 2 * g._n_parameters()
698::CODE;;bic = 2 * n_samples * sgh + np.log(n_samples) * g._n_parameters()
699::CODE;;bound = n_features / np.sqrt(n_samples)
700::CODE;;assert (g.aic(X) - aic) / n_samples < bound
701::CODE;;assert (g.bic(X) - bic) / n_samples < bound

192::CODE;;Non-deterministic iterable over random candidate combinations for hyper-
193::CODE;;parameter search. If all parameters are presented as a list,
194::CODE;;sampling without replacement is performed. If at least one parameter
195::CODE;;is given as a distribution, sampling with replacement is used.
196::CODE;;It is highly recommended to use continuous distributions for continuous
197::CODE;;parameters.
198::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <grid_search>`.
199::CODE;;Parameters
200::CODE;;----------

202::CODE;;Dictionary with parameters names (`str`) as keys and distributions
203::CODE;;or lists of parameters to try. Distributions must provide a ``rvs``
204::CODE;;method for sampling (such as those from scipy.stats.distributions).
205::CODE;;If a list is given, it is sampled uniformly.
206::CODE;;If a list of dicts is given, first a dict is sampled uniformly, and
207::CODE;;then a parameter is sampled using that dict as above.
208::CODE;;n_iter : int

211::CODE;;Pseudo random number generator state used for random uniform sampling

214::CODE;;function calls.

216::CODE;;Returns

220::CODE;;as sampled value.

601::CODE;;X_original : {ndarray, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
602::CODE;;Result of the `inverse_transform` function for `X` based on the
603::CODE;;estimator with the best found parameters.
610::CODE;;Only available when `refit=True`.
626::CODE;;Only available when `refit=True` and the estimator is a classifier.
632::CODE;;This method, implemented in sub-classes, makes it possible to
633::CODE;;customize the scheduling of evaluations: GridSearchCV and
634::CODE;;RandomizedSearchCV schedule evaluations for their whole parameter
635::CODE;;search space at once but other more sequential approaches are also
636::CODE;;possible: for instance is possible to iteratively schedule evaluations
637::CODE;;for new regions of the parameter search space based on previously
638::CODE;;collected evaluation results. This makes it possible to implement
639::CODE;;Bayesian optimization or more generally sequential model-based
640::CODE;;optimization by deriving from the BaseSearchCV abstract base class.
641::CODE;;For example, Successive Halving is implemented by calling
642::CODE;;`evaluate_candidates` multiples times (once per iteration of the SH
643::CODE;;process), each time passing a different set of candidates with `X`
644::CODE;;and `y` of increasing sizes.
645::CODE;;Parameters
646::CODE;;----------
647::CODE;;evaluate_candidates : callable
648::CODE;;This callback accepts:
649::CODE;;- a list of candidates, where each candidate is a dict of
650::CODE;;parameter settings.
651::CODE;;- an optional `cv` parameter which can be used to e.g.
652::CODE;;evaluate candidates on different dataset splits, or
653::CODE;;evaluate candidates on subsampled data (as done in the
654::CODE;;Successive Halving estimators). By default, the original
655::CODE;;`cv` parameter is used, and it is available as a private
656::CODE;;`_checked_cv_orig` attribute.
657::CODE;;- an optional `more_results` dict. Each key will be added to
658::CODE;;the `cv_results_` attribute. Values should be lists of
659::CODE;;length `n_candidates`
660::CODE;;It returns a dict of all results so far, formatted like
661::CODE;;``cv_results_``.
662::CODE;;Important note (relevant whether the default cv is used or not):
663::CODE;;in randomized splitters, and unless the random_state parameter of
664::CODE;;cv was set to an int, calling cv.split() multiple times will
665::CODE;;yield different splits. Since cv.split() is called in
666::CODE;;evaluate_candidates, this means that candidates will be evaluated
667::CODE;;on different splits each time evaluate_candidates is called. This
668::CODE;;might be a methodological issue depending on the search strategy
669::CODE;;that you're implementing. To prevent randomized splitters from
670::CODE;;being used, you may use _split._yields_constant_splits()
671::CODE;;Examples
672::CODE;;--------
673::CODE;;::
