1499::CODE;;Determines cross-validated training and test scores for different training
1500::CODE;;set sizes.
1501::CODE;;A cross-validation generator splits the whole dataset k times in training
1502::CODE;;and test data. Subsets of the training set with varying sizes will be used
1503::CODE;;to train the estimator and a score for each training subset size and the
1504::CODE;;test set will be computed. Afterwards, the scores will be averaged over
1505::CODE;;all k runs for each training subset size.
1506::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <learning_curve>`.
1507::CODE;;Parameters
1508::CODE;;----------
1509::CODE;;estimator : object type that implements the "fit" method
1510::CODE;;An object of that type which is cloned for each validation. It must
1511::CODE;;also implement "predict" unless `scoring` is a callable that doesn't
1512::CODE;;rely on "predict" to compute a score.
1513::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
1514::CODE;;Training vector, where `n_samples` is the number of samples and
1515::CODE;;`n_features` is the number of features.
1516::CODE;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_outputs) or None
1517::CODE;;Target relative to X for classification or regression;
1518::CODE;;None for unsupervised learning.
1519::CODE;;groups : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
1520::CODE;;Group labels for the samples used while splitting the dataset into
1521::CODE;;train/test set. Only used in conjunction with a "Group" :term:`cv`
1522::CODE;;instance (e.g., :class:`GroupKFold`).
1523::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.6
1524::CODE;;``groups`` can only be passed if metadata routing is not enabled
1525::CODE;;via ``sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)``. When routing
1526::CODE;;is enabled, pass ``groups`` alongside other metadata via the ``params``
1527::CODE;;argument instead. E.g.:
1528::CODE;;``learning_curve(..., params={'groups': groups})``.
1529::CODE;;train_sizes : array-like of shape (n_ticks,), \
1530::CODE;;default=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 5)
1531::CODE;;Relative or absolute numbers of training examples that will be used to
1532::CODE;;generate the learning curve. If the dtype is float, it is regarded as a
1533::CODE;;fraction of the maximum size of the training set (that is determined
1534::CODE;;by the selected validation method), i.e. it has to be within (0, 1].
1535::CODE;;Otherwise it is interpreted as absolute sizes of the training sets.
1536::CODE;;Note that for classification the number of samples usually has to
1537::CODE;;be big enough to contain at least one sample from each class.
1538::CODE;;cv : int, cross-validation generator or an iterable, default=None
1539::CODE;;Determines the cross-validation splitting strategy.
1540::CODE;;Possible inputs for cv are:
1541::CODE;;- None, to use the default 5-fold cross validation,
1542::CODE;;- int, to specify the number of folds in a `(Stratified)KFold`,
1543::CODE;;- :term:`CV splitter`,
1544::CODE;;- An iterable yielding (train, test) splits as arrays of indices.
1545::CODE;;For int/None inputs, if the estimator is a classifier and ``y`` is
1546::CODE;;either binary or multiclass, :class:`StratifiedKFold` is used. In all
1547::CODE;;other cases, :class:`KFold` is used. These splitters are instantiated
1548::CODE;;with `shuffle=False` so the splits will be the same across calls.
1549::CODE;;Refer :ref:`User Guide <cross_validation>` for the various
1550::CODE;;cross-validation strategies that can be used here.
1551::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.22
1552::CODE;;``cv`` default value if None changed from 3-fold to 5-fold.
1553::CODE;;scoring : str or callable, default=None
1554::CODE;;Scoring method to use to evaluate the training and test sets.
1555::CODE;;- str: see :ref:`scoring_string_names` for options.
1556::CODE;;- callable: a scorer callable object (e.g., function) with signature
1557::CODE;;``scorer(estimator, X, y)``. See :ref:`scoring_callable` for details.
1558::CODE;;- `None`: the `estimator`'s
1559::CODE;;:ref:`default evaluation criterion <scoring_api_overview>` is used.
1560::CODE;;exploit_incremental_learning : bool, default=False
1561::CODE;;If the estimator supports incremental learning, this will be
1562::CODE;;used to speed up fitting for different training set sizes.
1563::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
1564::CODE;;Number of jobs to run in parallel. Training the estimator and computing
1565::CODE;;the score are parallelized over the different training and test sets.
1566::CODE;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
1567::CODE;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
1568::CODE;;for more details.
1569::CODE;;pre_dispatch : int or str, default='all'
1570::CODE;;Number of predispatched jobs for parallel execution (default is
1571::CODE;;all). The option can reduce the allocated memory. The str can
1572::CODE;;be an expression like '2*n_jobs'.
1573::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
1574::CODE;;Controls the verbosity: the higher, the more messages.

1884::CODE;;else (train_scores, test_scores)
1885::CODE;;)
1886::CODE;;return np.array(ret).T
1887::CODE;;@validate_params(
1888::CODE;;{
1889::CODE;;"estimator": [HasMethods(["fit"])],
1890::CODE;;"X": ["array-like", "sparse matrix"],
1891::CODE;;"y": ["array-like", None],
1892::CODE;;"param_name": [str],
1893::CODE;;"param_range": ["array-like"],
1894::CODE;;"groups": ["array-like", None],
1895::CODE;;"cv": ["cv_object"],
1896::CODE;;"scoring": [StrOptions(set(get_scorer_names())), callable, None],
1897::CODE;;"n_jobs": [Integral, None],
1898::CODE;;"pre_dispatch": [Integral, str],
1899::CODE;;"verbose": ["verbose"],
1900::CODE;;"error_score": [StrOptions({"raise"}), Real],
1901::CODE;;"params": [dict, None],
1902::CODE;;},
1904::CODE;;)
1905::CODE;;def validation_curve(
1906::CODE;;estimator,
1907::CODE;;X,
1908::CODE;;y,
1909::CODE;;*,
1910::CODE;;param_name,
1911::CODE;;param_range,
1912::CODE;;groups=None,
1913::CODE;;cv=None,
1914::CODE;;scoring=None,
1915::CODE;;n_jobs=None,
1916::CODE;;pre_dispatch="all",
1917::CODE;;verbose=0,
1918::CODE;;error_score=np.nan,
1919::CODE;;params=None,
1920::CODE;;):
2032::CODE;;_check_groups_routing_disabled(groups)
2033::CODE;;params = {} if params is None else params
2034::CODE;;X, y, groups = indexable(X, y, groups)
2035::CODE;;cv = check_cv(cv, y, classifier=is_classifier(estimator))
2036::CODE;;scorer = check_scoring(estimator, scoring=scoring)
2037::CODE;;if _routing_enabled():
2038::CODE;;router = (
2039::CODE;;MetadataRouter(owner="validation_curve")
2040::CODE;;.add(
2041::CODE;;estimator=estimator,
2042::CODE;;method_mapping=MethodMapping().add(caller="fit", callee="fit"),
2043::CODE;;)
2044::CODE;;.add(
2045::CODE;;splitter=cv,
2046::CODE;;method_mapping=MethodMapping().add(caller="fit", callee="split"),
2047::CODE;;)
2048::CODE;;.add(
2049::CODE;;scorer=scorer,
2050::CODE;;method_mapping=MethodMapping().add(caller="fit", callee="score"),
2051::CODE;;)
2052::CODE;;)
2053::CODE;;try:
2054::CODE;;routed_params = process_routing(router, "fit", **params)
2055::CODE;;except UnsetMetadataPassedError as e:
2060::CODE;;raise UnsetMetadataPassedError(
2061::CODE;;message=str(e).replace("validation_curve.fit", "validation_curve"),
2062::CODE;;unrequested_params=e.unrequested_params,
2063::CODE;;routed_params=e.routed_params,
2064::CODE;;)
2065::CODE;;else:
2066::CODE;;routed_params = Bunch()
2067::CODE;;routed_params.estimator = Bunch(fit=params)
2068::CODE;;routed_params.splitter = Bunch(split={"groups": groups})
2069::CODE;;routed_params.scorer = Bunch(score={})
2070::CODE;;parallel = Parallel(n_jobs=n_jobs, pre_dispatch=pre_dispatch, verbose=verbose)
2071::CODE;;results = parallel(
2072::CODE;;delayed(_fit_and_score)(
2073::CODE;;clone(estimator),
2074::CODE;;X,
2075::CODE;;y,
2076::CODE;;scorer=scorer,
2077::CODE;;train=train,
2078::CODE;;test=test,
2079::CODE;;verbose=verbose,
2080::CODE;;parameters={param_name: v},
2081::CODE;;fit_params=routed_params.estimator.fit,
2082::CODE;;score_params=routed_params.scorer.score,
2083::CODE;;return_train_score=True,
2084::CODE;;error_score=error_score,
2085::CODE;;)
2087::CODE;;for train, test in cv.split(X, y, **routed_params.splitter.split)
2088::CODE;;for v in param_range
2089::CODE;;)
2090::CODE;;n_params = len(param_range)
2091::CODE;;results = _aggregate_score_dicts(results)
2092::CODE;;train_scores = results["train_scores"].reshape(-1, n_params).T
2093::CODE;;test_scores = results["test_scores"].reshape(-1, n_params).T
2094::CODE;;return train_scores, test_scores
2095::CODE;;def _aggregate_score_dicts(scores):
2113::CODE;;return {
2114::CODE;;key: (
2115::CODE;;np.asarray([score[key] for score in scores])
2116::CODE;;if isinstance(scores[0][key], numbers.Number)
2117::CODE;;else [score[key] for score in scores]
2118::CODE;;)
2119::CODE;;for key in scores[0]
2120::CODE;;}

108::CODE;;class _ConstantPredictor(BaseEstimator):
158::CODE;;If `self.estimators_[0]` has the attr, then its safe to assume that other
159::CODE;;estimators have it too. We raise the original `AttributeError` if `attr`
160::CODE;;does not exist. This function is used together with `available_if`.
176::CODE;;Also known as one-vs-all, this strategy consists in fitting one classifier
177::CODE;;per class. For each classifier, the class is fitted against all the other
178::CODE;;classes. In addition to its computational efficiency (only `n_classes`
179::CODE;;classifiers are needed), one advantage of this approach is its
180::CODE;;interpretability. Since each class is represented by one and one classifier
181::CODE;;only, it is possible to gain knowledge about the class by inspecting its
182::CODE;;corresponding classifier. This is the most commonly used strategy for
183::CODE;;multiclass classification and is a fair default choice.
184::CODE;;OneVsRestClassifier can also be used for multilabel classification. To use
185::CODE;;this feature, provide an indicator matrix for the target `y` when calling
186::CODE;;`.fit`. In other words, the target labels should be formatted as a 2D
187::CODE;;binary (0/1) matrix, where [i, j] == 1 indicates the presence of label j
188::CODE;;in sample i. This estimator uses the binary relevance method to perform
189::CODE;;multilabel classification, which involves training one binary classifier
190::CODE;;independently for each label.
191::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <ovr_classification>`.
192::CODE;;Parameters
193::CODE;;----------
194::CODE;;estimator : estimator object
195::CODE;;A regressor or a classifier that implements :term:`fit`.
196::CODE;;When a classifier is passed, :term:`decision_function` will be used
197::CODE;;in priority and it will fallback to :term:`predict_proba` if it is not
198::CODE;;available.
199::CODE;;When a regressor is passed, :term:`predict` is used.
200::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
201::CODE;;The number of jobs to use for the computation: the `n_classes`
202::CODE;;one-vs-rest problems are computed in parallel.
203::CODE;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
204::CODE;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
205::CODE;;for more details.
206::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.20
207::CODE;;`n_jobs` default changed from 1 to None
208::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
209::CODE;;The verbosity level, if non zero, progress messages are printed.
210::CODE;;Below 50, the output is sent to stderr. Otherwise, the output is sent
211::CODE;;to stdout. The frequency of the messages increases with the verbosity
212::CODE;;level, reporting all iterations at 10. See :class:`joblib.Parallel` for
213::CODE;;more details.
214::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
215::CODE;;Attributes
216::CODE;;----------
217::CODE;;estimators_ : list of `n_classes` estimators
218::CODE;;Estimators used for predictions.
219::CODE;;classes_ : array, shape = [`n_classes`]
220::CODE;;Class labels.
221::CODE;;n_classes_ : int
222::CODE;;Number of classes.
223::CODE;;label_binarizer_ : LabelBinarizer object
224::CODE;;Object used to transform multiclass labels to binary labels and
225::CODE;;vice-versa.
226::CODE;;multilabel_ : boolean
227::CODE;;Whether a OneVsRestClassifier is a multilabel classifier.
228::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
229::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
230::CODE;;underlying estimator exposes such an attribute when fit.
231::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
232::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
233::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
234::CODE;;underlying estimator exposes such an attribute when fit.
235::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
236::CODE;;See Also
237::CODE;;--------
238::CODE;;OneVsOneClassifier : One-vs-one multiclass strategy.
239::CODE;;OutputCodeClassifier : (Error-Correcting) Output-Code multiclass strategy.
240::CODE;;sklearn.multioutput.MultiOutputClassifier : Alternate way of extending an
241::CODE;;estimator for multilabel classification.
242::CODE;;sklearn.preprocessing.MultiLabelBinarizer : Transform iterable of iterables
243::CODE;;to binary indicator matrix.
244::CODE;;Examples
245::CODE;;--------
246::CODE;;>>> import numpy as np
247::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.multiclass import OneVsRestClassifier
248::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.svm import SVC
249::CODE;;>>> X = np.array([
250::CODE;;... [10, 10],
251::CODE;;... [8, 10],
252::CODE;;... [-5, 5.5],
253::CODE;;... [-5.4, 5.5],
254::CODE;;... [-20, -20],
255::CODE;;... [-15, -20]
256::CODE;;... ])
257::CODE;;>>> y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2])
258::CODE;;>>> clf = OneVsRestClassifier(SVC()).fit(X, y)
259::CODE;;>>> clf.predict([[-19, -20], [9, 9], [-5, 5]])
260::CODE;;array([2, 0, 1])

410::CODE;;Predicted multi-class targets.
440::CODE;;The returned estimates for all classes are ordered by label of classes.
441::CODE;;Note that in the multilabel case, each sample can have any number of
442::CODE;;labels. This returns the marginal probability that the given sample has
443::CODE;;the label in question. For example, it is entirely consistent that two
444::CODE;;labels both have a 90% probability of applying to a given sample.

446::CODE;;sum to 1.

454::CODE;;Returns the probability of the sample for each class in the model,
455::CODE;;where classes are ordered as they are in `self.classes_`.

41::CODE;;class _BaseNB(ClassifierMixin, BaseEstimator, metaclass=ABCMeta):
46::CODE;;I.e. ``log P(c) + log P(x|c)`` for all rows x of X, as an array-like of
47::CODE;;shape (n_samples, n_classes).
48::CODE;;Public methods predict, predict_proba, predict_log_proba, and
49::CODE;;predict_joint_log_proba pass the input through _check_X before handing it
50::CODE;;over to _joint_log_likelihood. The term "joint log likelihood" is used
51::CODE;;interchangibly with "joint log probability".
56::CODE;;Only used in predict* methods.
60::CODE;;For each row x of X and class y, the joint log probability is given by
61::CODE;;``log P(x, y) = log P(y) + log P(x|y),``
62::CODE;;where ``log P(y)`` is the class prior probability and ``log P(x|y)`` is
63::CODE;;the class-conditional probability.
64::CODE;;Parameters
65::CODE;;----------
66::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
67::CODE;;The input samples.
68::CODE;;Returns
69::CODE;;-------
70::CODE;;C : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_classes)
71::CODE;;Returns the joint log-probability of the samples for each class in
72::CODE;;the model. The columns correspond to the classes in sorted
73::CODE;;order, as they appear in the attribute :term:`classes_`.
80::CODE;;Perform classification on an array of test vectors X.
81::CODE;;Parameters
82::CODE;;----------
83::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
84::CODE;;The input samples.

137::CODE;;Gaussian Naive Bayes (GaussianNB).
138::CODE;;Can perform online updates to model parameters via :meth:`partial_fit`.
139::CODE;;For details on algorithm used to update feature means and variance online,
140::CODE;;see `Stanford CS tech report STAN-CS-79-773 by Chan, Golub, and LeVeque

147::CODE;;adjusted according to the data.

231::CODE;;@staticmethod
232::CODE;;def _update_mean_variance(n_past, mu, var, X, sample_weight=None):
261::CODE;;xp, _ = get_namespace(X)
262::CODE;;if X.shape[0] == 0:
263::CODE;;return mu, var
265::CODE;;if sample_weight is not None:
266::CODE;;n_new = float(xp.sum(sample_weight))
267::CODE;;if np.isclose(n_new, 0.0):
268::CODE;;return mu, var
269::CODE;;new_mu = _average(X, axis=0, weights=sample_weight, xp=xp)
270::CODE;;new_var = _average((X - new_mu) ** 2, axis=0, weights=sample_weight, xp=xp)
271::CODE;;else:
272::CODE;;n_new = X.shape[0]
273::CODE;;new_var = xp.var(X, axis=0)
274::CODE;;new_mu = xp.mean(X, axis=0)
275::CODE;;if n_past == 0:
276::CODE;;return new_mu, new_var
277::CODE;;n_total = float(n_past + n_new)
280::CODE;;total_mu = (n_new * new_mu + n_past * mu) / n_total
284::CODE;;old_ssd = n_past * var
285::CODE;;new_ssd = n_new * new_var
286::CODE;;total_ssd = old_ssd + new_ssd + (n_new * n_past / n_total) * (mu - new_mu) ** 2
287::CODE;;total_var = total_ssd / n_total
288::CODE;;return total_mu, total_var

323::CODE;;def _partial_fit(self, X, y, classes=None, _refit=False, sample_weight=None):
345::CODE;;if _refit:
346::CODE;;self.classes_ = None

351::CODE;;if sample_weight is not None:
352::CODE;;sample_weight = _check_sample_weight(sample_weight, X, dtype=float_dtype)
353::CODE;;xp_y, _ = get_namespace(y)
358::CODE;;self.epsilon_ = self.var_smoothing * xp.max(xp.var(X, axis=0))
359::CODE;;if first_call:
362::CODE;;n_features = X.shape[1]
363::CODE;;n_classes = self.classes_.shape[0]
364::CODE;;self.theta_ = xp.zeros(
365::CODE;;(n_classes, n_features), dtype=float_dtype, device=device_
366::CODE;;)
367::CODE;;self.var_ = xp.zeros(
368::CODE;;(n_classes, n_features), dtype=float_dtype, device=device_
369::CODE;;)
370::CODE;;self.class_count_ = xp.zeros(n_classes, dtype=float_dtype, device=device_)
373::CODE;;if self.priors is not None:
374::CODE;;priors = xp.asarray(self.priors, dtype=float_dtype, device=device_)
376::CODE;;if priors.shape[0] != n_classes:
377::CODE;;raise ValueError("Number of priors must match number of classes.")
379::CODE;;if not xpx.isclose(xp.sum(priors), 1.0):
380::CODE;;raise ValueError("The sum of the priors should be 1.")
382::CODE;;if xp.any(priors < 0):
383::CODE;;raise ValueError("Priors must be non-negative.")
384::CODE;;self.class_prior_ = priors
385::CODE;;else:
387::CODE;;self.class_prior_ = xp.zeros(
388::CODE;;self.classes_.shape[0], dtype=float_dtype, device=device_
389::CODE;;)
390::CODE;;else:
391::CODE;;if X.shape[1] != self.theta_.shape[1]:
392::CODE;;msg = "Number of features %d does not match previous data %d."
393::CODE;;raise ValueError(msg % (X.shape[1], self.theta_.shape[1]))
395::CODE;;self.var_[:, :] -= self.epsilon_
396::CODE;;classes = self.classes_
397::CODE;;unique_y = xp_y.unique_values(y)
398::CODE;;unique_y_in_classes = _isin(unique_y, classes, xp=xp_y)
399::CODE;;if not xp_y.all(unique_y_in_classes):
400::CODE;;raise ValueError(
401::CODE;;"The target label(s) %s in y do not exist in the initial classes %s"
402::CODE;;% (unique_y[~unique_y_in_classes], classes)
403::CODE;;)
404::CODE;;for y_i in unique_y:
405::CODE;;i = int(xp_y.searchsorted(classes, y_i))
406::CODE;;y_i_mask = xp.asarray(y == y_i, device=device_)
407::CODE;;X_i = X[y_i_mask]
408::CODE;;if sample_weight is not None:
409::CODE;;sw_i = sample_weight[y_i_mask]
410::CODE;;N_i = xp.sum(sw_i)
411::CODE;;else:
412::CODE;;sw_i = None
413::CODE;;N_i = X_i.shape[0]
414::CODE;;new_theta, new_sigma = self._update_mean_variance(
415::CODE;;self.class_count_[i], self.theta_[i, :], self.var_[i, :], X_i, sw_i
416::CODE;;)
417::CODE;;self.theta_[i, :] = new_theta
418::CODE;;self.var_[i, :] = new_sigma
419::CODE;;self.class_count_[i] += N_i
420::CODE;;self.var_[:, :] += self.epsilon_
422::CODE;;if self.priors is None:
424::CODE;;self.class_prior_ = self.class_count_ / xp.sum(self.class_count_)
425::CODE;;return self
426::CODE;;def _joint_log_likelihood(self, X):
427::CODE;;xp, _ = get_namespace(X)
428::CODE;;joint_log_likelihood = []
429::CODE;;for i in range(size(self.classes_)):
430::CODE;;jointi = xp.log(self.class_prior_[i])
431::CODE;;n_ij = -0.5 * xp.sum(xp.log(2.0 * xp.pi * self.var_[i, :]))
432::CODE;;n_ij = n_ij - 0.5 * xp.sum(
433::CODE;;((X - self.theta_[i, :]) ** 2) / (self.var_[i, :]), axis=1
434::CODE;;)
435::CODE;;joint_log_likelihood.append(jointi + n_ij)
436::CODE;;joint_log_likelihood = xp.stack(joint_log_likelihood).T
437::CODE;;return joint_log_likelihood

756::CODE;;The Complement Naive Bayes classifier was designed to correct the "severe
757::CODE;;assumptions" made by the standard Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier. It is
758::CODE;;particularly suited for imbalanced data sets.
759::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <complement_naive_bayes>`.
760::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
761::CODE;;Parameters
762::CODE;;----------
763::CODE;;alpha : float or array-like of shape (n_features,), default=1.0
764::CODE;;Additive (Laplace/Lidstone) smoothing parameter
765::CODE;;(set alpha=0 and force_alpha=True, for no smoothing).
766::CODE;;force_alpha : bool, default=True
767::CODE;;If False and alpha is less than 1e-10, it will set alpha to
768::CODE;;1e-10. If True, alpha will remain unchanged. This may cause
769::CODE;;numerical errors if alpha is too close to 0.
770::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
771::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.4
772::CODE;;The default value of `force_alpha` changed to `True`.
773::CODE;;fit_prior : bool, default=True
774::CODE;;Only used in edge case with a single class in the training set.
775::CODE;;class_prior : array-like of shape (n_classes,), default=None
776::CODE;;Prior probabilities of the classes. Not used.
777::CODE;;norm : bool, default=False
778::CODE;;Whether or not a second normalization of the weights is performed. The
779::CODE;;default behavior mirrors the implementations found in Mahout and Weka,
780::CODE;;which do not follow the full algorithm described in Table 9 of the
781::CODE;;paper.
782::CODE;;Attributes
783::CODE;;----------
784::CODE;;class_count_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
785::CODE;;Number of samples encountered for each class during fitting. This
786::CODE;;value is weighted by the sample weight when provided.
787::CODE;;class_log_prior_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
788::CODE;;Smoothed empirical log probability for each class. Only used in edge
789::CODE;;case with a single class in the training set.
790::CODE;;classes_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
791::CODE;;Class labels known to the classifier
792::CODE;;feature_all_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
793::CODE;;Number of samples encountered for each feature during fitting. This
794::CODE;;value is weighted by the sample weight when provided.
795::CODE;;feature_count_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes, n_features)
796::CODE;;Number of samples encountered for each (class, feature) during fitting.
797::CODE;;This value is weighted by the sample weight when provided.
798::CODE;;feature_log_prob_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes, n_features)
799::CODE;;Empirical weights for class complements.
800::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
801::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
802::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
803::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
804::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
805::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
806::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
807::CODE;;See Also
808::CODE;;--------
809::CODE;;BernoulliNB : Naive Bayes classifier for multivariate Bernoulli models.
810::CODE;;CategoricalNB : Naive Bayes classifier for categorical features.
811::CODE;;GaussianNB : Gaussian Naive Bayes.
812::CODE;;MultinomialNB : Naive Bayes classifier for multinomial models.

658::CODE;;or (n_queries, n_indexed) if metric == 'precomputed', default=None

661::CODE;;In this case, the query point is not considered its own neighbor.
662::CODE;;n_neighbors : int, default=None

672::CODE;;neigh_ind : ndarray of shape (n_queries, n_neighbors)
673::CODE;;Indices of the nearest points in the population matrix.
674::CODE;;Examples
675::CODE;;--------
676::CODE;;In the following example, we construct a NearestNeighbors
677::CODE;;class from an array representing our data set and ask who's
678::CODE;;the closest point to [1,1,1]
679::CODE;;>>> samples = [[0., 0., 0.], [0., .5, 0.], [1., 1., .5]]
680::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
681::CODE;;>>> neigh = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1)
682::CODE;;>>> neigh.fit(samples)
683::CODE;;NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1)
684::CODE;;>>> print(neigh.kneighbors([[1., 1., 1.]]))
685::CODE;;(array([[0.5]]), array([[2]]))
686::CODE;;As you can see, it returns [[0.5]], and [[2]], which means that the
687::CODE;;element is at distance 0.5 and is the third element of samples
688::CODE;;(indexes start at 0). You can also query for multiple points:
689::CODE;;>>> X = [[0., 1., 0.], [1., 0., 1.]]
690::CODE;;>>> neigh.kneighbors(X, return_distance=False)
691::CODE;;array([[1],
692::CODE;;[2]]...)
832::CODE;;Parameters
833::CODE;;----------
834::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_queries, n_features), \
835::CODE;;or (n_queries, n_indexed) if metric == 'precomputed', default=None
836::CODE;;The query point or points.
837::CODE;;If not provided, neighbors of each indexed point are returned.
838::CODE;;In this case, the query point is not considered its own neighbor.

840::CODE;;(n_queries, n_indexed). Otherwise the shape should be

901::CODE;;def _radius_neighbors_reduce_func(self, dist, start, radius, return_distance):
921::CODE;;neigh_ind = [np.where(d <= radius)[0] for d in dist]
922::CODE;;if return_distance:
923::CODE;;if self.effective_metric_ == "euclidean":
924::CODE;;dist = [np.sqrt(d[neigh_ind[i]]) for i, d in enumerate(dist)]
925::CODE;;else:
926::CODE;;dist = [d[neigh_ind[i]] for i, d in enumerate(dist)]
927::CODE;;results = dist, neigh_ind
928::CODE;;else:
929::CODE;;results = neigh_ind
930::CODE;;return results

39::CODE;;Parameters
40::CODE;;----------
41::CODE;;n_neighbors : int, default=5
42::CODE;;Number of neighbors to use by default for :meth:`kneighbors` queries.
43::CODE;;weights : {'uniform', 'distance'}, callable or None, default='uniform'
44::CODE;;Weight function used in prediction. Possible values:
45::CODE;;- 'uniform' : uniform weights. All points in each neighborhood
46::CODE;;are weighted equally.
47::CODE;;- 'distance' : weight points by the inverse of their distance.
48::CODE;;in this case, closer neighbors of a query point will have a
49::CODE;;greater influence than neighbors which are further away.
50::CODE;;- [callable] : a user-defined function which accepts an
51::CODE;;array of distances, and returns an array of the same shape
52::CODE;;containing the weights.
53::CODE;;Refer to the example entitled
54::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neighbors_plot_classification.py`
55::CODE;;showing the impact of the `weights` parameter on the decision
56::CODE;;boundary.
57::CODE;;algorithm : {'auto', 'ball_tree', 'kd_tree', 'brute'}, default='auto'
58::CODE;;Algorithm used to compute the nearest neighbors:
59::CODE;;- 'ball_tree' will use :class:`BallTree`
60::CODE;;- 'kd_tree' will use :class:`KDTree`
61::CODE;;- 'brute' will use a brute-force search.
62::CODE;;- 'auto' will attempt to decide the most appropriate algorithm
63::CODE;;based on the values passed to :meth:`fit` method.
64::CODE;;Note: fitting on sparse input will override the setting of
65::CODE;;this parameter, using brute force.
66::CODE;;leaf_size : int, default=30
67::CODE;;Leaf size passed to BallTree or KDTree. This can affect the
68::CODE;;speed of the construction and query, as well as the memory
69::CODE;;required to store the tree. The optimal value depends on the
70::CODE;;nature of the problem.
71::CODE;;p : float, default=2
72::CODE;;Power parameter for the Minkowski metric. When p = 1, this is equivalent
73::CODE;;to using manhattan_distance (l1), and euclidean_distance (l2) for p = 2.
74::CODE;;For arbitrary p, minkowski_distance (l_p) is used. This parameter is expected
75::CODE;;to be positive.
76::CODE;;metric : str or callable, default='minkowski'
77::CODE;;Metric to use for distance computation. Default is "minkowski", which
78::CODE;;results in the standard Euclidean distance when p = 2. See the
79::CODE;;documentation of `scipy.spatial.distance
80::CODE;;<https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/spatial.distance.html>`_ and
81::CODE;;the metrics listed in
82::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise.distance_metrics` for valid metric
83::CODE;;values.
84::CODE;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a distance matrix and
85::CODE;;must be square during fit. X may be a :term:`sparse graph`, in which
86::CODE;;case only "nonzero" elements may be considered neighbors.
87::CODE;;If metric is a callable function, it takes two arrays representing 1D
88::CODE;;vectors as inputs and must return one value indicating the distance
89::CODE;;between those vectors. This works for Scipy's metrics, but is less
90::CODE;;efficient than passing the metric name as a string.
91::CODE;;metric_params : dict, default=None
92::CODE;;Additional keyword arguments for the metric function.
93::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
94::CODE;;The number of parallel jobs to run for neighbors search.
95::CODE;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
96::CODE;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
97::CODE;;for more details.
98::CODE;;Doesn't affect :meth:`fit` method.

198::CODE;;"Inputs within the same classes for at least 1 feature are identical."

200::CODE;;err_msg = "All features have zero variance. Division by zero."
201::CODE;;if is_X_sparse and np.all((X.max(axis=0) - X.min(axis=0)).toarray() == 0):
202::CODE;;raise ValueError(err_msg)
203::CODE;;elif not is_X_sparse and np.all(np.ptp(X, axis=0) == 0):
204::CODE;;raise ValueError(err_msg)
205::CODE;;dataset_centroid_ = X.mean(axis=0)
207::CODE;;m = np.sqrt((1.0 / nk) - (1.0 / n_samples))
210::CODE;;s = self.within_class_std_dev_ + np.median(self.within_class_std_dev_)
212::CODE;;ms = mm * s
213::CODE;;self.deviations_ = np.array(
214::CODE;;(self.centroids_ - dataset_centroid_) / ms, copy=False
215::CODE;;)
218::CODE;;if self.shrink_threshold:
219::CODE;;signs = np.sign(self.deviations_)
220::CODE;;self.deviations_ = np.abs(self.deviations_) - self.shrink_threshold
221::CODE;;np.clip(self.deviations_, 0, None, out=self.deviations_)
222::CODE;;self.deviations_ *= signs
224::CODE;;msd = ms * self.deviations_
225::CODE;;self.centroids_ = np.array(dataset_centroid_ + msd, copy=False)
226::CODE;;return self
227::CODE;;def predict(self, X):
239::CODE;;check_is_fitted(self)
240::CODE;;if np.isclose(self.class_prior_, 1 / len(self.classes_)).all():
242::CODE;;ensure_all_finite = (
243::CODE;;"allow-nan" if get_tags(self).input_tags.allow_nan else True
244::CODE;;)
245::CODE;;X = validate_data(
246::CODE;;self,
247::CODE;;X,
248::CODE;;ensure_all_finite=ensure_all_finite,
249::CODE;;accept_sparse="csr",
250::CODE;;reset=False,
251::CODE;;)
252::CODE;;return self.classes_[
253::CODE;;pairwise_distances_argmin(X, self.centroids_, metric=self.metric)
254::CODE;;]
255::CODE;;else:
256::CODE;;return super().predict(X)
257::CODE;;def _decision_function(self, X):
259::CODE;;check_is_fitted(self, "centroids_")
260::CODE;;X_normalized = validate_data(
261::CODE;;self, X, copy=True, reset=False, accept_sparse="csr", dtype=np.float64
262::CODE;;)
263::CODE;;discriminant_score = np.empty(
264::CODE;;(X_normalized.shape[0], self.classes_.size), dtype=np.float64
265::CODE;;)
266::CODE;;mask = self.within_class_std_dev_ != 0
267::CODE;;X_normalized[:, mask] /= self.within_class_std_dev_[mask]
268::CODE;;centroids_normalized = self.centroids_.copy()
269::CODE;;centroids_normalized[:, mask] /= self.within_class_std_dev_[mask]
270::CODE;;for class_idx in range(self.classes_.size):
271::CODE;;distances = pairwise_distances(
272::CODE;;X_normalized, centroids_normalized[[class_idx]], metric=self.metric
273::CODE;;).ravel()
274::CODE;;distances **= 2
275::CODE;;discriminant_score[:, class_idx] = np.squeeze(
276::CODE;;-distances + 2.0 * np.log(self.class_prior_[class_idx])
277::CODE;;)
278::CODE;;return discriminant_score

17::CODE;;The target is predicted by local interpolation of the targets
18::CODE;;associated of the nearest neighbors in the training set.
19::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <regression>`.
20::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.9
21::CODE;;Parameters
22::CODE;;----------
23::CODE;;n_neighbors : int, default=5
24::CODE;;Number of neighbors to use by default for :meth:`kneighbors` queries.
25::CODE;;weights : {'uniform', 'distance'}, callable or None, default='uniform'
26::CODE;;Weight function used in prediction. Possible values:
27::CODE;;- 'uniform' : uniform weights. All points in each neighborhood
28::CODE;;are weighted equally.
29::CODE;;- 'distance' : weight points by the inverse of their distance.
30::CODE;;in this case, closer neighbors of a query point will have a
31::CODE;;greater influence than neighbors which are further away.
32::CODE;;- [callable] : a user-defined function which accepts an
33::CODE;;array of distances, and returns an array of the same shape
34::CODE;;containing the weights.
35::CODE;;Uniform weights are used by default.
36::CODE;;See the following example for a demonstration of the impact of
37::CODE;;different weighting schemes on predictions:
38::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neighbors_plot_regression.py`.
39::CODE;;algorithm : {'auto', 'ball_tree', 'kd_tree', 'brute'}, default='auto'
40::CODE;;Algorithm used to compute the nearest neighbors:
41::CODE;;- 'ball_tree' will use :class:`BallTree`
42::CODE;;- 'kd_tree' will use :class:`KDTree`
43::CODE;;- 'brute' will use a brute-force search.
44::CODE;;- 'auto' will attempt to decide the most appropriate algorithm
45::CODE;;based on the values passed to :meth:`fit` method.
46::CODE;;Note: fitting on sparse input will override the setting of
47::CODE;;this parameter, using brute force.
48::CODE;;leaf_size : int, default=30
49::CODE;;Leaf size passed to BallTree or KDTree. This can affect the
50::CODE;;speed of the construction and query, as well as the memory
51::CODE;;required to store the tree. The optimal value depends on the
52::CODE;;nature of the problem.
53::CODE;;p : float, default=2
54::CODE;;Power parameter for the Minkowski metric. When p = 1, this is
55::CODE;;equivalent to using manhattan_distance (l1), and euclidean_distance
56::CODE;;(l2) for p = 2. For arbitrary p, minkowski_distance (l_p) is used.
57::CODE;;metric : str, DistanceMetric object or callable, default='minkowski'
58::CODE;;Metric to use for distance computation. Default is "minkowski", which
59::CODE;;results in the standard Euclidean distance when p = 2. See the
60::CODE;;documentation of `scipy.spatial.distance
61::CODE;;<https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/spatial.distance.html>`_ and
62::CODE;;the metrics listed in
63::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise.distance_metrics` for valid metric
64::CODE;;values.
65::CODE;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a distance matrix and
66::CODE;;must be square during fit. X may be a :term:`sparse graph`, in which
67::CODE;;case only "nonzero" elements may be considered neighbors.
68::CODE;;If metric is a callable function, it takes two arrays representing 1D
69::CODE;;vectors as inputs and must return one value indicating the distance
70::CODE;;between those vectors. This works for Scipy's metrics, but is less
71::CODE;;efficient than passing the metric name as a string.
72::CODE;;If metric is a DistanceMetric object, it will be passed directly to
73::CODE;;the underlying computation routines.
74::CODE;;metric_params : dict, default=None
75::CODE;;Additional keyword arguments for the metric function.
76::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
77::CODE;;The number of parallel jobs to run for neighbors search.
78::CODE;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
79::CODE;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
80::CODE;;for more details.
81::CODE;;Doesn't affect :meth:`fit` method.
82::CODE;;Attributes
83::CODE;;----------
84::CODE;;effective_metric_ : str or callable
85::CODE;;The distance metric to use. It will be same as the `metric` parameter
86::CODE;;or a synonym of it, e.g. 'euclidean' if the `metric` parameter set to
87::CODE;;'minkowski' and `p` parameter set to 2.
88::CODE;;effective_metric_params_ : dict
89::CODE;;Additional keyword arguments for the metric function. For most metrics
90::CODE;;will be same with `metric_params` parameter, but may also contain the
91::CODE;;`p` parameter value if the `effective_metric_` attribute is set to
92::CODE;;'minkowski'.
93::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
94::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.

96::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
97::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`

99::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
100::CODE;;n_samples_fit_ : int
101::CODE;;Number of samples in the fitted data.

106::CODE;;KNeighborsClassifier : Classifier implementing the k-nearest neighbors vote.
107::CODE;;RadiusNeighborsClassifier : Classifier implementing

13::CODE;;def compute_kernel_slow(Y, X, kernel, h):
14::CODE;;if h == "scott":
15::CODE;;h = X.shape[0] ** (-1 / (X.shape[1] + 4))
16::CODE;;elif h == "silverman":
17::CODE;;h = (X.shape[0] * (X.shape[1] + 2) / 4) ** (-1 / (X.shape[1] + 4))
18::CODE;;d = np.sqrt(((Y[:, None, :] - X) ** 2).sum(-1))
19::CODE;;norm = kernel_norm(h, X.shape[1], kernel) / X.shape[0]
20::CODE;;if kernel == "gaussian":
21::CODE;;return norm * np.exp(-0.5 * (d * d) / (h * h)).sum(-1)
22::CODE;;elif kernel == "tophat":
23::CODE;;return norm * (d < h).sum(-1)
24::CODE;;elif kernel == "epanechnikov":
25::CODE;;return norm * ((1.0 - (d * d) / (h * h)) * (d < h)).sum(-1)
26::CODE;;elif kernel == "exponential":
27::CODE;;return norm * (np.exp(-d / h)).sum(-1)
28::CODE;;elif kernel == "linear":
29::CODE;;return norm * ((1 - d / h) * (d < h)).sum(-1)
30::CODE;;elif kernel == "cosine":
31::CODE;;return norm * (np.cos(0.5 * np.pi * d / h) * (d < h)).sum(-1)
32::CODE;;else:
33::CODE;;raise ValueError("kernel not recognized")
34::CODE;;def check_results(kernel, bandwidth, atol, rtol, X, Y, dens_true):
35::CODE;;kde = KernelDensity(kernel=kernel, bandwidth=bandwidth, atol=atol, rtol=rtol)
36::CODE;;log_dens = kde.fit(X).score_samples(Y)
37::CODE;;assert_allclose(np.exp(log_dens), dens_true, atol=atol, rtol=max(1e-7, rtol))
38::CODE;;assert_allclose(
39::CODE;;np.exp(kde.score(Y)), np.prod(dens_true), atol=atol, rtol=max(1e-7, rtol)
40::CODE;;)
41::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize(
42::CODE;;"kernel", ["gaussian", "tophat", "epanechnikov", "exponential", "linear", "cosine"]
43::CODE;;)
44::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("bandwidth", [0.01, 0.1, 1, "scott", "silverman"])

1399::CODE;;metric_params=metric_params,
1400::CODE;;)

36::CODE;;V_mahalanobis = np.dot(V_mahalanobis, V_mahalanobis.T)
37::CODE;;DIMENSION = 3
38::CODE;;METRICS = {
39::CODE;;"euclidean": {},
40::CODE;;"manhattan": {},
41::CODE;;"minkowski": dict(p=3),
42::CODE;;"chebyshev": {},
43::CODE;;"seuclidean": dict(V=rng.random_sample(DIMENSION)),
44::CODE;;"mahalanobis": dict(V=V_mahalanobis),

46::CODE;;KD_TREE_METRICS = ["euclidean", "manhattan", "chebyshev", "minkowski"]
47::CODE;;BALL_TREE_METRICS = list(METRICS)
48::CODE;;def dist_func(x1, x2, p):
49::CODE;;return np.sum((x1 - x2) ** p) ** (1.0 / p)
50::CODE;;def compute_kernel_slow(Y, X, kernel, h):
51::CODE;;d = np.sqrt(((Y[:, None, :] - X) ** 2).sum(-1))
52::CODE;;norm = kernel_norm(h, X.shape[1], kernel)
53::CODE;;if kernel == "gaussian":
54::CODE;;return norm * np.exp(-0.5 * (d * d) / (h * h)).sum(-1)
55::CODE;;elif kernel == "tophat":
56::CODE;;return norm * (d < h).sum(-1)
57::CODE;;elif kernel == "epanechnikov":
58::CODE;;return norm * ((1.0 - (d * d) / (h * h)) * (d < h)).sum(-1)
59::CODE;;elif kernel == "exponential":
60::CODE;;return norm * (np.exp(-d / h)).sum(-1)
61::CODE;;elif kernel == "linear":
62::CODE;;return norm * ((1 - d / h) * (d < h)).sum(-1)
63::CODE;;elif kernel == "cosine":
64::CODE;;return norm * (np.cos(0.5 * np.pi * d / h) * (d < h)).sum(-1)
65::CODE;;else:
66::CODE;;raise ValueError("kernel not recognized")
67::CODE;;def brute_force_neighbors(X, Y, k, metric, **kwargs):
68::CODE;;D = DistanceMetric.get_metric(metric, **kwargs).pairwise(Y, X)
69::CODE;;ind = np.argsort(D, axis=1)[:, :k]
70::CODE;;dist = D[np.arange(Y.shape[0])[:, None], ind]
71::CODE;;return dist, ind
72::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("Cls", [KDTree, BallTree])
73::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize(

75::CODE;;)
76::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("h", [0.01, 0.1, 1])
77::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("rtol", [0, 1e-5])
78::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("atol", [1e-6, 1e-2])
79::CODE;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("breadth_first", [True, False])
80::CODE;;def test_kernel_density(
81::CODE;;Cls, kernel, h, rtol, atol, breadth_first, n_samples=100, n_features=3
82::CODE;;):
83::CODE;;rng = check_random_state(1)
84::CODE;;X = rng.random_sample((n_samples, n_features))
85::CODE;;Y = rng.random_sample((n_samples, n_features))
86::CODE;;dens_true = compute_kernel_slow(Y, X, kernel, h)

1141::CODE;;Parameters
1142::CODE;;----------
1143::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
1144::CODE;;The input data.
1145::CODE;;Returns
1146::CODE;;-------
1147::CODE;;y_prob : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_classes)
1148::CODE;;The predicted probability of the sample for each class in the
1149::CODE;;model, where classes are ordered as they are in `self.classes_`.
1165::CODE;;This model optimizes the squared error using LBFGS or stochastic gradient
1166::CODE;;descent.
1167::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1168::CODE;;Parameters
1169::CODE;;----------
1170::CODE;;loss : {'squared_error', 'poisson'}, default='squared_error'
1171::CODE;;The loss function to use when training the weights. Note that the
1172::CODE;;"squared error" and "poisson" losses actually implement
1173::CODE;;"half squares error" and "half poisson deviance" to simplify the
1174::CODE;;computation of the gradient. Furthermore, the "poisson" loss internally uses
1175::CODE;;a log-link (exponential as the output activation function) and requires
1176::CODE;;``y >= 0``.
1177::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
1178::CODE;;Added parameter `loss` and option 'poisson'.
1179::CODE;;hidden_layer_sizes : array-like of shape(n_layers - 2,), default=(100,)
1180::CODE;;The ith element represents the number of neurons in the ith
1181::CODE;;hidden layer.
1182::CODE;;activation : {'identity', 'logistic', 'tanh', 'relu'}, default='relu'
1183::CODE;;Activation function for the hidden layer.
1184::CODE;;- 'identity', no-op activation, useful to implement linear bottleneck,
1185::CODE;;returns f(x) = x
1186::CODE;;- 'logistic', the logistic sigmoid function,
1187::CODE;;returns f(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)).
1188::CODE;;- 'tanh', the hyperbolic tan function,
1189::CODE;;returns f(x) = tanh(x).
1190::CODE;;- 'relu', the rectified linear unit function,
1191::CODE;;returns f(x) = max(0, x)
1192::CODE;;solver : {'lbfgs', 'sgd', 'adam'}, default='adam'
1193::CODE;;The solver for weight optimization.
1194::CODE;;- 'lbfgs' is an optimizer in the family of quasi-Newton methods.
1195::CODE;;- 'sgd' refers to stochastic gradient descent.
1196::CODE;;- 'adam' refers to a stochastic gradient-based optimizer proposed by
1197::CODE;;Kingma, Diederik, and Jimmy Ba
1198::CODE;;For a comparison between Adam optimizer and SGD, see
1199::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neural_networks_plot_mlp_training_curves.py`.
1200::CODE;;Note: The default solver 'adam' works pretty well on relatively
1201::CODE;;large datasets (with thousands of training samples or more) in terms of
1202::CODE;;both training time and validation score.
1203::CODE;;For small datasets, however, 'lbfgs' can converge faster and perform
1204::CODE;;better.
1205::CODE;;alpha : float, default=0.0001
1206::CODE;;Strength of the L2 regularization term. The L2 regularization term
1207::CODE;;is divided by the sample size when added to the loss.
1208::CODE;;batch_size : int, default='auto'
1209::CODE;;Size of minibatches for stochastic optimizers.
1210::CODE;;If the solver is 'lbfgs', the regressor will not use minibatch.
1211::CODE;;When set to "auto", `batch_size=min(200, n_samples)`.
1212::CODE;;learning_rate : {'constant', 'invscaling', 'adaptive'}, default='constant'
1213::CODE;;Learning rate schedule for weight updates.
1214::CODE;;- 'constant' is a constant learning rate given by
1215::CODE;;'learning_rate_init'.
1216::CODE;;- 'invscaling' gradually decreases the learning rate ``learning_rate_``
1217::CODE;;at each time step 't' using an inverse scaling exponent of 'power_t'.
1218::CODE;;effective_learning_rate = learning_rate_init / pow(t, power_t)
1219::CODE;;- 'adaptive' keeps the learning rate constant to
1220::CODE;;'learning_rate_init' as long as training loss keeps decreasing.
1221::CODE;;Each time two consecutive epochs fail to decrease training loss by at
1222::CODE;;least tol, or fail to increase validation score by at least tol if
1223::CODE;;'early_stopping' is on, the current learning rate is divided by 5.
1224::CODE;;Only used when solver='sgd'.
1225::CODE;;learning_rate_init : float, default=0.001
1226::CODE;;The initial learning rate used. It controls the step-size
1227::CODE;;in updating the weights. Only used when solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
1228::CODE;;power_t : float, default=0.5
1229::CODE;;The exponent for inverse scaling learning rate.
1230::CODE;;It is used in updating effective learning rate when the learning_rate
1231::CODE;;is set to 'invscaling'. Only used when solver='sgd'.
1232::CODE;;max_iter : int, default=200
1233::CODE;;Maximum number of iterations. The solver iterates until convergence
1234::CODE;;(determined by 'tol') or this number of iterations. For stochastic
1235::CODE;;solvers ('sgd', 'adam'), note that this determines the number of epochs
1236::CODE;;(how many times each data point will be used), not the number of
1237::CODE;;gradient steps.
1238::CODE;;shuffle : bool, default=True
1239::CODE;;Whether to shuffle samples in each iteration. Only used when
1240::CODE;;solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
1241::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
1242::CODE;;Determines random number generation for weights and bias
1243::CODE;;initialization, train-test split if early stopping is used, and batch
1244::CODE;;sampling when solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
1245::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
1246::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
1247::CODE;;tol : float, default=1e-4
1248::CODE;;Tolerance for the optimization. When the loss or score is not improving
1249::CODE;;by at least ``tol`` for ``n_iter_no_change`` consecutive iterations,
1250::CODE;;unless ``learning_rate`` is set to 'adaptive', convergence is
1251::CODE;;considered to be reached and training stops.
1252::CODE;;verbose : bool, default=False
1253::CODE;;Whether to print progress messages to stdout.
1254::CODE;;warm_start : bool, default=False
1255::CODE;;When set to True, reuse the solution of the previous
1256::CODE;;call to fit as initialization, otherwise, just erase the
1257::CODE;;previous solution. See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
1258::CODE;;momentum : float, default=0.9

1481::CODE;;def partial_fit(self, X, y, sample_weight=None):
1497::CODE;;return self._fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight, incremental=True)
21::CODE;;A Restricted Boltzmann Machine with binary visible units and
22::CODE;;binary hidden units. Parameters are estimated using Stochastic Maximum
23::CODE;;Likelihood (SML), also known as Persistent Contrastive Divergence (PCD)
24::CODE;;[2].
25::CODE;;The time complexity of this implementation is ``O(d ** 2)`` assuming
26::CODE;;d ~ n_features ~ n_components.
27::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <rbm>`.
28::CODE;;Parameters
29::CODE;;----------
30::CODE;;n_components : int, default=256
31::CODE;;Number of binary hidden units.
32::CODE;;learning_rate : float, default=0.1
33::CODE;;The learning rate for weight updates. It is *highly* recommended
34::CODE;;to tune this hyper-parameter. Reasonable values are in the
35::CODE;;10**[0., -3.] range.
36::CODE;;batch_size : int, default=10
37::CODE;;Number of examples per minibatch.
38::CODE;;n_iter : int, default=10
39::CODE;;Number of iterations/sweeps over the training dataset to perform
40::CODE;;during training.
41::CODE;;verbose : int, default=0
42::CODE;;The verbosity level. The default, zero, means silent mode. Range
43::CODE;;of values is [0, inf].
44::CODE;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
45::CODE;;Determines random number generation for:
46::CODE;;- Gibbs sampling from visible and hidden layers.
47::CODE;;- Initializing components, sampling from layers during fit.
48::CODE;;- Corrupting the data when scoring samples.
49::CODE;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
50::CODE;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
51::CODE;;Attributes
52::CODE;;----------
53::CODE;;intercept_hidden_ : array-like of shape (n_components,)
54::CODE;;Biases of the hidden units.
55::CODE;;intercept_visible_ : array-like of shape (n_features,)
56::CODE;;Biases of the visible units.
57::CODE;;components_ : array-like of shape (n_components, n_features)
58::CODE;;Weight matrix, where `n_features` is the number of
59::CODE;;visible units and `n_components` is the number of hidden units.
60::CODE;;h_samples_ : array-like of shape (batch_size, n_components)
61::CODE;;Hidden Activation sampled from the model distribution,
62::CODE;;where `batch_size` is the number of examples per minibatch and
63::CODE;;`n_components` is the number of hidden units.
64::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
65::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
66::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
67::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
68::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
69::CODE;;has feature names that are all strings.
70::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
71::CODE;;See Also
72::CODE;;--------
73::CODE;;sklearn.neural_network.MLPRegressor : Multi-layer Perceptron regressor.
74::CODE;;sklearn.neural_network.MLPClassifier : Multi-layer Perceptron classifier.
75::CODE;;sklearn.decomposition.PCA : An unsupervised linear dimensionality
76::CODE;;reduction model.
77::CODE;;References
78::CODE;;----------
79::CODE;;[1] Hinton, G. E., Osindero, S. and Teh, Y. A fast learning algorithm for
80::CODE;;deep belief nets. Neural Computation 18, pp 1527-1554.
81::CODE;;https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/fastnc.pdf
82::CODE;;[2] Tieleman, T. Training Restricted Boltzmann Machines using
83::CODE;;Approximations to the Likelihood Gradient. International Conference

62::CODE;;learning_rate_init : float, default=0.1
63::CODE;;The initial learning rate used. It controls the step-size in updating
64::CODE;;the weights
65::CODE;;lr_schedule : {'constant', 'adaptive', 'invscaling'}, default='constant'
66::CODE;;Learning rate schedule for weight updates.
67::CODE;;-'constant', is a constant learning rate given by
68::CODE;;'learning_rate_init'.
69::CODE;;-'invscaling' gradually decreases the learning rate 'learning_rate_' at
70::CODE;;each time step 't' using an inverse scaling exponent of 'power_t'.
71::CODE;;learning_rate_ = learning_rate_init / pow(t, power_t)
72::CODE;;-'adaptive', keeps the learning rate constant to
73::CODE;;'learning_rate_init' as long as the training keeps decreasing.
74::CODE;;Each time 2 consecutive epochs fail to decrease the training loss by
75::CODE;;tol, or fail to increase validation score by tol if 'early_stopping'
76::CODE;;is on, the current learning rate is divided by 5.
77::CODE;;momentum : float, default=0.9
78::CODE;;Value of momentum used, must be larger than or equal to 0
79::CODE;;nesterov : bool, default=True
80::CODE;;Whether to use nesterov's momentum or not. Use nesterov's if True
81::CODE;;power_t : float, default=0.5
82::CODE;;Power of time step 't' in inverse scaling. See `lr_schedule` for
83::CODE;;more details.

65::CODE;;def test_adam_optimizer():
66::CODE;;params = [np.zeros(shape) for shape in shapes]
67::CODE;;lr = 0.001
68::CODE;;epsilon = 1e-8
69::CODE;;rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
70::CODE;;for beta_1 in np.arange(0.9, 1.0, 0.05):
71::CODE;;for beta_2 in np.arange(0.995, 1.0, 0.001):
72::CODE;;optimizer = AdamOptimizer(params, lr, beta_1, beta_2, epsilon)
73::CODE;;ms = [rng.random_sample(shape) for shape in shapes]
74::CODE;;vs = [rng.random_sample(shape) for shape in shapes]
75::CODE;;t = 10
76::CODE;;optimizer.ms = ms
77::CODE;;optimizer.vs = vs
78::CODE;;optimizer.t = t - 1
79::CODE;;grads = [rng.random_sample(shape) for shape in shapes]
80::CODE;;ms = [beta_1 * m + (1 - beta_1) * grad for m, grad in zip(ms, grads)]
81::CODE;;vs = [beta_2 * v + (1 - beta_2) * (grad**2) for v, grad in zip(vs, grads)]
82::CODE;;learning_rate = lr * np.sqrt(1 - beta_2**t) / (1 - beta_1**t)
83::CODE;;updates = [
84::CODE;;-learning_rate * m / (np.sqrt(v) + epsilon) for m, v in zip(ms, vs)
85::CODE;;]
86::CODE;;expected = [param + update for param, update in zip(params, updates)]
87::CODE;;optimizer.update_params(params, grads)
88::CODE;;for exp, param in zip(expected, params):
89::CODE;;assert_array_equal(exp, param)
43::CODE;;Parameters
44::CODE;;----------
45::CODE;;sub_pipeline : Pipeline
46::CODE;;The sub-pipeline to be used for transformation.
47::CODE;;cache : dict
48::CODE;;The cache dictionary to store the transformed values.
49::CODE;;param_name : str
50::CODE;;The name of the parameter to be transformed.
51::CODE;;param_value : object
52::CODE;;The value of the parameter to be transformed.
53::CODE;;transform_params : dict
54::CODE;;The metadata to be used for transformation. This passed to the
55::CODE;;`transform` method of the sub-pipeline.
56::CODE;;Returns
57::CODE;;-------
58::CODE;;transformed_value : object
59::CODE;;The transformed value of the parameter.
76::CODE;;A sequence of data transformers with an optional final predictor.
77::CODE;;`Pipeline` allows you to sequentially apply a list of transformers to
78::CODE;;preprocess the data and, if desired, conclude the sequence with a final
79::CODE;;:term:`predictor` for predictive modeling.
80::CODE;;Intermediate steps of the pipeline must be transformers, that is, they
81::CODE;;must implement `fit` and `transform` methods.
82::CODE;;The final :term:`estimator` only needs to implement `fit`.
83::CODE;;The transformers in the pipeline can be cached using ``memory`` argument.
84::CODE;;The purpose of the pipeline is to assemble several steps that can be
85::CODE;;cross-validated together while setting different parameters. For this, it
86::CODE;;enables setting parameters of the various steps using their names and the
87::CODE;;parameter name separated by a `'__'`, as in the example below. A step's
88::CODE;;estimator may be replaced entirely by setting the parameter with its name
89::CODE;;to another estimator, or a transformer removed by setting it to
90::CODE;;`'passthrough'` or `None`.
91::CODE;;For an example use case of `Pipeline` combined with
92::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV`, refer to
93::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_compose_plot_compare_reduction.py`. The
94::CODE;;example :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_compose_plot_digits_pipe.py` shows how
95::CODE;;to grid search on a pipeline using `'__'` as a separator in the parameter names.
96::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <pipeline>`.
97::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.5
98::CODE;;Parameters
99::CODE;;----------
100::CODE;;steps : list of tuples
101::CODE;;List of (name of step, estimator) tuples that are to be chained in
102::CODE;;sequential order. To be compatible with the scikit-learn API, all steps
103::CODE;;must define `fit`. All non-last steps must also define `transform`. See
104::CODE;;:ref:`Combining Estimators <combining_estimators>` for more details.
105::CODE;;transform_input : list of str, default=None
106::CODE;;The names of the :term:`metadata` parameters that should be transformed by the
107::CODE;;pipeline before passing it to the step consuming it.
108::CODE;;This enables transforming some input arguments to ``fit`` (other than ``X``)
109::CODE;;to be transformed by the steps of the pipeline up to the step which requires
110::CODE;;them. Requirement is defined via :ref:`metadata routing <metadata_routing>`.
111::CODE;;For instance, this can be used to pass a validation set through the pipeline.
112::CODE;;You can only set this if metadata routing is enabled, which you
113::CODE;;can enable using ``sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)``.
114::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
115::CODE;;memory : str or object with the joblib.Memory interface, default=None
116::CODE;;Used to cache the fitted transformers of the pipeline. The last step
117::CODE;;will never be cached, even if it is a transformer. By default, no
118::CODE;;caching is performed. If a string is given, it is the path to the
119::CODE;;caching directory. Enabling caching triggers a clone of the transformers
120::CODE;;before fitting. Therefore, the transformer instance given to the
121::CODE;;pipeline cannot be inspected directly. Use the attribute ``named_steps``
122::CODE;;or ``steps`` to inspect estimators within the pipeline. Caching the
123::CODE;;transformers is advantageous when fitting is time consuming. See
124::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neighbors_plot_caching_nearest_neighbors.py`
125::CODE;;for an example on how to enable caching.
126::CODE;;verbose : bool, default=False
127::CODE;;If True, the time elapsed while fitting each step will be printed as it
128::CODE;;is completed.
129::CODE;;Attributes
130::CODE;;----------
131::CODE;;named_steps : :class:`~sklearn.utils.Bunch`
132::CODE;;Dictionary-like object, with the following attributes.
133::CODE;;Read-only attribute to access any step parameter by user given name.
134::CODE;;Keys are step names and values are steps parameters.
135::CODE;;classes_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
136::CODE;;The classes labels. Only exist if the last step of the pipeline is a
137::CODE;;classifier.
138::CODE;;n_features_in_ : int
139::CODE;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
140::CODE;;underlying first estimator in `steps` exposes such an attribute
141::CODE;;when fit.
142::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
143::CODE;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
144::CODE;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
145::CODE;;underlying estimator exposes such an attribute when fit.
146::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
147::CODE;;See Also
148::CODE;;--------
149::CODE;;make_pipeline : Convenience function for simplified pipeline construction.
150::CODE;;Examples
151::CODE;;--------
152::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.svm import SVC
153::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
154::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
155::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
156::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
157::CODE;;>>> X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
158::CODE;;>>> X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y,
159::CODE;;... random_state=0)
160::CODE;;>>> pipe = Pipeline([('scaler', StandardScaler()), ('svc', SVC())])
163::CODE;;>>> pipe.fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_test, y_test)
164::CODE;;0.88
166::CODE;;>>> pipe.set_params(svc__C=10).fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_test, y_test)
167::CODE;;0.76
183::CODE;;Calling `set_output` will set the output of all estimators in `steps`.
184::CODE;;Parameters
185::CODE;;----------
186::CODE;;transform : {"default", "pandas", "polars"}, default=None
187::CODE;;Configure output of `transform` and `fit_transform`.
188::CODE;;- `"default"`: Default output format of a transformer
189::CODE;;- `"pandas"`: DataFrame output
190::CODE;;- `"polars"`: Polars output
191::CODE;;- `None`: Transform configuration is unchanged
192::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.4
193::CODE;;`"polars"` option was added.
194::CODE;;Returns
195::CODE;;-------
196::CODE;;self : estimator instance
197::CODE;;Estimator instance.
204::CODE;;Returns the parameters given in the constructor as well as the
205::CODE;;estimators contained within the `steps` of the `Pipeline`.
206::CODE;;Parameters
207::CODE;;----------

210::CODE;;contained subobjects that are estimators.
211::CODE;;Returns
212::CODE;;-------
213::CODE;;params : mapping of string to any
214::CODE;;Parameter names mapped to their values.
219::CODE;;Valid parameter keys can be listed with ``get_params()``. Note that
220::CODE;;you can directly set the parameters of the estimators contained in
221::CODE;;`steps`.
222::CODE;;Parameters
223::CODE;;----------
224::CODE;;**kwargs : dict
225::CODE;;Parameters of this estimator or parameters of estimators contained
226::CODE;;in `steps`. Parameters of the steps may be set using its name and
227::CODE;;the parameter name separated by a '__'.
228::CODE;;Returns
229::CODE;;-------
230::CODE;;self : object
231::CODE;;Pipeline class instance.
269::CODE;;Generate (idx, (name, trans)) tuples from self.steps
270::CODE;;When filter_passthrough is True, 'passthrough' and None transformers
271::CODE;;are filtered out.
283::CODE;;Returns the length of the Pipeline
288::CODE;;Indexing with an integer will return an estimator; using a slice
289::CODE;;returns another Pipeline instance which copies a slice of this
290::CODE;;Pipeline. This copy is shallow: modifying (or fitting) estimators in
291::CODE;;the sub-pipeline will affect the larger pipeline and vice-versa.
292::CODE;;However, replacing a value in `step` will not affect a copy.
293::CODE;;See
294::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_feature_selection_plot_feature_selection_pipeline.py`
295::CODE;;for an example of how to use slicing to inspect part of a pipeline.
312::CODE;;Read-only attribute to access any step by given name.
362::CODE;;This transforms the metadata up to this step if required, which is
363::CODE;;indicated by the `transform_input` parameter.
364::CODE;;If a param in `step_params` is included in the `transform_input` list,
365::CODE;;it will be transformed.
366::CODE;;Parameters
367::CODE;;----------
368::CODE;;step_idx : int
369::CODE;;Index of the step in the pipeline.
370::CODE;;step_params : dict
371::CODE;;Parameters specific to the step. These are routed parameters, e.g.
372::CODE;;`routed_params[name]`. If a parameter name here is included in the
373::CODE;;`pipeline.transform_input`, then it will be transformed. Note that
374::CODE;;these parameters are *after* routing, so the aliases are already
375::CODE;;resolved.
376::CODE;;all_params : dict
377::CODE;;All parameters passed by the user. Here this is used to call
378::CODE;;`transform` on the slice of the pipeline itself.
379::CODE;;Returns
380::CODE;;-------
381::CODE;;dict
382::CODE;;Parameters to be passed to the step. The ones which should be
383::CODE;;transformed are transformed.
432::CODE;;routed_params is the output of `process_routing`
433::CODE;;raw_params is the parameters passed by the user, used when `transform_input`

1130::CODE;;def _name_estimators(estimators):
1150::CODE;;This is a shorthand for the :class:`Pipeline` constructor; it does not
1151::CODE;;require, and does not permit, naming the estimators. Instead, their names
1152::CODE;;will be set to the lowercase of their types automatically.
1153::CODE;;Parameters
1154::CODE;;----------
1155::CODE;;*steps : list of Estimator objects
1156::CODE;;List of the scikit-learn estimators that are chained together.
1157::CODE;;memory : str or object with the joblib.Memory interface, default=None
1158::CODE;;Used to cache the fitted transformers of the pipeline. The last step
1159::CODE;;will never be cached, even if it is a transformer. By default, no
1160::CODE;;caching is performed. If a string is given, it is the path to the
1161::CODE;;caching directory. Enabling caching triggers a clone of the transformers
1162::CODE;;before fitting. Therefore, the transformer instance given to the
1163::CODE;;pipeline cannot be inspected directly. Use the attribute ``named_steps``
1164::CODE;;or ``steps`` to inspect estimators within the pipeline. Caching the
1165::CODE;;transformers is advantageous when fitting is time consuming.
1166::CODE;;transform_input : list of str, default=None
1167::CODE;;This enables transforming some input arguments to ``fit`` (other than ``X``)
1168::CODE;;to be transformed by the steps of the pipeline up to the step which requires
1169::CODE;;them. Requirement is defined via :ref:`metadata routing <metadata_routing>`.
1170::CODE;;This can be used to pass a validation set through the pipeline for instance.
1171::CODE;;You can only set this if metadata routing is enabled, which you
1172::CODE;;can enable using ``sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)``.
1173::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
1174::CODE;;verbose : bool, default=False
1175::CODE;;If True, the time elapsed while fitting each step will be printed as it
1176::CODE;;is completed.
1177::CODE;;Returns
1178::CODE;;-------
1179::CODE;;p : Pipeline
1180::CODE;;Returns a scikit-learn :class:`Pipeline` object.
1181::CODE;;See Also
1182::CODE;;--------
1183::CODE;;Pipeline : Class for creating a pipeline of transforms with a final
1184::CODE;;estimator.
1185::CODE;;Examples
1186::CODE;;--------
1187::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
1188::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
1189::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
1190::CODE;;>>> make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), GaussianNB(priors=None))
1191::CODE;;Pipeline(steps=[('standardscaler', StandardScaler()),
1192::CODE;;('gaussiannb', GaussianNB())])
1202::CODE;;Parameters
1203::CODE;;----------
1204::CODE;;transformer : estimator
1205::CODE;;Estimator to be used for transformation.
1206::CODE;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
1207::CODE;;Input data to be transformed.
1208::CODE;;y : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
1209::CODE;;Ignored.
1210::CODE;;weight : float
1211::CODE;;Weight to be applied to the output of the transformation.
1212::CODE;;params : dict
1213::CODE;;Parameters to be passed to the transformer's ``transform`` method.
1214::CODE;;This should be of the form ``process_routing()["step_name"]``.
1225::CODE;;Fits ``transformer`` to ``X`` and ``y``. The transformed result is returned
1226::CODE;;with the fitted transformer. If ``weight`` is not ``None``, the result will
1227::CODE;;be multiplied by ``weight``.
1228::CODE;;``params`` needs to be of the form ``process_routing()["step_name"]``.
1243::CODE;;Fits ``transformer`` to ``X`` and ``y``.
1249::CODE;;This estimator applies a list of transformer objects in parallel to the
1250::CODE;;input data, then concatenates the results. This is useful to combine
1251::CODE;;several feature extraction mechanisms into a single transformer.
1252::CODE;;Parameters of the transformers may be set using its name and the parameter
1253::CODE;;name separated by a '__'. A transformer may be replaced entirely by
1254::CODE;;setting the parameter with its name to another transformer, removed by
1255::CODE;;setting to 'drop' or disabled by setting to 'passthrough' (features are
1256::CODE;;passed without transformation).
1257::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <feature_union>`.
1258::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.13
1259::CODE;;Parameters
1260::CODE;;----------
1261::CODE;;transformer_list : list of (str, transformer) tuples
1262::CODE;;List of transformer objects to be applied to the data. The first
1263::CODE;;half of each tuple is the name of the transformer. The transformer can
1264::CODE;;be 'drop' for it to be ignored or can be 'passthrough' for features to
1265::CODE;;be passed unchanged.
1266::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
1267::CODE;;Added the option `"passthrough"`.
1268::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.22
1269::CODE;;Deprecated `None` as a transformer in favor of 'drop'.
1270::CODE;;n_jobs : int, default=None
1271::CODE;;Number of jobs to run in parallel.
1272::CODE;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
1273::CODE;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
1274::CODE;;for more details.
1275::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: v0.20
1276::CODE;;`n_jobs` default changed from 1 to None
1277::CODE;;transformer_weights : dict, default=None
1278::CODE;;Multiplicative weights for features per transformer.
1279::CODE;;Keys are transformer names, values the weights.
1280::CODE;;Raises ValueError if key not present in ``transformer_list``.
1281::CODE;;verbose : bool, default=False
1282::CODE;;If True, the time elapsed while fitting each transformer will be
1283::CODE;;printed as it is completed.
1284::CODE;;verbose_feature_names_out : bool, default=True
1285::CODE;;If True, :meth:`get_feature_names_out` will prefix all feature names
1286::CODE;;with the name of the transformer that generated that feature.
1287::CODE;;If False, :meth:`get_feature_names_out` will not prefix any feature
1288::CODE;;names and will error if feature names are not unique.
1289::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 1.5
1290::CODE;;Attributes
1291::CODE;;----------

2185::CODE;;This method transforms the features to follow a uniform or a normal
2186::CODE;;distribution. Therefore, for a given feature, this transformation tends
2187::CODE;;to spread out the most frequent values. It also reduces the impact of
2188::CODE;;(marginal) outliers: this is therefore a robust preprocessing scheme.
2189::CODE;;The transformation is applied on each feature independently. First an
2190::CODE;;estimate of the cumulative distribution function of a feature is
2191::CODE;;used to map the original values to a uniform distribution. The obtained
2192::CODE;;values are then mapped to the desired output distribution using the
2193::CODE;;associated quantile function. Features values of new/unseen data that fall
2194::CODE;;below or above the fitted range will be mapped to the bounds of the output
2195::CODE;;distribution. Note that this transform is non-linear. It may distort linear
2196::CODE;;correlations between variables measured at the same scale but renders
2197::CODE;;variables measured at different scales more directly comparable.

2655::CODE;;array([...])
2672::CODE;;Power transforms are a family of parametric, monotonic transformations
2673::CODE;;that are applied to make data more Gaussian-like. This is useful for
2674::CODE;;modeling issues related to heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance),
2675::CODE;;or other situations where normality is desired.
2676::CODE;;Currently, PowerTransformer supports the Box-Cox transform and the
2677::CODE;;Yeo-Johnson transform. The optimal parameter for stabilizing variance and
2678::CODE;;minimizing skewness is estimated through maximum likelihood.
2679::CODE;;Box-Cox requires input data to be strictly positive, while Yeo-Johnson
2680::CODE;;supports both positive or negative data.
2681::CODE;;By default, zero-mean, unit-variance normalization is applied to the
2682::CODE;;transformed data.
2683::CODE;;For an example visualization, refer to :ref:`Compare PowerTransformer with
2684::CODE;;other scalers <plot_all_scaling_power_transformer_section>`. To see the
2685::CODE;;effect of Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson transformations on different
2686::CODE;;distributions, see:
2687::CODE;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_preprocessing_plot_map_data_to_normal.py`.
2688::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <preprocessing_transformer>`.
2689::CODE;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
2690::CODE;;Parameters
2691::CODE;;----------

2693::CODE;;The power transform method. Available methods are:
2694::CODE;;- 'yeo-johnson' [1]_, works with positive and negative values
2695::CODE;;- 'box-cox' [2]_, only works with strictly positive values

2851::CODE;;The inverse of the Yeo-Johnson transformation is given by::
2852::CODE;;if X >= 0 and lambda_ == 0:
2853::CODE;;X_original = exp(X) - 1
2854::CODE;;elif X >= 0 and lambda_ != 0:
2855::CODE;;X_original = (X * lambda_ + 1) ** (1 / lambda_) - 1
2856::CODE;;elif X < 0 and lambda_ != 2:
2857::CODE;;X_original = 1 - (-(2 - lambda_) * X + 1) ** (1 / (2 - lambda_))
2858::CODE;;elif X < 0 and lambda_ == 2:
2859::CODE;;X_original = 1 - exp(-X)
2860::CODE;;Parameters
2861::CODE;;----------
2862::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
2863::CODE;;The transformed data.
2864::CODE;;Returns
2865::CODE;;-------
2866::CODE;;X_original : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features)
2867::CODE;;The original data.
2896::CODE;;transform with parameter lambda.
2913::CODE;;parameter lambda.
2930::CODE;;MLE, for observed data x.
2931::CODE;;We here use scipy builtins which uses the brent optimizer.
2942::CODE;;transform by MLE, for observed data x.
2943::CODE;;Like for Box-Cox, MLE is done via the brent optimizer.
2966::CODE;;Parameters
2967::CODE;;----------
2968::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
2969::CODE;;in_fit : bool
2970::CODE;;Whether or not `_check_input` is called from `fit` or other
2971::CODE;;methods, e.g. `predict`, `transform`, etc.
2972::CODE;;check_positive : bool, default=False
2973::CODE;;If True, check that all data is positive and non-zero (only if
2974::CODE;;``self.method=='box-cox'``).
2975::CODE;;check_shape : bool, default=False
2976::CODE;;If True, check that n_features matches the length of self.lambdas_
3013::CODE;;Power transforms are a family of parametric, monotonic transformations
3014::CODE;;that are applied to make data more Gaussian-like. This is useful for
3015::CODE;;modeling issues related to heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance),
3016::CODE;;or other situations where normality is desired.
3017::CODE;;Currently, power_transform supports the Box-Cox transform and the
3018::CODE;;Yeo-Johnson transform. The optimal parameter for stabilizing variance and
3019::CODE;;minimizing skewness is estimated through maximum likelihood.
3020::CODE;;Box-Cox requires input data to be strictly positive, while Yeo-Johnson
3021::CODE;;supports both positive or negative data.
3022::CODE;;By default, zero-mean, unit-variance normalization is applied to the
3023::CODE;;transformed data.
3024::CODE;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <preprocessing_transformer>`.
3025::CODE;;Parameters
3026::CODE;;----------
3027::CODE;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
3028::CODE;;The data to be transformed using a power transformation.
3029::CODE;;method : {'yeo-johnson', 'box-cox'}, default='yeo-johnson'
3030::CODE;;The power transform method. Available methods are:
3031::CODE;;- 'yeo-johnson' [1]_, works with positive and negative values
3032::CODE;;- 'box-cox' [2]_, only works with strictly positive values
3033::CODE;;.. versionchanged:: 0.23
3034::CODE;;The default value of the `method` parameter changed from
3035::CODE;;'box-cox' to 'yeo-johnson' in 0.23.
3036::CODE;;standardize : bool, default=True
3037::CODE;;Set to True to apply zero-mean, unit-variance normalization to the
3038::CODE;;transformed output.
3039::CODE;;copy : bool, default=True
3040::CODE;;If False, try to avoid a copy and transform in place.
3041::CODE;;This is not guaranteed to always work in place; e.g. if the data is
3042::CODE;;a numpy array with an int dtype, a copy will be returned even with
3043::CODE;;copy=False.
3044::CODE;;Returns
3045::CODE;;-------
3046::CODE;;X_trans : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features)
3047::CODE;;The transformed data.
3048::CODE;;See Also
3049::CODE;;--------
3050::CODE;;PowerTransformer : Equivalent transformation with the
3051::CODE;;Transformer API (e.g. as part of a preprocessing
3052::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline`).
3053::CODE;;quantile_transform : Maps data to a standard normal distribution with
3054::CODE;;the parameter `output_distribution='normal'`.
3055::CODE;;Notes
3056::CODE;;-----
3057::CODE;;NaNs are treated as missing values: disregarded in ``fit``, and maintained
3058::CODE;;in ``transform``.
3059::CODE;;For a comparison of the different scalers, transformers, and normalizers,
3060::CODE;;see: :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_preprocessing_plot_all_scaling.py`.
3061::CODE;;References
3062::CODE;;----------
3063::CODE;;.. [1] I.K. Yeo and R.A. Johnson, "A new family of power transformations to
3064::CODE;;improve normality or symmetry." Biometrika, 87(4), pp.954-959,
3065::CODE;;(2000).
3066::CODE;;.. [2] G.E.P. Box and D.R. Cox, "An Analysis of Transformations", Journal
3067::CODE;;of the Royal Statistical Society B, 26, 211-252 (1964).
3068::CODE;;Examples
3069::CODE;;--------
3070::CODE;;>>> import numpy as np
3071::CODE;;>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import power_transform
3072::CODE;;>>> data = [[1, 2], [3, 2], [4, 5]]
3073::CODE;;>>> print(power_transform(data, method='box-cox'))
3074::CODE;;[[-1.332 -0.707]
3075::CODE;;[ 0.256 -0.707]
3076::CODE;;[ 1.076 1.414]]
3077::CODE;;.. warning:: Risk of data leak.
3078::CODE;;Do not use :func:`~sklearn.preprocessing.power_transform` unless you
3079::CODE;;know what you are doing. A common mistake is to apply it to the entire
3080::CODE;;data *before* splitting into training and test sets. This will bias the
3081::CODE;;model evaluation because information would have leaked from the test
3082::CODE;;set to the training set.
3083::CODE;;In general, we recommend using
3084::CODE;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PowerTransformer` within a
3085::CODE;;:ref:`Pipeline <pipeline>` in order to prevent most risks of data
3086::CODE;;leaking, e.g.: `pipe = make_pipeline(PowerTransformer(),
3087::CODE;;LogisticRegression())`.
